Between 2004 and 2013, the Pierre Auger Observatory detected 29 unusually large cosmic-ray events with energies exceeding 4 EeV, where the standard deviation of flux fluctuations falls within the 8.7% mark for homogeneously distributed events of this size. These rare, large-scale cosmic-ray patterns spanning roughly 2 billion light years, exceed the predicted density based on fractal principles and are more frequent than expected at 8.7% per decade for areas of this scale, suggesting a cosmological origin and possibly linking to sources of quasars that illuminate the early universe. A thorough study of cosmic-ray arrival directions showed no significant patterns, nor any correlation with nearby extragalactic objects, and since the fluctuations are on a cosmic scale, the term "ultra-clustering" is used to describe them. A theoretical framework based on flux fluctuations and identified features in cosmic-ray spectra, suggests that more of these events will be detected with the expansion of cosmic-ray observatories, and that their study will provide a new and powerful tool for exploring the early universe. A supplement to this paper includes an update of the fluctuation analysis with the expanded and complete dataset from the Pierre Auger Observatory. Quantum mechanics can be reimagined using a noncommutative coordinate system, characterized by the commutator of two coordinate operators representing a fundamental length in proportion to the Planck length. This fundamental aspect maintains the consistency of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, even in a noncommutative setting. When based on Lie algebras such as $su(2)$ or $u(2)$, the relationship between the noncommutative coordinates simplifies to a commutative algebra under a specific rescaling. The latter property enables an equivalent representation of the algebra in relation to classical Lie groups like $SU(2)$ or $U(2)$. The article explores the distinction between commutative and noncommutative descriptions, examining whether the latter can contribute to an explanation of dark matter, an issue that persists in standard quantum mechanics. The article also examines various approaches to noncommutative geometry, before settling on a specific $SU(2)$-based framework with unique properties, including an explanation for the formation of molecules and the universality of the Planck constant, leaving little scope for the influence of dark matter in atomic and molecular physics. The article also delves into the unique characteristics of this particular noncommutative setting, including an interpretation of the Gravitational Force, an examination of dark energy, and a discussion on the implications for quantum gravity. The article also discusses various experimental tests that can validate or refute its hypotheses. The article is a continuation of the author's earlier work, 'Noncommutative Quantum Mechanics Linking Lie Algebras and Classical Lie Groups', arXiv:2012.04010, 'The article arXiv:2012.04010 in Review', arXiv:2109.14303 and 'The Article in JHEP - 20 (2021): 082', arXiv:2012.04011, with the exception of the discussion on monopoles, and introduces a new hypothesis on the noncommutative origin of quark masses and the recent discovery of sterile neutrinos by the KATRIN group, and presents a new theoretical prediction for the value of the fine structure constant. The article also concludes with an outline of a new experimental project that could provide further evidence for this theory. The article is also accompanied by an appendix that outlines the derivation of the monopole operator, the discussion on magnetic charge, magnetic field strength, instantons, soliton, and anyon, and the presentation of additional experimental data

In evaluating the potential of a cancer treatment, Tumor Infiltrating Lymphocytes are a crucial factor and their impact is typically categorized into three levels: favorable, uncertain, or unfavorable. To automate this categorization process, researchers have explored deep learning-based approaches in image analysis. However, these models require extensive, high-quality training datasets that are difficult to obtain due to the time-consuming and costly process of annotating lymphocytes in medical images. This challenge prompted us to explore a novel approach, where only coarse annotations are used to train a lymphocyte detection model and subsequently a classification network is trained to predict IHC scores from the extracted regions of interest, rather than relying on explicit lymphocyte segmentation in histopathological images. This method was applied in a study involving 1,500 images from four sites, with three categories of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and achieved notable accuracy of 73.7%, 74.2%, and 74.5% in three-fold validations, respectively. Notably, our approach achieved comparable or better classification performance in comparison to traditional annotation methods while significantly reducing annotation requirements. This method was further tested in a federated learning framework, involving five sites with diverse datasets and achieved comparable or better performance in every federation trial, with a mean accuracy of 74.3%. This research offers a groundbreaking solution to the long-standing challenge of medical image annotation, demonstrating the feasibility of a more flexible and less expensive annotation method that reduces the burden of medical image annotation. This approach has far-reaching implications, potentially making it more feasible to develop robust and generalizable models in medical imaging with annotation costs scaled linearly. Deep learning-based models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) have gained popularity in anomaly detection with varying data sizes and cadences. To deliver TCN's high accuracy, a significant amount of computational power and memory is required, mainly due to the model's extensive parameter count and linear attention mechanism. In real-world applications, improving latency and efficiency is crucial, as models may be deployed on devices with limited resources and with streaming data input. This paper introduces a new optimization technique called Trimming In Time (PIT), a network trimming method that reduces the parameter count by eliminating unnecessary filter weights before training. We also present a method to trim self-attention mechanisms by decreasing the number of key and value vectors used. Following evaluation on six public datasets for various anomaly detection scenarios, PIT has shown significant improvements in reducing parameter count, requiring no additional training or hyperparameter tuning. The optimized PIT models have achieved comparable or better performance compared to the original models, with an average 62% decrease in parameter count. For linear TCNs, we introduced a new method to trim TCN filters and combined it with a simplified attention trimming technique, resulting in significant reductions in both memory and latency requirements. The optimized PIT models have shown a 62% decrease in parameter count, 2.5x decrease in memory usage, and 3.5x decrease in latency compared to the original models, making them more suitable for deployment on devices with limited resources. The code for the proposed algorithm has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/IBM/trimming-in-time. The evaluation results for both non-causal and causal TCNs can be found in the accompanying presentation and the detailed evaluation results in the appendix. The findings indicate that trriming the parameter count of linear TCNs leads to substantial latency, memory, and parameter reduction while maintaining detection performance, and the technique may be applied to other streaming models with attention mechanisms and variable input cadences. The research also sheds light on the fact that the attention mechanism's latency requirement is proportional to the input sequence length and the number of attention heads used, and there is a significant reduction in latency and memory usage achievable by reducing the number of self-attention heads and key and value vectors in linear TCNs. The evaluation of the proposed algorithm has shown a 62% decrease in parameter count, 2.5x decrease in memory usage, and 3.5x decrease in latency compared to the original models, making them more suitable for deployment on devices with limited resources. Furthermore, the intensity of elliptical flow is influenced by initial conditions, resulting in significant azimuthal fluctuations. This study in the LHC at a 5.02 TeV collision energy with the CMS detector reveals significant fluctuations in stream angle and flow intensity in lead-lead collisions, providing valuable insights into the complex interplay of final-state interactions and initial condition properties. These fluctuations are found to be substantial, accounting for more than half of total elliptical flow volatility, and are in line with theoretical models predicting similar volatility in flow intensity and angle. The data analysis is performed using a four-dimensional $v_2$ fluctuation parameter and a corresponding volatility parameter, and the results are in line with those obtained in smaller colliding systems with lower energies. However, the present findings offer more precise constraints on flow model parameters due to more detailed information at higher LHC energies. The SiD detector concept for the ILC has remained largely unchanged since the 2007 Higgs working group report. Given the significant progress made in detector R&D since that time, it is essential to re-evaluate and potentially revise the SiD design in light of new discovery tools and background reduction techniques that have become available. This proceeding provides an overview of the considered revisions to the SiD silicon vertex tracker and central magnetic calorimeter, explaining in detail the underlying motivations and reasons for the proposed changes.

For the SVT, we examined two main alternatives to the existing disk design with potential issues. The first is a radial silicon vertex tracker that extends the interaction point access and reduces the overall material, while the second is a barrel-forward design featuring separate components to address potential cooling challenges and reduce costs. Both of these options maintain the minimum hit requirements specified in the design report.

The central calorimeter design has been the subject of two main revisions since the last report. Initially, there were considerations for the SiD detector's hadronic performance, which led to expanding the central section and increasing the overall energy threshold. However, this resulted in increased material and limitations on the vertex resolution due to the increased radiation length from the additional steel. As an alternative, we evaluated a design with a smaller central angle and reduced material, which presents a trade-off between hadronic energy measurement and vertex reconstruction performance. Despite these changes, the calorimeter's overall characteristics still exceed the minimum requirements outlined in the design report. Furthermore, simulations indicate that both revised central calorimeter designs can achieve the desired discovery potential for the ILC. Lastly, we examined the overall detector performance and found that both revised concepts meet the design report's overall specifications and requirements, which include a 5 sigma discovery of a 250 GeV Higgs boson in 1 year of operation at 250 GeV, and a 1 in 10^6 sensitivity for missing energy events. Additionally, both revised detectors demonstrate compatibility with the SiD forward pixel detector for JLC and CLIC, highlighting their versatility and adaptability. Ultimately, this proceeding presents the case for retaining the SiD detector concept's original design while incorporating the latest advancements and technological breakthroughs in detector development. As such, it remains an attractive option for the ILC, capable of delivering both precise calorimeter and vertexing measurements, along with a unique missing energy detection system. Therefore, further R&D and testing of the SiD detector design are both warranted and recommended. System combinations such as the one presented here will continue to serve

We employed the APOGEE-2 spectroscopic survey to investigate the multiple-line-of-sight blending in the bright elliptical galaxy Tonantzintla 2, which hosts an intrinsically important field of foreground turnoff stars, globular clusters, and several background asymptotic giant branch stars. Using a novel approach to data analysis known as spectroscopic tomography, we resolved the superposition of Tonantzintla 2's various components by deconvolving the observed APOGEE-2 spectra. Our research revealed detailed 1-dimensional radiative transfer models for each major component, including a foreground field of 1-dimensional turnoff stars and white dwarfs, two distinct globular clusters with low-metallicities, and three asymptotic giant branch stars with varying chemical compositions. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs, a comprehensive collection of research proofs developed with Isabelle, has grown substantially since its creation in 2007. To facilitate further development and refinement of this archive in line with modern proof-assisting tools, we conducted a thorough examination of 50 selected theories with the Isabelle Framework. Our evaluation focused on several aspects, including theory structure, proof methodology, and documentation. We observed both positive trends and areas for improvement. Within the archive, we found an average of 210 individual files per theory, often resulting in diffused proof assets, in contrast to the Isabelle Framework's recommended component-based approach. Additionally, our analysis revealed instances of unnecessarily complex proofs, along with opportunities for optimizing proof performance and enhancing readability. Furthermore, some theories lacked essential metadata, failed to employ the Isabelle Framework's recommended naming conventions, and did not leverage its features such as session structure and interconnectivity. We outline strategies for improving the archive's theories by refining proofs, reorganizing proof assets, and enhancing metadata, along with suggestions for future development with the Isabelle Framework. Our examination and the resulting improvements can serve as a starting point for further enhancements to the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs in relation to the Isabelle Framework. We study Yang-Lee edges in massive $O(N)$ models, varying $N$ from 1 to infinity. For $N$ equal to 1, 2, and infinity, we calculate the positions of Yang-Lee edges directly. For $N$ values between 1 and 2, and 2 and infinity, we use a scaling and renormalization group method to make approximate calculations. With this information, we create a universal equation that makes predictions about Yang-Lee edge positions for all $N$ values. Our theoretical predictions match experimental findings in Ising and Fermi liquids in (3+1)D space-time. Our research provides a foundation for similar investigations in classical and quantum universality classes in other settings. In classical settings, we explore the specific situations of ferromagnetic and binary Lozenge tiling, both resulting in identical edge positions that align with our universal equation. Similarly, in quantum settings, we examine the situations of spinor Bose-Einstein condensate and monodromy Ising models, again finding their edge positions match our predictions. Our research suggests that the positions of Yang-Lee edges are inherently universal, defined by the characteristics of a given universality class rather than the specifics of a particular model. Our proposed universal equation provides a clear and concise definition of these positions. It is crucial to note that this universal edge position definition relies on an alternative criticality where the Zeeman field is set to zero, as required for our experimental methods that rely on tunable, synthetic magnetic fields. In this context, our research offers a groundbreaking contribution towards a better comprehension of critical behavior in non-uniform settings, where traditional uniform approaches are ineffectual. It is worth noting that our experimental techniques not only allow for edge position calculations but also provide access to other critical properties that may vary depending on the specific model and universality class. It is also interesting to note that some of our experimental models feature interacting particles with multiple universal regimes corresponding to both classical and quantum settings, as evidenced by the results presented in this study. Furthermore, our research raises fundamental questions regarding the positions of Yang-Lee edges in other universality classes and models that are yet to be explored and our proposed universal equation serves as a guiding framework for this research. In statistics and machine learning, the Bethe Hessian and its second mate, the generalized Hessian, play significant roles in optimizing parameters for various graphical models. By examining the properties of these matrices, we demonstrate the concavity of a specific objective function, extending the methods of Bethe Hessian optimization and its variants, such as the generalized Hessian and successive convex approximation methods, including Sudakov-Fernique's recent work, by providing a more general framework for these methods, ultimately showing the validity of their results. Our findings are independent of specific functions and applications, making the paper a general theoretical contribution. Building upon this foundation, we derive a more localized consequence, establishing the local concavity of a particular function and its corresponding Hessian, despite its non-contractible domain. This achievement is notable because it is challenging to verify the Hessian's positive definiteness at an approximate fixed point, especially in cases where the Hessian and its Hessian do not share similar eigenvalue distributions. Our solution involves demonstrating the generalized Hessian's positive definiteness within a limited area and using this result to show the existence of a convex approximation for a specific function in a limited area, even when the Hessian's eigenvalues follow a power-law distribution. Our work is a combination of the contributions of Benigni, Cooper, Gammerman, Gómez-Vacas, Rudi, Sleder, Szabó, Vanervald, and Vigoda.

This study introduces a deep learning approach known as the Electron Configuration
Potential Network, which achieves remarkable accuracy in predicting potential energies
for complex electron interactions from scratch, without relying on potential energy
annihilation or up/down spin separation. We demonstrated this capability using a simple
electron-coupled potential network that effectively models the interactions of up to 10
electrons in simple orbits by learning a vast number of precomputed CI coefficients.
Interestingly, we found that fine-tuning the pretrained model on a relatively small set
of contracted configuration data leads to a general understanding of the electron
interaction potential energy, surpassing the accuracy of its original performance.
Interestingly, when applied to a scenario involving an external potential, the learned
electron potential energy model exhibits an interesting duality, where the learned model
for the interacting electrons is equivalent to a model of the interacting potential, as
validated through the application of an operator that distinguishes the two. We also
examined the feasibility of extending this approach to more complex situations using a
higher-dimensional electron configuration potential network, as an initial exploration.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using only one object image has gained significant attention. By leveraging deep learning techniques, this task has become more manageable, especially when using real-world datasets. Nonetheless, existing methods primarily focus on easily identifiable objects with straightforward backgrounds, leaving a broader range of scenarios, such as those with overlapping or similarly colored objects and complex backgrounds, unresolved. To address this, we propose a groundbreaking approach called DeepHMap++, which tackles two major challenges in this area: (1) determining a suitable projection, and (2) learning object correspondences, in a single step, using a unified network called Unified-2SNet. By integrating projection grouping, corresponding learning, and maximum likelihood estimation, we have achieved notable improvements over baseline models, including a proposed method that learns correspondences through a weakly supervised approach called Correspondence-2SNet, resulting in pose estimation results that outperform current state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. Experimental evaluations using real-world datasets, such as LINEMOD, MODAL, and IUPR-BOP, have shown that our proposed method has the ability to accurately estimate the poses of difficult objects with complex backgrounds, and has achieved industry-leading average precision (AP) scores of 43.1%, 45.5%, and 35.5% on the LINEMOD, MODAL, and IUPR-BOP benchmarks, respectively. Furthermore, we have observed that our approach not only excels in estimating the poses of easily identifiable objects but also has a robust performance in challenging scenarios, especially those with overlapping or similarly colored objects and complex backgrounds. Peridynamic theories have experienced significant growth over the past decade, becoming a widely accepted approach in modeling complex mechanical issues. This review focuses on bond-based peridynamics, an intuitive and accessible nonlocal framework. We have made substantial contributions to developing PD equations, establishing their equivalence to standard partial differential equations like Navier-Stolz and Reynolds equations through various simplifying assumptions. We have also explored PD modeling of fluid mechanics by applying PD operators to Riemann surfaces and leveraging the introduction of PD strain tensors. Notably, our research demonstrated the PD equivalent of the transport equation and revealed how PD can capture fluid-mechanics phenomena such as shock waves and contact discontinuities. We have methodically assessed the choice of PD bond-length parameter and investigated how it influences solution accuracy. We have introduced implicit algorithms for solving PD equations and demonstrated their efficiency in resolving time-dependent fluid-mechanics problems. Finally, we have discussed potential areas for further exploration within the field of peridynamic fluid mechanics. Through this review, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of the subject matter for which there is currently no centralized resource. Additionally, we have made our code freely available to the community for further development and to facilitate collaboration. Collective knowledge presented in this review will serve as a foundation for future research in the field of peridynamic fluid mechanics. These areas offer significant opportunities for advancing our understanding of complex phenomena and for addressing the challenges facing us in the present day. We present GGLasso, a Python-based library that offers an accessible framework for solving a wide range of matrix factorization problems rooted in Graphical Lasso variants. This framework is particularly useful for tackling various structured high-dimensional estimation challenges, including those with Lasso, group Lasso, weighted Lasso, and sparse principal component analysis structures. By providing a unified interface and a flexible framework for user-defined penalties, GGLasso enables users to easily compute a broad spectrum of generalized Lasso formulations. Additionally, it includes an automatic tool for measuring the R-LOD (relative least squares error) metric, which is a representative of a class of regression metrics that have an L1 penalty, and this metric is a critical performance indicator in many of its applications. The development of GGLasso is centered on a mixture of methodological research and computational experimentation, and the library is designed to be an open platform for collaborative research and development. It is available under the permissive MIT License and can be accessed through GitHub at https://github.com/TSaran/GGLasso. Furthermore, the corresponding RUMINA project, focused on user interface development, is available at https://github.com/TSaran/RUMINA. By offering an intuitive and customizable graphical user interface (GUI) through RUMINA, users can interactively explore and manipulate the factorization output from GGLasso. Together, GGLasso and RUMINA provide an effective and engaging framework for collaborative methodological research and development in statistics. Numerous configurational molecular models have been utilized in computational social science to analyze the spread of information, influence, and behavior, but existing methods for sampling configurations often have limitations, especially with high connectivity and variable time steps. To address this challenge, we propose a method for robust configurational sampling based on Langevin dynamics, which leverages the fundamental properties of the system to determine an optimal time step. Our approach is "time-step free" and independent of system connectivity, allowing it to efficiently produce high-quality configurations in a short time. We evaluated our method in a variety of scenarios, including Watts-Strogatz, Barabasi-Albert, and Erdos-Renyi networks, and compared it to alternative methods for configurational sampling, which involved utilizing proposals based on local mean squared displacements. Our results demonstrate that our method boasts increased efficiency, particularly in systems with high connectivity and variable time steps, and we found no differences in the metrics analyzed from configurations produced by our method and those given. Consequently, our study offers our proposed algorithm as an effective and dependable solution for the configurational sampling of dynamic stochastic networks. Additionally, we explored the application of our proposed algorithm to evaluate system-level properties by estimating averages through the use of multiple independent configurational sampling replicas, which showed excellent agreement with estimates derived from trajectories generated by Langevin dynamics and demonstrated our proposed algorithm's potential for handling complex systems with large numbers of agents. We made available our code in an user-friendly package for configurational sampling known as ConfigLangevin, which can be accessed through GitHub at https://github.com/alejandrojimenezg/ConfigLangevin, under the terms of the MIT License. Our study provides a thorough examination of our proposed algorithm and an exhaustive examination of configurational dynamics' underlying principles in the context of social science through an in-depth examination of existing research on various network types. Researchers utilized the black hole collision event GW150914 as a basis to test a new computational model for gravitational waves. This model incorporates the effects of matter and dark energy on the cosmos, specifically dark energy's influence on large scales. As a contrast, the current standard model of cosmology, known as LCDM, features distinct components for dark matter and dark energy with separate scales of interaction. To make predictions about the gravitational wave signal from black hole collisions under various dark energy cosmologies, researchers developed a multi-scale approach that bridges the gap between computational simulations and theoretical models of dark energy. This new method involves three components: a mesoscale numerical simulation of black hole mergers influenced by gravitational forces from surrounding matter; a higresolution numerical simulation of merging black holes with controlled initial conditions; and a macroscopic lattice simulation representing the structure of matter at a cosmological scale. Based on GW150914, this model was utilized to compare its predictions with actual data, and a similar approach was applied to simulated gravitational wave signals from black hole collisions under LCDM and dark energy wave cosmologies. As a result, this model demonstrated its capability to replicate actual gravitational wave data from black hole collisions and demonstrated a notable feature: wave dark energy cosmologies generate distinctive patterns in gravitational wave signals that are distinguishable from LCDM, specifically in the amplitude versus frequency correlation. Furthermore, this model discovered that wave dark energy cosmologies have a more pronounced effect on low-frequency gravitational wave signals, and it identified two distinct patterns in such signals: a standard LCDM pattern and an alternative one, which is unique to dark energy wave cosmologies and characterized by a different ratio of signal components. This model's findings are relevant to ongoing and future gravitational wave observatories that will provide more precise data and allow for the distinction between different dark energy cosmologies through gravitational wave signals from black hole collisions. Additionally, this model offers a framework for investigating the dark energy cosmos through gravitational wave signals from black hole collisions and other phenomena such as neutron star mergers and primordial black hole collisions. This model's computational tool, known as the computational fluid dynamics (CFD) framework, is highly versatile and can be applied to a wide range of gravitational wave sources and their corresponding signals in the frequency range of 1-10 Hz. This model's predictions and conclusions are based on simulations and data from the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) during its second observing run from design sensitivity to the actual data, and it provides new insights and a new perspective on dark energy

We have designed a novel acoustic lens material called HCT-1, which significantly enhances the effectiveness of wide-area detectors in photoacoustic breast tomography. Our research indicates that HCT-1 possesses exceptional total internal reflection properties, resulting in approximately 99.98% of incident photons being reflected back into the desired imaging area. In comparison to standard photoacoustic lenses, HCT-1 yields a remarkable enhancement of up to 15 times in photon recollection, collectively demonstrating its potential to greatly enhance low-light intensity imaging and reduce photoacoustic noise through improved light containment and redirection. Notably, this material exhibits unusually high conductivity when it contains defects in its triangular layers,

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, used by nearly everyone, and interactive systems like these are now an integral part of every operating system. Despite their widespread use, there is a significant issue with their reliability, as even small inaccuracies can cause them to fail. This problem is particularly pronounced when these systems are used in high-stakes situations, such as in customer service, financial transactions, and legal proceedings. This paper describes a novel machine testing system called ConvTest, which runs on a cloud-based platform and is designed to test the interaction between a conversational bot and a human user. This system is an advancement over traditional testing methods, which are inadequate for several reasons. For example, these methods test individual features in isolation, but conversational systems are fundamentally different, as they require a holistic approach that mirrors real-world conversations. Additionally, these methods are often time-consuming and require extensive human input, which can be a significant bottleneck. The increasing complexity of MRI acquisitions and sophisticated image reconstructions poses a challenge for ensuring the quality of MRI data. This problem is particularly pronounced in research that relies on large datasets, as even small deviations in data quality can have a significant impact. To address this issue, it's essential to develop methods that can effectively assess MRI data quality, taking into account various factors such as patient, scan, and reconstruction parameters. However, this task is complicated by the fact that quality is often subjectively classified on a continuous scale by experts, who may provide numerical scores or perform pairwise comparisons to prioritize images. This paper explores the idea of modeling MRI data quality as a multi-factorial continuous label, based on the opinions of multiple experts, and proposes a framework that combines neural networks with pairwise comparison data to achieve robust performance. Our results demonstrate the benefits of incorporating pairwise comparison data, leading to the development of a pre-training scheme that can be employed by other models. This approach has yielded promising evaluation metrics and model architectures on publicly available datasets, including those rated by a single expert and pairs of images compared in quality assessments. To facilitate further progress in this area, the authors have released the Expert-Label-Annotated MRI (ELAMRI) dataset, which includes a variety of brain MRI sequences along with their corresponding quality annotations derived from the opinions of multiple experts. This dataset is unique in that it is based on continuous quality labels and incorporates pairwise comparison data, providing a valuable resource for researchers working on this challenging problem. To further advance the field, the authors invite contributions from all interested parties, including data contributors, at the IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI) 2023. In addition to presenting the proposed framework and the ELAMRI dataset, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art in MRI data quality assessment, covering popular datasets, robust learning techniques, and cutting-edge models, as well as an exploration of expert annotation strategies for continuous quality labels. This includes an examination of pairwise comparison data, featuring an empirical analysis of the relationships between images in terms of quality, the development of methods to handle missing comparisons, and the exploration of comparison structures in different datasets. Our work is an attempt to address the multi-factorial generalization issue in MRI data quality assessment, with implications that extend to other domains involving the learning of subjective, continuous labels from multiple experts. We introduce an innovative symbolic computation approach to generate semi-analytical expressions for values of semi-Abelian functions at irreducible (non-rational) points, specifically those corresponding to the limits of Weierstrass points on genus-one curves as their weights approach zero. The resulting formulas, obtained using our method, are typically more concise and easier to work with than the equivalent expressions derived from geometric methods. We demonstrate our technique by producing formulas for values of CM and non-CM types of Weierstrass zeta and sigma functions at these limit points, as well as showing the connection between these values and modular forms for $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$. Our method also enables us to identify relationships between the values of Weierstrass zeta functions and elliptic integrals, including elliptic integral reductions related to the elliptic theta functions and elliptic gamma functions. Furthermore, we apply our approach to evaluate semi-Abelian integrals, including elliptic integrals of the first kind, with algebraic or transcendental results depending on the type and complexity of the input. We provide examples of the computation of quasi-linear formulas for Weierstrass zeta values and show that our method can handle expressions involving the algebraic addition formula for Weierstrass sigma functions. Building upon previous research, we extend our method to the computation of degenerate CM and non-CM values of quasi-Abelian varieties, including fields of definition and the evaluation of these values, for certain types of fields defined over number fields and $p$-adic fields. We also discuss an open problem related to the extension of our approach to the computation of Weierstrass beta functions. Deep neural network-based object classifiers are often tested for their accuracy in identifying images based on their labels, but it's common to see them struggle when presented with contextual information. This research seeks to create a comprehensive framework for evaluating how much context these classifiers can handle. It's worth noting that existing evaluation metrics can be misleading due to the limited nature of training data or the simplicity of the image scenarios. To address this issue, our proposed framework includes a diverse set of criteria that assess a classifier's performance in various aspects, such as its ability to process visual details, recognize relationships between objects, and handle positional information. These criteria are designed to be versatile and adaptable to different types of object classifiers. Our experiments involve evaluating two popular object classifiers using our proposed framework and providing insights into their performance. For instance, we discovered that the contextual information processed by these classifiers can be quite different even when they are based on the same architecture. Our research demonstrates the value of carefully selecting images for each criterion to gain a more accurate understanding of a classifier's strengths and weaknesses. Our findings suggest that certain evaluation metrics used in our study may not always reflect the performance seen in real-world scenarios. Our research data is available for public access through our website. Due to the diverse nature of object recognition tasks, it's unlikely that a single universal standard will be established, but our proposal aims to provide a clear direction for researchers and practitioners in this field. The main objective of this paper is to establish criteria for boundedness of solutions to a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system in a bounded area within R^n ($n\geq2$). The system in question involves a singular Trudinger-Moser type inequality with a nonuniform growth term. We intend to demonstrate here that these criteria are applicable and sufficient for proving the existence of a compact solution to the system in a particular subdomain of R^n ($n\geq2$), and that this solution is characterized by a unique set of functions satisfying a certain relationship within that subdomain. The method employed in this paper is an extension of the techniques developed by Li and Yang in their study on a uniform Kirchhoff type elliptic system, and also builds upon the work of Yang and Yang in their investigation on a nonuniform Kirchhoff type elliptic equation. The approach presented in this paper involves modifying the inequality in question to eliminate the nonuniform term, and then utilizing a fixed point theorem within a suitable functional space to prove the existence of a compact solution to the system in a particular subdomain of R^n ($n\geq2$). The key innovation in this paper is the demonstration that this approach is applicable and efficient for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system in a particular subdomain of R^n ($n\geq2$). The main contribution of this paper is the establishment of a new inequality in question, and the proof of the existence of a compact solution to the system in a particular subdomain of R^n ($n\geq2$). The paper also provides an alternative and simpler proof of the existence of a compact solution to the system in a particular subdomain of R^n ($n\geq2$), and this proof is based on the properties of the singular Trudinger-Moser expansion and the Kirchhoff type elliptic system in question. The paper is organized as follows: the first section provides an overview of the singular Trudinger-Moser expansion and the Kirchhoff type elliptic system in question, and the second section presents the main criteria for proving the existence of a compact solution to the system in a particular subdomain of R^n ($n\geq2$). The third section is devoted to the discussion of the main contribution of this paper, and the fourth section is devoted to the conclusion. The appendix is devoted to the discussion of the singular Trudinger-Moser expansion and the Kirchhoff type elliptic system in question. The paper ends

This paper presents an entity suggestion model based on a Wikipedia graph.
It employs a two-tiered graph structure, incorporating a coarse-level entity
suggestion network and a fine-level detailed network.
The former is a high-level abstract representation used for entity categorization,
while the latter is a concrete network providing specific information for each
entity category.
To train the model, a combination of a categorical prediction method and
respective detailed information extraction techniques are applied.
Our experimental findings show that this approach yields superior entity
suggestion performance in comparison to baseline methods.
Furthermore, our entity suggestion framework based on Wikipedia outperforms
another established knowledge graph, yielding a notable performance boost of
12% in precision and 10% in recall.
Our entity suggestion system has been implemented and is currently in use at
Yahoo! Japan.

In response, implicit kernel methods have emerged as a viable alternative, leveraging mathematical structures like operator algebras and Gelfand triples to define implicit feature mappings. These constructions offer a more flexible and systematic approach to implicit feature transformation, enabling exploration of diverse mathematical frameworks that can underpin implicit kernels. This survey delves into the underlying principles of implicit kernels, tracing the evolution of such methods from their roots in functional analysis to their current form, and explores open research questions and potential future directions along three key dimensions: theoretical foundations, implicit kernel practices, and connections to other areas of machine learning. By providing an overview of the subject through the lens of an implicit kernel framework, we hope to inspire further research into the broader concepts and to create a foundation for the development of new implicit kernel methods. Recent studies utilizing neural networks for sentiment analysis have shown them to be effective, yet it's unclear whether these models truly grasp the underlying polarity dimensions as defined by Loughran-McDonald. To address this, we re-examined and expanded upon the original Loughran-McDonald corpus to account for multiple aspects, such as negation, which previous research failed to consider. Our findings indicate that although neural networks excel in classification tasks, they are essentially equivalent to feature vectors, which are derived from word representations that can be either learned or fixed. When testing these word representations on a variety of evaluation metrics, including semantic similarity and sentence similarity, we discovered that they are susceptible to artificial negation and masking, which significantly boosts their performance. As a result, we conclude that these representations are primarily based on superficial patterns rather than a deep understanding of the underlying polarity structures. To mitigate this, we propose a method called sequential classification, which considers the sequence of words to be more crucial than the word representations alone. When using this approach in a system that accounts for negation and other grammatical components, we found that the performance could be matched without relying on the word representations. Consequently, we suggest that the use of these word representations in the context of the Loughran-McDonald dataset should be reevaluated and alternative methods explored. Furthermore, we believe that our findings are applicable to other sentiment analysis tasks that involve the interpretation of the underlying structure of text. In light of this, we have made our dataset and evaluation metrics available for the broader research community to explore these results and potential solutions. In particular, we invite researchers to investigate our proposed sequential classification approach and the accompanying dataset, which can be downloaded from https://github.com/zhengyangwang/word-representations-for-sentiment-analysis. For further information regarding this work, the authors are more than happy to provide an oral presentation at the conference in response to questions and feedback from the audience. Additionally, the study has been formally published in the Proceedings of the 2022 Conference of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-2022). The interpretation of experimental data through theoretical tools relies heavily on functional descriptions, such as PDFs and FFs, which are subject to constraints from a broader set of data that has not been directly measured. These unconstrained quantities pose uncertainty when translating partonic measurements into physical outcomes, affecting predictions across scales and processes that involve parton participation. As experimental evidence accumulates, enriching the fit variables and PDF parameters, new considerations arise, such as the impact of model assumptions and potential biases, which necessitate a formal framework for evaluating the fit's integrity and influencing model choices that shape the fit. This paper outlines an evaluation framework that addresses these aspects through explicit calculation of PDF bias and a proposal for a robust assessment of model alternatives, which informs the choice of methods for evaluating model uncertainty. This framework is employed to examine two widely used fit methodologies, xQCD and HOF, which yield $W$-mass predictions that differ by 1.7 Sigmas, prompting a reevaluation of PDF uncertainty in this context. Additionally, this study presents guidance for experimental analyses, emphasizing the importance of providing data in a form that facilitates objective interpretation and suggests ways to compare fit methodologies implicitly, which is particularly crucial for unprecedented measurements. As new data and analyses emerge, this framework is poised to contribute to the ongoing discussion of best practices for PDF evaluation and to facilitate a comprehensive understanding of theoretical uncertainties in experiments rooted in partonic interpretations. This is because it addresses two key issues with conventional approaches: the inconsistent nature of gradient estimates and the slow learning process. This study introduces a new variance-reducing replay buffer population strategy that prioritizes diverse experiences. This is represented mathematically as minimizing the mean squared error subject to constraints on data diversity. This leads to an efficient and scalable solution. Our proposed framework, known as VDER, is then compared to existing methods, demonstrating its advantages in terms of convergence speed, robustness, and accuracy. Furthermore, VDER is applied to two prominent algorithms: DQN and TD3, resulting in significant improvements over baseline models, as evidenced by reduced variance, converged values, and superior performance. Our findings are supported by comprehensive numerical experiments and a theoretical analysis. This includes a discussion on the implications of the Euler scheme and a convergence rate analysis for the optimized experience replay buffer population problem. Systematic simulations reveal the influence of parameters, such as variance, diversity constraints, and population size on the VDER framework. We employed x-ray emission spectroscopy in combination with density functional theory to determine the electronic structure of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, and investigated its relation to superconducting properties. The results show that removing electrons from a d-x^2-y^2 orbital in the DFS (Fe-based superconductors) phase and transferring them to a d-z^2 orbital in the FS (free electron gas) phase can facilitate superconductivity. Furthermore, we found that replacing barium with potassium on the surface of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ can alter the DFS structure to an FS structure, effectively enhancing electron transfer between the two states and thus boosting superconducting critical temperature (Tc). The optimal Tc of around 7 K can be achieved by adjusting the ratio of barium to potassium. The proposed model offers an innovative method for designing high Tc superconductors. 
  The described surface structure and superconducting property alteration are experimentally verified through scanning tunneling microscopy and resistivity measurements under potassium coverage. The study reveals a previously unobserved surface structure in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ and demonstrates the potential of controlling superconducting properties through surface composition. 
  The discovered relationship between the surface structure and superconducting properties can be applied to other Fe-based superconductors, and the study provides valuable insights for the fundamental understanding of superconductivity and material design. 
  The proposed model can be employed to design high Tc superconductors by adjusting the composition of metal and transition metal elements within the DFS and FS phases. 
  The study offers a perspective for the theoretical and experimental investigation of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ and related Fe-based superconductors through the analysis of surface composition and superconducting properties under metal coverage.

A certain transformation, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, was previously proposed by Nishida for Gaussian matrices. We have shown here that this transformation can be expressed in the form of the superbosonization equation, a more universal formula that produces bosonic representations for both fermions and Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) fermions. As a result, the HBST transformation loses its unique status, and its utility is now seen as a direct application of the superbosonization equation with a specific choice of variables. We have demonstrated this equivalence by illustrating examples involving both $t$-$J$ and Hubbard models, and these examples can also be treated as examples for the superbosonization equation. We have also used the HBST transformation with a spin-triplet $XX$-matrix to examine the inter-relationship between three different types of Gaussian matrices: the $sp(2k)$, $so(2k+1)$, and $u(2k)$ symmetries. The discussion of super-soliton systems resulting from both the HBST transformation and the superbosonization equation has led to an equivalent expression for the BKT central charge $c=1$, and we have derived a new general formula for the super-soliton central extension. MultiTalk is a large-scale, highly-branching dialogue dataset designed to tackle a key challenge in conversational AI research: handling extensive, real-world conversation trees. Many current datasets are limited to shallow tree structures, which can lead to biased training data and limited testing for conversational models. To address this issue, we present a new dataset featuring 32 starting topics, with each topic spanning 10 distinct subtopics, resulting in over 1 million unique conversation turns through human interaction. Unlike previous datasets, MultiTalk showcases conversation trees that extend far beyond 3-4 levels of depth, with an average of nearly 7 branches per conversation. To further complicate matters, each conversation is allowed to explore any subtopic at any time, without pre-set constraints, which can lead to unpredictable branching patterns. With human evaluators assessing every conversation turn for relevance and coherence, MultiTalk serves as an exhaustive testbed for conversational systems, with each conversation turn counted towards the final evaluation metric rather than just relying on overall conversation scores. To facilitate seamless integration with existing datasets, MultiTalk shares the same format as the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset, which is widely used for evaluating conversational systems. To demonstrate the difficulties posed by this testbed, we present a series of rigorous evaluation experiments, which reveal significant performance disparities between different evaluation metrics and different system assumptions, which we classify into three primary categories: strict, loose, and intermediate systems. These findings provide valuable insights for future research in this domain, with a proposed new evaluation framework that balances practical considerations with theoretical limitations, which we term the 7-branch rule, which we plan to explore in depth in an upcoming companion paper. With its unprecedented level of complexity and branching, MultiTalk sets a new benchmark for the field, with a strong emphasis on real-world applicability, which we believe will serve as an ideal testbed for evaluating the maturity of conversational AI systems in the future. Our research enhances the understanding of intelligent reflective surfaces (IRS) by examining their capacity to induce ergodicity in multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems, considering the effects of correlated and non-correlated subarray reflections and co-arrays. We develop and analyze two practical models for describing these phenomena, creating a mathematical framework that enables the derivation of ergodic capacity in IRS-assisted MIMO systems. We then investigate and compare the results obtained from both models, demonstrating that the effects of correlated and non-correlated subarray reflections and co-arrays significantly impact the ergodic capacity in IRS-assisted MIMO systems. Moreover, we find that the model incorporating non-correlated reflections yields the highest ergodic capacity, while the model considering correlated reflections may provide a closer estimate in certain scenarios, especially those with large and randomly distributed co-arrays, ultimately highlighting the potential for IRS to induce ergodicity in MIMO systems. Our research is also a foundation for exploring other aspects of IRS-assisted MIMO systems, such as sum-ergodic capacity and outage probability, which we hope to investigate in our future work. We anticipate that our results, particularly the development of an 8-dimensional path loss model, will contribute to the creation of a more comprehensive and standardized model for describing the performance of IRS-assisted MIMO systems, enabling more precise simulations and analyses. Additionally, we believe that our study on the impact of correlated and non-correlated subarray reflections and co-arrays will facilitate the design and optimization of IRS in real-world scenarios, ultimately leading to the realization of its full potential. However, there are several aspects of our research that require further extension and refinement, including the analysis of correlated Rician fading, the development of optimized phase-shift modeling, and the exploration of other innovative techniques for enhancing the performance of IRS-assisted MIMO systems. Building upon our research, we plan to investigate these areas in more detail, with a focus on investigating the ergodic capacity of IRS-assisted MIMO systems under the influence of correlated Rician fading and exploring alternative designs for co-arrays, as well as considering the effects of line-of-sight (LoS) links in both IRS-assisted and LoS systems. This platform offers free, open-source software for performing $N$-body simulations quickly, typically within a few hours for $N=65536$. Each simulation consists of $13$ billion time steps. The code is designed to be user-friendly and is paired with a suite of computational tools that facilitate easy interpretation of results. To validate our method, we simulated a standard $\Lambda$CDM universe and compared our findings to established numerical simulations, showing that our approach is precise. The platform includes two types of force calculation algorithms: a direct multigrid method and a user-friendly interface for leveraging precomputed gravitational potentials, allowing for the exploration of a broad range of $N$ values. By integrating several key features, WorkingWiki has improved upon MediaWiki in the following areas: a more efficient and intuitive page editing system; better organization and categorization tools; enhanced support for data input in various numerical and graphical formats; improved collaboration features, including real-time chat and streamlined revision tracking; as well as enhanced administration and security functionalities. Our case study at the University of California, Berkeley, involving graduate students across multiple disciplines, demonstrates the viability of WorkingWiki. This research project, supported by a combination of staff guidance and student self-regulation, successfully leverages WorkingWiki's strengths to facilitate effective collaboration and produce high-quality outcomes within a relatively short timeframe. This work contributes valuable insights to the development of effective technologies for supporting collaborative research efforts. By building upon established platforms like MediaWiki, researchers and developers can create derivative systems like WorkingWiki that provide valuable tools for managing research projects, data, and outcomes. Our analysis indicates that certain unstable flame modes can interact with acoustic waves in complex ways, depending on factors such as frequency and flow conditions.
These mode-acoustic interactions can be both localized and extended in nature.
Some modes exhibit similar behavior to their steady-state counterparts under specific conditions.
However, our findings suggest that in general, mode-acoustic interactions result in mode behavior that is distinct from its steady-state equivalent.
Our research also reveals that certain modes can transfer their energy to other modes through acoustic waves, a phenomenon we term active flame response.
This phenomenon enables flames to respond actively to acoustic waves, potentially leading to enhanced mixing and heat release.
As a result, we believe that using active flame models can provide a more accurate representation of turbulent flame behavior under forced conditions.
Our analysis indicates that a linearized framework can capture the active flame response and mode-acoustic interactions that lead to enhanced mixing and heat release.
However, our research also reveals that this framework may not capture all aspects of turbulent flame behavior under forced conditions, a topic in need of further investigation.

High-resolution spectroscopy and the asteroseismology of stars are interlinked through a field known as exo-seismology. It involves the analysis of a star's seismic data to gather information about the characteristics of another star, typically a exoplanet-hosting one. This process is often a two-step approach where the properties of the star are determined first and then used in the subsequent phase. 

Recently, researchers have discovered a category of vibrations in stars with complex internal structures, specifically those with molecular layers in low-mass stars and convective core borders in intermediate and heavy stars. These vibrations are connected to the geometric shape of the star and its boundary layers and are referred to as geometric modes. They possess unique period characteristics that set them apart from standard p- and g-modes. 

A new method has been developed to the adiabatic frequency expansion of these modes by using a perturbation approach that is applicable to various mode types, including those with complex structures and boundary layers. Using this method, theoretical frequency predictions were made for both fundamental and secondary geometric modes in both standard and cool stars, resulting in their period characteristics deviating from the typical period-luminosity relations. 

These new modes and the developed method hold promise for their detection via high-resolution spectroscopy, especially when combined with the latest observational techniques that are more sensitive to certain frequency ranges. If detected, these modes will provide valuable insights into a star's structural characteristics and can be an additional factor in the interpretation of exo-seismology data. Moreover, they will also serve as an indicator to evaluate the accuracy of stellar seismic analysis software, used in the interpretation of spectroscopic data, when applying it to the detection of exoplanets. 

The cutting-edge technique of time-domain spectroscopy, which is highly sensitive to frequency ranges of $10^{-3}$ d$^{-1}$, offers the possibility of detecting these modes in a short period of $10$ days. This is significantly quicker than the months or even years required by traditional techniques. If successful, the detection of these modes will not only open up new avenues for the study of stars but also contribute to the development of advanced algorithms and observational techniques.

We present a novel method to pinpoint traveling chimeras and synchronized clusters within a larger network of interlinked oscillating nodes. Our method is built upon a reduced set of variables that dynamically capture the level of coherence among any subset of the network's nodes. By observing these variables in time and space, we can visually identify the desired coherent groups. Specifically, we can determine the Granger causality between any nodes to establish their connection, and then derive a metric that quantifies the level of coherence within any subnetwork. With these coherence measures, we can create a simplified phase-space representation that showcases the level of synchronization among the network's components over time, and also facilitate a geometrical interpretation to identify traveling cluster waves. We demonstrated our method's effectiveness on three different spiking network models. Firstly, we found traveling chimeras in a ring of 50 nodes, where a specific group of three nodes formed an intra-connected spiral wave pattern, moving at a speed of one node length per time step. Secondly, we discovered a cluster wave in an 80-node ring, where 16 nodes synchronized with each other to form a coherent group, moving at a speed of half a node per time step. Lastly, we identified a big island of synchronized states in a 50x50 grid of 250 nodes, where traveling cluster waves emerged when the internal frequency of the grid nodes differed. All of the obtained results were verified using our method and further confirmed by numerical solutions obtained with the method of time and phase embedding, and the clarification of the method's results with a specific example is also provided. Additionally, we outline the potential of our method to be adapted for other types of networks, and the source code is made available at the following link https://github.com/aleksandar-eric-kostic/robust-cluster-identification, where it can be downloaded from. This process is significant when the dark matter wavelength is comparable to or larger than the de Broglie wavelength of neutrinos. As a result, we can expect a diminished neutrino heat flux in high-flux environments, such as in big-bang nucleosynthesis, and this effect is found to be consistent with observational standards. Furthermore, we find that neutrinos' interaction with ultralight dark matter may exceed the half-life limit for 0νββ decay imposed by existing data in half of the dark matter mass range, thus potentially being detected in next-generation experiments. The unification of Galaxies, Superclusters and Cosmics Rays origins relies heavily on the presence of Ultra High Energy photons. These photons, with energies above $10^{19}$ eV, are thought to originate from distant sources and travel long distances through the cosmos. It is essential to determine how they interact with the magnetic fields of the solar system and other intergalactic fields in order to establish their path and potential for continued travel. In this paper, a model is developed to calculate the behavior of these high energy photons when they enter the solar magnetic field. It is shown that these photons can enter the solar system at nearly any angle and can travel significant distances before being deflected by more than 0.1 radians. This occurs when the solar system is positioned between the source and the observer, and the major axis of this triangle is within the 45 degree to 141 degree range. This condition must be met for the photon flux to be isotropic. Therefore, it is not the high energy photons themselves that cause the distortion, but rather the large angle photon flux caused by the redirection of photons within the solar magnetic field. This model also demonstrates that when the solar system is not situated between the source and the observer, the photon flux is not isotropic and its behavior is influenced by the angle of the major axis, resulting in a more complex relationship that cannot be defined by a second order polynomial. This model provides a framework to analyze the behavior of high energy photons in various magnetic fields and could be applied to other contexts such as particle acceleration in magnetic fields. Nonlocal Gravity is a theoretical framework that modifies General Relativity to include nonlocal effects while maintaining the principle of general covariance. This report outlines a novel approach to formulating Nonlocal Gravity, characterized by the use of 'essential tetrads' which are defined by a covariant four-dimensional construction that identifies the fundamental spacetime volume. Within this framework, the metric tensor is redefined and expressed as the dot product of the essential tetrads. A constitutive equation is then established to link this new metric with the Einstein tensor, and its connection is shown to act as an additional gravitational potential. Ultimately, this formulation demonstrates that Nonlocal Gravity can be viewed as an emergent effect within Nonlocal Gravity from to its constitutive equation. This report also provides an overview of the theoretical foundation and key predictions of Nonlocal Gravity, including a discussion on cosmological solutions and the possibility of gravitational wave production. This work is a part of ongoing research aimed at developing a new paradigm for particle physics, grounded on a modified approach to gravity that can facilitate natural Compton scales in energy, essentially paving the way for a more intuitive understanding of fundamental particle interactions. This new perspective on Nonlocal Gravity, fueled by its potential to resolve long-standing issues in quantum physics, is being explored. Distributed systems with multiple participants require a high level of data consistency assurance across all users. User applications can take various actions such as reading or writing data, making it essential to develop robust data structures that function effectively under potentially conflicting updates from multiple processes. Although many replicated data structures have been created to handle this kind of scenario, they often lack a clear design foundation and fail to address the fundamental issue of handling conflicts. This paper proposes a novel design framework called Eliminate-Win to address this issue. It categorizes user actions into either eliminative or winny actions. Eliminative actions either remove existing values or supplement them, whereas winny actions overwrite existing values, necessitating conflict handling. The framework ensures that all conflicts are resolved through the eliminative action, thereby ensuring that replicated data structures are free from conflicts. This framework's application is demonstrated through the creation of a fully functional version of the Eliminate-Win replicated queue using the Eliminate-Win framework and verifying its correctness with the help of the Tamarin prover. Additionally, the paper discusses its key characteristics as well as potential use cases and potential future research directions. Eliminate-Win provides a clear design for replicated data structures that are conflict-free, allowing for easier maintenance and troubleshooting, in comparison to earlier approaches as Base-Case With Win, System F+R. The framework's conflict-free aspect ensures user satisfaction, yet it imposes certain limitations on user actions, such as read operations, which could potentially conflicts and, therefore, are not supported. Nonetheless, Eliminate-Win has the potential to significantly contribute to the creation of robust and conflict-free replicated data structures in distributed systems. The corresponding author for this paper is Janez Brest. Janez Brest is an associate professor at the University of Maribor, Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Information Technology, in Slovenia. His research interests include distributed systems, optimization techniques for solving complex mathematical problems, and their real-world applications, as well as the development of robust algorithms in the presence of various types of attacks and errors. To supply a comprehensive view of current genomic findings, a joint initiative among 17 international research groups analyzed genome-wide association data for 18 human disorders and examined the functional implications of associated variants. This collaborative effort involved a thorough examination of nearly 300 previously identified loci associated with each disorder, across all 18, and a more in-depth analysis of over 1,000 newly discovered loci for 10 of these conditions. A sophisticated computational tool called FUMA was utilized to interpret more than 280 million genome-wide association findings from over 80 different studies, encompassing over 150,000 individuals with each disorder, across all 18. In addition to identifying many disease-associated genes through a variety of methods, this analysis revealed several key patterns in genomic data, including a higher prevalence of immune-related genes among those linked to autoimmune disorders, a greater association with cancer genes in certain conditions, and a higher prevalence of developmental genes in disorders that affect development. Furthermore, when comparing all 18 conditions, a notable disparity was observed in the proportion of associated loci that are specific to each disorder, with certain conditions, such as inflammatory bowel disease and type 2 diabetes, having a relatively high number of unique genetic links, whereas others, like heart disease and stroke, had a significantly lower number of distinct genomic connections. These findings provide valuable insights into the complex genetic underpinnings of each disorder and highlight the need for further research aimed at clarifying the functional implications of associated variants and the structural organization of genetic links within each condition. In this case, we focus on a specific subset of EFTs - the operator subsets associated with electroweak and QCD sub-systems that are not fundamental - and explore their fundamental descriptions through the exchange of heavy particles below the cutoff scale. We reframe the cross-section calculations in a manner that emphasizes the interaction between these sub-systems and a 4-year dataset from the LHC, available at 13 TeV and in various forms (inclusive, vector boson scattering, di-boson, and heavy vector bosos). We found all available LHC data to be consistent with a set of general effective assumptions and determined the relevant constraints on the effective parameters up to a certain order. Observations of many low-mass X-ray binary systems have revealed a significant population of objects that exhibit no outbursts. This study aims to explain this lack of activity using a theoretical approach. Rather than relying on the "natural selection" hypothesis that outbursts are necessary for these systems to survive, this research proposes a more complex model in which some systems lack the required conditions for outbursts to occur. A key factor in this model is the presence of a recurring pattern in the outbursts of active systems, which was first identified by Patruno et al. in 2011. A specific range for the spin period of these systems has been deduced through data analysis and is characterized by a ratio of the spin period to the orbital period being less than one. Our research reveals that long-lasting, narrow shocks can maintain their velocity and heat surrounding stellar envelopes even in complex, curved geometries, ultimately producing massive amounts of optically thick cooling at temperatures above 10e4 K. Conversely, broad, shallow shocks at similar velocities lead to significant heating in thinner layers, producing massive amounts of optically thick cooling, while narrow, deep shocks with similar velocities fail to significantly impact the surrounding environment. We highlight the overlooked significance of phonon effects on dynamic electron behavior, particularly spin, using first-principle calculations on copper. Conversations involve an exchange of statements with varying meanings and inferences, yet the majority of existing NLP models are developed with isolated tests of language understanding. This work expands natural language inference to multiple contexts, mirroring the semantic variety found in conversations. Six hundred pairs of sentences with different meanings and inferences, derived from NLI datasets with additional context, will serve as the basis for evaluation and refinement of NLI models in multi-turn settings. Our findings show that NLI models perform better when the context supports their current beliefs, but struggle with more complex situations involving new information, where they significantly underperform human performance. These results highlight the limitations of current NLI models and suggest several paths for improvement, including adding variety to training datasets, incorporating different semantic roles, and developing methods to handle inference in multiple contexts. Our datasets and code are available at https://github.com/harvardnlp/semantics-in-conversation. This work is an initial exploration of the implications of semantic variety in conversations, and future research will be necessary to fully address these challenges. Nonetheless, our key insight is that NLI models require significant improvement before they can accurately capture the variety of semantic contexts found in conversations. This is reflected in our proposed evaluation metric, which prioritizes models that perform well even with less favorable contexts. This priority will be crucial for future researchers working to refine NLI models for these settings. Our results with the proposed evaluation metric and NLI models pre-trained with multi-turn settings suggest that these models are still far from adequate for these settings. This work will also provide a foundation for further study into the variety of semantic contexts found in conversations and how they are managed in comparison to monologic settings. This will be particularly true as more research is conducted around these exchange of statements with varying meanings and inferences found in conversations and how they differ from situations involving the reading of a single passage. This work will also be a starting point for a more in-depth exploration of the implications of these differences on models of natural language understanding and how they are tested and refined. Next-generation self-driving vehicles rely on artificial intelligence to anticipate and prevent collisions, particularly during lane changes. However, existing systems are hindered by their inability to accurately identify potential hazards in the target lane. To address this limitation, this research leverages advanced computer vision techniques to classify video segments associated with lane changes as safe or hazardous. A novel deep learning framework, dubbed Semi-supervised 4D Network, is proposed to achieve this classification. This proposed framework builds on existing spatial and temporal segmentation techniques by incorporating a feature extraction method that utilizes masked features from related scenes. Furthermore, this research employs a mask transfer approach to accelerate training with only lane change video data. Results show that the proposed framework yields superior performance compared to existing systems, surpassing top performance by 25% with limited annotated data. Moreover, this research demonstrates the efficacy of a mask transfer approach in semi-supervised learning through the enhancement of lane change detection. Notably, this detection approach achieves 85% accuracy with only 100 annotated video segments. This research provides a foundation for the development of a system capable of predicting lane change-related hazards in next-generation self-driving vehicles. Code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuan-wu/hazards-recognition. With continuous advancements in computer vision and the collection of more annotated data, this system is poised to significantly improve, ultimately becoming a crucial component of self-driving vehicles. However, several challenges need to be addressed prior to its deployment, including the integration of system latency and the development of a decision-making framework in conjunction with existing systems used in vehicles. This framework is essential for real-time lane change-related hazard prediction used in vehicles equipped with sensing technology, given that it is approximately 100ms slower than similar systems employed in stationary computers.
