The exact mechanisms behind Type II supernovae that result in rotating neutron star and black hole formations are not yet fully understood and are still a topic of active research. It is widely accepted that these extreme objects should rotate rapidly due to angular momentum conservation from their progenitor's rotation. However, current theoretical models fail to produce the high rotation rates observed in these objects, particularly in four-step explosion scenarios. To fill this gap in our knowledge, researchers have developed a sophisticated computational model that simulates the collapse of rotating stellar objects, including both main-sequence and lower-mass stars, as well as brown dwarfs and planets, in various environments and with diverse compositions. This model is highly versatile and is used to investigate how various factors influence the structure and behavior of rotating stars, such as the presence or absence of magnetic fields, convective patterns, and shock waves in their cores. By exploring both fundamental and explosion-driven collapse scenarios, scientists have discovered several possible pathways that could lead to high rotation rates in neutron stars and black holes, including the conversion of kinetic energy into internal energy during the collapse, as well as the effects of angular velocity conservation and magnetic field generation. These findings have shed new light on the rotation characteristics of compact objects and have provided a framework that can be used to make predictions about the structure and behavior of pulsar planets, pulsar winds, and relativistic shock waves, as well as the formation of pulsar binaries with small separations. This research has also identified potential signatures for detecting pulsar formation through gravitational waves, as well as new types of gravitational wave sources, such as the merger of rotating neutron stars with large magnetic fields and pulsar planets, whose production mechanisms are still not well understood. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of the rotation characteristics of compact objects and the formation of pulsar binaries, as well as the detection of gravitational waves, and have opened up a new area of research in the physics of dense matter and neutron star physics. Additionally, these models have contributed to a paper that has been submitted to the Astrophysical Journal Letters and is currently under review. The significance of amplitude measurements in particle physics research is underscored by their effectiveness in fine-tuning instrument adjustments, filtering signal from background, and ultimately enhancing detection efficiency and accuracy. While often indispensable, this importance can be challenging to quantify, making it a subjective variable in data analysis. Subjectivity can be minimized by factoring in instrumental fluctuations that affect measurement results and, in turn, downstream interpretations. A comprehensive description of experimental uncertainties associated with amplitude measurements and their impact on derived variables is provided in this study. Specifically, central value and standard deviation estimates are determined for three variables derived from amplitude measurements, including one that is theoretically significant, such as a ratio or R-value, and two that are experimentally significant, such as efficiency and yield. These estimates are validated through simulated test data analysis, and the associated uncertainty metrics for the three variables are found to be in the range of 0.01-0.05, indicating that amplitude measurement precision generally prioritizes accuracy over precision, except in cases involving binomial distribution, where the standard deviation is significantly higher. These findings are applicable to most particle physics experiments that involve amplitude-based analyses, such as scattering angle, mass, and decay width determinations, and are further illustrated by a concrete example from a stransverse momentum distribution fit, where a R-value of 2.58 and a yield of 106.2 were obtained with associated standard deviations of 0.03, 0.02, and 0.01 for the R-value, yield, and width, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of amplitude measurements in enhancing detection efficiency and accuracy and the experimental significance of such variables, and serve as a guideline for uncertainty estimation in future analyses. A supplemental section provides a theoretical justification for the uncertainty metric formula, and a further section outlines a proposed future experiment that leverages amplitude analysis in the search for chiral momentum transport in heavy-ion collisions at RHIC with the STAR detector. Imbalanced incremental learning poses a significant challenge for continuous learning due to shifting data and class imbalances. Real-world scenarios, such as medical diagnosis and credit risk assessment, frequently exhibit substantial class imbalances. Existing research has primarily focused on developing incremental methods for addressing single imbalanced learning problems, neglecting the dual challenge of data that shifts over time. In this work, we address this gap by introducing a novel evaluation framework that simulates incremental learning scenarios in a comprehensive manner. To validate our framework, we conducted comprehensive experiments to compare the performance of four prominent calibration techniques – Kullback-Leibler Divergence, Maximum Likelihood Estimation, Rényi Divergence, and Weighted Minimum Squares Error – in relation to their ability to address the dual challenge of data that shifts over time due to class imbalances. Our empirical findings revealed that calibration techniques can effectively remedy the issue of imbalanced learning but are less impactful when dealing with data that shifts over time. Conversely, our results indicate that the selection of the divergence or loss function has a more pronounced impact on model performance in such scenarios. Notably, the Kullback-Leibler Divergence exhibited the worst performance, while the Weighted Minimum Squares Error outperformed the other methods in our evaluation. Our study offers a thorough assessment of the performance of calibration techniques in the context of imbalanced incremental learning and provides a framework for a comprehensive evaluation of such challenges. Furthermore, we provide experimental code in the appendix in accordance with the guidelines set forth by the Deep Learning Competitions and Surveys (DL-COS) norms. Our research lays the groundwork for a more in-depth exploration of the performance of calibration techniques in scenarios involving data that shifts over time due to class imbalances. In the near future, we plan to expand our evaluation framework to a broader range of scenarios and incorporate additional methods for dealing with the dual challenge of data that shifts over time due to class imbalances. This evaluation framework is a critical component of our research, and we anticipate it to contribute substantially to the field of imbalanced incremental learning. In the long-term, we aim to explore innovative approaches to processing data in real-world scenarios through our research. In the appendix, we provide a detailed description of each calibration technique, along with a comprehensive overview of our evaluation framework and all experimental configurations used in our evaluation. Additionally, we include a discussion on potential future research directions in the field of imbalanced incremental learning. As energy efficiency becomes the primary performance metric for CPU design, an emerging issue with today's systems is the limited capacity to run older software. This problem arises because legacy applications are optimized for simpler, less efficient memory models that can't be seamlessly integrated into the latest programming frameworks. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel memory model called HyperShared, which combines the advantages of different memory paradiggs through a reimagined hardware structure. We implemented HyperShared in an actual CPU and achieved significant improvements in energy efficiency and performance for older software. Specifically, we observed a $4.5\times$ to $7.6\times$ decrease in energy consumption and a $2.3\times$ to $3.3\times$ increase in processing speed compared to traditional in-order and out-of-order cores, respectively. We also developed an automated technique to convert modern workloads into forms that can take advantage of HyperShared's capabilities and found it could process legacy applications at speeds $1.3\times$ to $3.5\times$ faster than baseline cores. To further explore the potential of HyperShared, we created a software framework that can easily convert numerous legacy applications into versions that can utilize its benefits, resulting in a significant $2\times$ to $4\times$ improvement in performance and a $2\times$ to $6\times$ decrease in energy consumption for various workloads. We call this framework HyperConverter and it can handle a vast range of applications but still faces limitations when dealing with very old or very complex software. To address these challenges, we designed an enhanced version of HyperShared called HyperShared2 that can support a wider range of programming models while providing even greater performance and energy efficiency gains. We believe our research can open up new avenues for the development of more adaptable and backward-compatible CPU architectures that can efficiently run older software and provide faster and more efficient performance. We also hope to contribute to the exploration of new possibilities for improving the performance and energy efficiency of legacy software and to facilitate the development of more versatile and backward-compatible hardware and software systems. We are confident that our research will not only facilitate the efficient processing of older software but also provide valuable insights that can be applied to the development of more adaptable and backward-compatible CPU architectures that can efficiently run not just legacy applications but also newer software that can take advantage of their unique features and capabilities. We are excited to share our research with other experts in this field and look forward to their valuable feedback and input. We would like to express our gratitude

In 1871, P. T. de Sainte-Catherine reported to P. L. Dulong that he observed in sulfur a variation of density with pressure, leading to a decrease in volume without a corresponding decrease in mass. Dulong was skeptical and requested a repeat of the experiment which indeed held true. This discovery sparked a debate between chemists and physicists regarding the underlying principles, with some advocating for the immutability of chemical substances and the creation of "intermediate substances" with varying properties, while others proposed more complex ideas such as the presence of air within sulfur. To resolve this issue, a theoretical analysis based on the thermodynamic theory of irreversibility is presented, along with a hypothesis that certain materials can exhibit diverse compositions, leading to distinct gradients in these regions. A proposed model, the "heterogeneous stock model," simulates this phenomenon by combining two elements with varying proportions and distinct gradients, resulting in a decrease in volume without a corresponding decrease in mass when subjected to pressure. This model demonstrates that the principles of chemistry are maintained while explaining the experimental results of Sainte-Catherine, providing a more plausible explanation than the idea of "intermediate substances" and offering a basis for further exploration of the relationship between chemical structure and physical properties. This concept is then applied to a discussion on the diffusion of light through matter, leading to a query as to whether it may pass through equal proportions by volume of any two substances, or if there are certain substances to which light cannot pass, and if so, what implications this may have for the fundamental principles of chemistry and physics. This debate is further contributed to by an experiment that demonstrates the power of high-pressure jets of water, indicating that water at such pressures behaves as an impenetrable mass, leading to the consideration of additional experiments that could shed light on this phenomenon, along with a discussion on the potential for these principles to influence the generation of power through the use of high-pressure jets of water and the extraction of heat from all natural bodies that are in a state of flux, suggesting that there may be a deeper connection between these concepts and the fundamental principles of chemistry and physics, and expressing a desire to explore these ideas further with the assistance of the Academy of Sciences. Deep neural network models excel at classifying most images in a test set, but their performance is often severely impaired on specific examples. Understanding and measuring this phenomenon is crucial, especially as high-stakes applications rely on these models. Currently, evaluation metrics like accuracy and AUROC overlook the models' behavior on individual images. We introduce a new framework that assesses the diversity of predictions made on each image in a dataset and identifies a key aspect of deep learning models: even if they make widespread, confident predictions, they can still fail catastrophically on a minority of images. We demonstrate the versatility of our framework by investigating multiple aspects of deep learning models, including their performance on easy and difficult images, with ambiguous labels, and with natural and anomalous data. Notably, we discovered that current benchmark datasets for image classification contain a significant minority of images that are misclassified even by chance, and that these models perform much better on the remaining images. These findings shed light on the significant disparity between the average and worst-case performance of deep learning models and may have implications for evaluating and selecting models for high-stakes applications. We hope our proposed framework will be a useful tool for the broader computer vision community. To accomplish this, we utilized GlossBERT, a state-of-the-art BERT-based system for WMC, as our basis and made improvements upon it. Originally, BERT-based models like GlossBERT generate word glossaries in their own words, which are then evaluated against the original definitions. To enhance the clarity of these definitions, we replaced the classification task with a generation task that mirrors the definitions found in the WordNet database. To facilitate this, we assembled a new dataset containing just the definition portions of WordNet entries. This dataset was utilized to fine-tune both GlossBERT and BERT, which in turn enabled them to effectively generate clear word definitions. We assessed these models against the classification-based GlossBERT and discovered them to be inferior in the classification context but vastly superior in definition-to-sentence matching tasks, which is the more natural way to view WMC. Experts like chefs operate within this paradigm, working from written recipes while preparing meals and presenting them visually for serving purposes. Our study simulates this scenario by presenting Kitchen54, a 3D cooking environment that demands both culinary and presentation expertise, as judged by human evaluators who consult written recipe guides that also need to be followed visually. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this metric by showing that learning models performance on Kitchen360 exceeds that of human culinarians and experts in the following areas: the overall sequence of steps, step-by-step sequences, and both written and visual instructional sequences. Furthermore, we discovered that Kitchen360 distinguishes between models that have been trained on Kitchen54 and those that have not, and that it offers valuable insights that are verified by human annotators, including the fact that it prioritizes sequential coherence and expertise over irrelevant information. This research focuses on creating Molmer-Sorensen gates with frequency stability using a combination of multiple laser frequencies that share equal contributions from various motional modes in a trapped ion chain. By sharing frequencies, the peak amplitude of each motional mode can be reduced, minimizing the effects of amplitude fluctuations and laser noise, thus achieving higher gate fidelity. Using a 4-ion chain as an example, we've demonstrated the potential for molmer-sorensen gates to operate at 100 kHz, 500 kHz, and 5 MHz, respectively, for different numbers of laser frequencies and mode participations, without compromising the desired equal contributions from the modes. A theoretical Molmer-Sorensen gate setup with three frequencies in a 9-dimensional mode space showed an extremely low requirement for peak amplitude, approximately 0.18 in a 4-ion chain, resulting in very minimal effects from amplitude fluctuations and laser noise, enabling the possibility of achieving very high molmer-sorensen gate fidelities even in the presence of moderate laser amplitude fluctuations and noise. A related simulation found that frequency-stable MS gates can operate with very low residual heating rates below 0.002 2π kHz in a 4-ion chain, even at higher laser frequencies. A discussion on the potential for implementing this gate type in larger ion chains, using a 9-ion chain as an example, also highlights the importance of controlling the mode participation in a desirable equal contributions range, indicating that only very low residual heating rates below 0.002 2π kHz can be maintained in larger mode spaces. A proposed method for dynamically adjusting the mode participations in a controlled manner has been outlined, based on a novel approach for real-time spectral analysis of the ion's fluorescence signal. This method allows for the swift adjustment of mode participations to maintain the required equal contributions even in a larger mode space, enabling frequency-stable molmer-sorensen gates in a wider range of applications. A comparison of frequency-stable MS gates with a proposed robust superconducting qubit gate suggests that both gates have similar requirements and both can achieve high fidelities even in the presence of moderate amplitude fluctuations and laser noise. Despite being peptide-free, our findings reveal that certain peptide molecules can form complex arrangements within the perovskite lattice, potentially reducing the necessary concentration required for triggering ferroelectricity. Furthermore, we found that some of these structures exhibit unique characteristics, serving as templates that can be used to explain the exceptional electric properties exhibited by peptide-containing perovskites. Neural models like Transformer have been the standard for text generation,
according to a recent evaluation. This research reveals that a simple $n$-gram
model can effectively produce high-quality texts by working in tandem with
these complex neural models. It's shown that a combination of $n$-gram and
transformer models results in high scores in various evaluation metrics. This
surprising finding can be understood through a residual learning perspective,
where neural models primarily correct $n$-gram errors and noise. As a result, it
is feasible to generate texts using a $n$-gram model in a limited domain setting
without needing neural models. This insight enables the creation of a system
that can produce not just texts but also other neural objects like dialogs and
images from neural prototypes. For instance, a dialog consists of a sequence of
texts, each of which can be produced with a $n$$^2$-gram model. This approach
also results in significant reductions in model sizes and computational costs. It
is demonstrated that the proposed models achieve comparable or better performance
as compared to fully-fledged neural models in multiple evaluation settings. The
source code of all experiments along with models and datasets can be found at
https://github.com/yondivargas/residual-learning-neural-text-creation. This work

We present a comprehensive attention-based bidirectional framework that leverages both forward and backward language models to enhance single-channel speech. Our proposed system utilizes a bidirectional neural network to compensate for the limitations of conventional neural network architectures, which typically focus on processing input sequences in a single direction. By exploring both forward and backward contexts, we can tap into the underlying semantic relationships within a speech utterance. However, challenging issues arise when applying contextual attention across bidirectional sequences, including the risk of primitive meaning loss and difficulties in training the model. To address these concerns, we employed a method that combines the sum of both forward and backward hidden state representations to maintain contextual information. Furthermore, we introduced an auxiliary attention mechanism to facilitate model training and overcome the challenge of speech utterance length. The proposed system was tested on the WSJ0-2mix dataset and demonstrated significant improvements in sentence-wise SE, MI, and SI-SNR, with scores of 20.72, 1.28 bits/channel, and 10.55 dB respectively, indicating a 12.6%, 11.5%, and 2.5 dB improvement respectively to a established baseline. The proposed system was found to be effective even when trained with a relatively small dataset of 5200 utterances, achieving a SI-SNR of 10.55 dB, indicating potential for low-data speech enhancement applications. Yeast serves as a model for studying eukaryotic cellular functions and dysfunctions, given its biochemically similar cellular makeup to humans. However, yeast research has historically been limited to laboratory settings by the necessity for sterile conditions. To overcome this constraint, a novel system has been developed that allows genetically engineered S. cerevisae to colonize decomposing fruit, enabling the study of complex interactions between microbes and their environments in a more natural setting. Building upon this system, an investigation was conducted into the spread of engineered S. cerevisiae through fruit fly populations using 16S rRNA gene sequencing to characterize the microbial communities present on the flies. The study revealed that flies infected with engineered yeast that produce the antibiotic streptomycin are infested with a higher abundance of bacteria associated with the genus Drosophhilus, which is normally found only in small quantities. Further analysis uncovered that this overabundance is caused by the antibiotic's ability to select for bacteria resistant to its effects over time. This study tackles the challenge of developing a learning paradigm that can effectively leverage a massive dataset under minimal labeling expense, specifically the ImageNet dataset, which serves as a foundational dataset for many large-scale learning tasks. Our investigation reveals that existing approaches, although they have reached seemingly optimal performance, still fall short of the mark when compared to human performance. To address this, we propose a novel theory that learning from a large dataset with diverse samples is analogous to combining the knowledge of multiple experts, each representing a specific sub-prototype within the data distribution. Our framework, Dynamic Learning, is an extension of this theory, where a fixed number of sub-prototypes are identified through clustering at the start of each training iteration. This allows for the focusing of expert attention on sub-prototypes with the highest loss scores, resulting in targeted updates of model parameters. Our implementation of this theory in Dynamic Learning, utilizing a straightforward approach with only minor adjustments to existing code, resulted in notable improvements of up to 4.7% in top-1 accuracy and 6.5% in top-5 accuracy when evaluated across multiple ResNets and Inception architectures. Moreover, our method reduces the number of required training iterations by at least 5-fold while achieving comparable or better performance, underscoring its efficiency. Our successful findings across diverse models and evaluations provide a compelling foundation for further research aimed at refining and optimizing Dynamic Learning, with a particular emphasis on exploring more effective clustering strategies and integrating this learning paradigm into unified frameworks for comprehensive evaluation and comparison. Context-aware action recognition is a current focus in computer vision, where the goal is to identify activities within a video by considering both temporal and context-based context. It is challenging because context can be both visual and temporal, as reflected in various real-world applications like activity understanding in daily life, sports analysis, and human behavior analysis. However, these methods often rely on narrowly defined boundary detection algorithms, which can lead to the exclusion of valuable information in surrounding context segments. We introduce a novel collision prevention method that leverages interrobot interactions to create dynamic vector fields, influencing each other's motion through a shared vortex potential landscape. We demonstrate in theory and practice that this approach forces robots to cooperate in avoiding each other, while also accommodating changes in the vortex field due to the creation of a new magnetic field, resulting from the introduction of additional robots. Our experiments, covering both simulated and actual environments, showcase the effectiveness of this method in maintaining cooperative robot behavior in response to external forces and in scenarios with varying vortex field intensity. Moreover, we explore the application of this approach to the creation of robust cooperative patterns of motion, such as circular paths and figure-eights, both in simulation and with real robots, observing that the dynamic vector fields facilitate the achievement of these patterns through the adjustment of the vortex field's parameters. Our method holds promise for the development of high-level cooperative behaviors in robots that rely on mutual magnetic influences to navigate, as well as for the creation of educational robotics lessons that combine code and the study of vector field dynamics. We also explore the potential expansion of this technique to more complex situations by conducting a systematic analysis of the characteristics of vortex fields that support cooperative behavior between magnetic robots, resulting in a playable game that enables human players to design cooperative robot trajectories in response to external forces and in scenarios with varying vortex field intensity. Furthermore, we explore a method for assigning positions to robots based on their place in a sequence, resulting in the creation of a quorum of cooperating robots even when there are multiple robots. We also experiment with both simulated and actual robots with different dynamic vector field patterns, such as gradient fields and fields with magnetic robot asymmetries, resulting in the creation of a design tool for the assignment of positions to robots based on their place in a sequence, leading to the creation of a suite of cooperative patterns, such as circular, figure-eight, and ladder patterns, as well as patterns with robots at rest, patterns with robots moving at different speeds, and patterns with magnetic robot asymmetries, leading to the award of an Academic Excellence Award in Robotics at the 2021 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). Intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) can dynamically change their reflection properties to optimize various wireless systems. We investigate the potential of an IRS to enhance target parameter estimation in a frequency-hopping radar system. We design an optimization framework that leverages the IRS's capabilities to maximize the radar cross-correlation function across multiple frequency hops. We demonstrate analytically that the proposed framework leads to a significant improvement in target parameter estimation, even with limited data. Interestingly, this estimation performance is comparable to a system that uses an ideal perfect reflector, which is theoretically unachievable. We also explore the practical implications of our findings in a simulation scenario. The results show that an IRS-assisted radar system can achieve a 10-20 dB improvement in the signal-to-noise ratio at the radar receiver, resulting in a marked improvement in target detection and a 50-70% reduction in the false alarm rate. Notably, this performance gain is sensitive to the radar frequency, target distance, and IRS resolution. We provide a qualitative analysis of these factors and identify potential design optimizations for an IRS in a radar system. The code for the numerical solutions and the plots is available in an open-source repository. In contrast to their limited performance in offline settings, pre-trained models have shown significant success in online continual learning tasks. This includes achieving low loss values and producing a few misclassified examples during evaluations of sequences that were never seen before. Our research involves testing the fundamental assumption underlying this success - that pre-trained models are necessary for online continual learning. We developed a simple baseline that replaces the backbone of these models with a similar model of the same type, but one that is trained from scratch at each sequence. Our results show this baseline achieves comparable performance to the original models in online continual learning tasks, as measured by loss values and the number of misclassified examples in each sequence. This includes results from rigorous real-world experiments that involve substantial changes in data distributions between sequences. These findings raise important questions about the current evaluation methods used in the field of continual learning. We also highlight the need for more robust evaluation methods that account for natural learning scenarios, where new information is continually added on top of existing knowledge. We hope our research will inspire a shift towards more practical evaluation methods that reflect real-world learning scenarios, alongside the open-source code and datasets available with our study. We conclude by exploring alternative methods that can be used to assess the performance of continual learning models, including those that involve fine-tuning models on sequences that were never seen during training. These methods reveal that the performance of models can be significantly worse when evaluated on sequences that were never seen during training, and this can apply to models trained on just a few examples as well as those trained on larger datasets. We also examine the role of the dataset itself in continual learning, asking whether the natural sequences present in real-world datasets provide sufficient context for continuous learning. We discuss the implications of our findings for other domains that involve continuous learning from natural sequences, and the opportunity that it presents for the development of novel evaluation methods that can capture the unique characteristics of these scenarios. We hope our research will spark a debate that will drive the development of more effective evaluation methods that can capture the unique characteristics of natural learning scenarios, and the code and datasets available with our study are a step in this direction. We investigated the effects of various interactions on 64Ni, specifically combining a mean-field and two-body interaction component. Our research revealed that a combination of the monopole and tensor components played a crucial role in explaining the coexistence phenomenon in 64Ni at zero spin. To validate our findings, we compared them with experimental data from the 32S(16O,32S) reaction. Our results show that the monopole tensor interaction combination significantly contributes to describing the coexistence state, particularly when considering the zero-spin forebody states. Conversely, other interactions fail to adequately account for these states without introducing tensions that could compromise the nucleus' stability. To achieve a satisfactory description of 64Ni without zero-spin states in the forebody and at the spin channel of interest, an excessive four-body interaction component was found to be necessary, resulting in an inelastic threshold that diverges from experimental data. Conversely, the monopole tensor interaction combination successfully describes 64Ni without zero-spin states in the forebody at zero spin without requiring an excessive four-body interaction component, thereby resolving the issue with the inelastic threshold. Notably, the intrinsic strength of the monopole tensor interaction combination lies within the range of in-medium corrections for the tensor interaction, which is approximately 20. For this particular interaction combination, a ratio of forebody and body intrinsically monopole strengths of 1:3 is found to be driving the coexistence in 64Ni. To achieve a satisfactory description of 64Ni without zero-spin states in the forebody at zero spin, the ratio of body intrinsically monopole strengths must be set to 2.8, which is marginally lower than 3. A comparison with 64Co, which does not exhibit the coexistence phenomenon, shows that the ratio of body intrinsically monopole strengths in 64Ni is sufficiently close to that of 64Co to prevent the appearance of zero-spin forebody states in 64Ni. In essence, the present study provides a theoretical justification for zero-spin forebody states in 64Ni driven by the monopole tensor interaction component, which is an essential low-spin phenomenon that demands a precise description in order to establish trust in experimental and theoretical findings. Machine learning models are often assessed using metrics like precision and recall, but their final performance significantly depends on the chosen validation method, especially in natural language processing, where models are easily affected by data splits due to linguistic complexities. As a result, it's essential to select a validation approach that provides a reliable estimate of the model's ability to generalize. In our research, we explored and compared various validation methods, including k-fold cross-validation, to determine how they impact NLP model adjustments. Our experiments demonstrated that j-k fold cross-validation, a lesser-known variation, is an effective way to reduce the variance of evaluation results. This approach is particularly useful for NLP when compared to traditional k-fold cross-validation, due to its simpler evaluation structure which is less prone to system slowdowns. We also found that increasing the number of folds in j-k cross-validation is an acceptable way to balance the variance and computational costs. Our research is ongoing, and we are exploring ways to integrate subword information into the validation method, which could further be applied to adapt pre-trained language models for new datasets. Our findings and research are presented in the paper, and we are open to collaborations and discussions with the community. Despite the progress made, building a knowledge-rich system with a substantial corpus requires an enormous amount of data, which is often obtained through extensive educator-pupil collaborations. This co-learning approach allows for the rapid development of systems that can learn from a range of formats, including real-world interactions, and combines the expertise of multiple educators, leveraging their individual knowledge bases with minimal flaws. This survey delves into various aspects of the educator-pupil framework, examining its applications, the diverse forms of pupil feedback, and the methods employed to tackle several key challenges this framework presents, including how to effectively utilize feedback from multiple pupils, dealing with the potential for low-quality data, and addressing the issue of system bias. We also discuss various ways to evaluate the performance of systems built using this framework and provide examples of systems developed through this method, before concluding with potential avenues for further research in this field. We believe that the educator-pupil framework holds the key to creating systems with a deep understanding of the world similar to human experts, including but not limited to, natural language processing, optical character recognition, and the solving of complex mathematical problems, and as such, it is an area that deserves the attention of both the machine learning and human-computer interaction communities. We hope that this survey will provide a useful foundation for the advancement of this field. A technique of measuring small changes in gas phase density is proposed that utilizes the absorption of a single laser beam by an ultracold strontium cloud. This method has the benefit of operating independently of background influences and the ability to provide continuous, spatially resolved data in response to changes in pressure, temperature, or the concentration of other gases. Key factors affecting this technique's sensitivity and response time are analyzed and it was found that, aside from the density itself, the most significant factors include the scattering of light off heat and atomic collisions within the cloud, the former limiting the technique's application and the latter offering potential for further improvement through the use of species with lower scattering cross-sections and lower atomic collision rates, such as offered by metastable states or near-resonance systems. When shear stress surpasses a certain threshold in a thickened suspension, sudden and drastic changes occur, where particles interlock and the fluid's viscosity skyrocket. This phenomenon is particularly evident in ancient descriptions of "drag thickening," documented in stories about sticky mud impeding progress. Researchers have attempted to explain this behavior through theories of particle aggregation and bridging, but the underlying causes remain unclear despite extensive study. This research seeks to provide a universal explanation by analyzing multiple shear thickening transitions in various polymer solutions and particulate mixtures subjected to high shear rates and observations of particle behavior, ultimately revealing a universal relationship between the size of clusters and shear thickening's critical point, and identifying distinct stages in the transition where particles go from aggregating to fracturing under the influence of shear forces. This newfound understanding offers a clear path for predicting the onset of shear thickening based on a material's composition and structure, and could potentially inform the design of materials with controlled properties of shear thickening and unbinding. This research is further validated through simulations of particle behavior, and the discovery of cluster fracturing is shown to contribute to the re-emergence of shear thinning following the transition, suggesting a more detailed examination of this transition using in-situ imaging of particle behavior would provide valuable insights into the complex dynamics at play. This research opens up possibilities for improving existing materials and discovering new applications for materials exhibiting shear thickening under high stress, such as stress waves in fluids, like ocean impacts or sonic waves in liquids, and could also contribute to better understanding and modeling of complex phenomena in materials science. This research is also relevant to fluid dynamics in everyday situations, such as mud's behavior during natural disasters or the flow of fluids with suspended particles in pipelines, and could inform strategies for scaling up laboratory experiments to replicate the behavior of materials in larger, more complex settings, like the flow of blood in human veins. We have derived a general mathematical formula to calculate the probability of detecting a certain energy range in a detector with a specific orientation, taking into account the incident direction of the WIMP and scattering angle. We investigated public opinion regarding a current event through a simulation of another event that occurred in the past, using a methodology that incorporates random sampling for search engine queries. Our approach involved asking 1500 participants from around the world to evaluate the relevance of 150 diverse search engine queries in relation to 9 different scenarios that were designed to be similar in nature to Wikipedia's featured articles' presentation style. Our research revealed that users' ability to detect important information is limited by their perception, with a significant disparity in detecting important information when comparing a generalized search engine to one that is personalized, such as Google's web search. Specifically, users were only able to detect 54.6% of the important information in searches that were personalized, in comparison to 71.5% in searches that were not personalized. We also found that users were more prone to relying on Wikipedia's biased information when the search results were personalized, in comparison to when the search results were not personalized. Our research provides experimental evidence for the significant impact of search engine personalization on the detection of important information, with a loss of up to 17% due to this personalization, with implications for the dissemination of biased information on the web. Furthermore, our research highlights the difficulty in assessing the impact of this personalization, with a loss of at least 12% that cannot be measured. Our research was conducted in collaboration with over 2000 search engines in 32 different languages, with a high level of consistency in the results. Our research has significant implications for the dissemination of biased information on the web, with potential solutions being the use of alternative search engines that are less prone to personalization, such as DuckDuckGo, or the development of methods that can account for this personalization, with a margin of error of up to 17%. Specifically, it focuses on the development of an approach to creating controller systems that can operate within predetermined safety boundaries, even when faced with unexpected external forces. These safety boundaries are defined in advance based on the system's characteristics and are represented by a specific geometric shape. The proposed controller system leverages Control Barrier Functions, which are an established concept, and builds upon previous work by introducing a method to create these functions using critical values from the system's equilibrium points, allowing for the incorporation of external forces that affect the system's dynamics. However, this research further identifies the limitation of previous work based on this approach, which assumes that the availability of state feedback is a given condition, thereby neglecting the practical challenge of ensuring the system's state is observable. Consequently, this research introduces the concept of partially observable secure control using a simplified model that is based on the system's most observable state variables, which are chosen based on the critical values of the system's equilibrium points. This approach is referred to as an Input Restricted Control Barrier Function. This research focuses on the container shipping industry, where it aims to create a comprehensive and integrated dataset consisting of freight rate, shipping volume, new ship prices, secondhand ship prices, and scrap prices from 1966 to present. Although it has become more manageable to access individual datasets through established sources, there is currently no unified platform offering a broad range of industry metrics over an extended time period. To address this gap, our team has collected and integrated 57 years' worth of data spanning from 1966 to 2022, utilizing five different sources and developing customized extraction algorithms to ensure a high level of accuracy. This integrated dataset holds great potential for researchers to explore various research questions and validate established models, as well as providing an opportunity for novel model testing and validation, such as state-of-the-art machine learning models and deep reinforcement learning frameworks, against real-world industry data and scenarios. To maintain data integrity and accessibility, this integrated dataset will be continuously updated and made available through a publicly accessible repository for the benefit of academic and industrial communities. In addition, our research includes initial analysis and verification of multiple industry hypotheses using our integrated dataset, along with a discussion on future research directions and potential areas for improvement. This integrated dataset addresses fundamental industry questions and sets the stage for novel research to address pressing industry challenges and concerns in the container transportation industry. Finally, our research demonstrates the value of collaborative data collection and the significance of accessible and unified industry datasets for both academic and industrial communities. As a result, this integrated dataset will be made available under the Creative Commons license to facilitate the development of future industry datasets in an analogous manner. This research is a model for creating and maintaining unified industry datasets in an analogous fashion, and it is our hope that it will inspire the creation of additional industry datasets with equal scope and breadth. This research is further accompanied by an accompanying code repository available at: https://github.com/kuang33/Unified-Container-Transport-Industry-Data. This code repository provides a comprehensive code framework that is compatible with both RStudio and Python, and it includes a detailed data collection and validation code framework. This code framework is designed to be transparent, reproducible, and easily adaptable for both academic and industrial communities. We've introduced the concept of fabric spaces as a unified framework for polyhedral cell complexes, and demonstrated its utility by drawing on its connections to regressive simplicial structures. This framework facilitates a natural integration of ideas from both areas. In this work, we explore how fabric spaces can be used to generalize the concept of simplicial complexes with the simplicial collapse property, and we provide an accessible overview of key definitions and results in this area. A primary focus is on Simpson's theorem regarding the simplicial collapse property, and on an enhancement of his result to fabric spaces of any degree. Our proof of this generalized result makes use of nondegenerate simplicial structures within the context of degenerate simplicial complexes. Additionally, we present an illustration of a family of projective simplicial spaces with collapsing structures that are compatible with their action on the projective plane, and we establish a connection between the sphere spectrum and the simplicial collapse property. Further research directions are also identified. Introductory materials and key results can be found in the provided appendices. Ultimately, this work aims to inspire others to explore the realm of changing triangulations. We invite readers to join us in this mathematical journey. Recent breakthroughs in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been driven by large-scale, extensively labeled datasets. Nonetheless, the cost of such data in terms of labeling expense and data quality poses a significant challenge. One possible solution to this issue is sparsely labeled supervised learning, where only a limited number of labels are assigned to each sample. To achieve this, reducing the number of labels required for each sample is crucial. In this paper, we introduce an innovative technique called labeled subgraph sparsification, where only critical subgraphs with labels are identified within each sample. Labeled node embeddings in these subgraphs are then combined to form the final representation. We propose an algorithm called LSS, which systematically identifies these critical subgraphs through a process of iterative refinement. LSS is a general framework that can be integrated with various GNN models. Our experiments demonstrate that LSS leads to a substantial reduction in labeling costs while maintaining or improving model performance, compared to baseline GNN models, especially in datasets with limited annotation data. The LSS framework is particularly effective at designating unlabeled nodes in each sample as irrelevant, thereby further reducing labeling expenses. Our results also highlight the sparsity achieved by LSS, where only 7-20% of nodes in each sample require labels, depending on the dataset. A notable aspect of LSS is its ability to produce interpretable models by focusing on critical subgraphs. These subgraphs often form dense clusters with significant semantic meaning, as evidenced by our experiments and qualitative analysis. We have made LSS available on GitHub at https://github.com/your-link, and our code has been incorporated into the PyTorch framework. Moreover, an extended version of this paper, including additional details and results, can be found at https://your-arxiv-link.com. Furthermore, a recorded presentation of this paper at the ICLR 2023 workshop titled "Interpretable Machine Learning for Graphs" is available at https://your-video-link.com. Finally, we have designed an LSS-App available at https://your-app-link.com that facilitates the generation of sparsely labeled graphs for evaluation and testing of GNN models. This app allows users to easily create and manage their own graph datasets with LSS and provides a user-friendly interface to configure LSS settings and model performance assessments using well-known GNN evaluation metrics. A recent study by Cotler et al., established an lower bound indicating that any linear sketch with arbitrary dimension $d$ necessitates $\Omega(d)$ storage to accurately estimate the $l_2$ norm of a vector sequence under certain conditions. This research builds upon Cotler et al.'s findings by examining various scenarios involving vector sequences with distinct characteristics. Specifically, we investigate the feasibility of estimating $X^{\dot 2}_n$ and $X^{\dot 4}_n$ with high probability, expanding upon the foundational assumptions and benchmarks set by Cotler et al. Our contributions include a demonstration that, even in the presence of relatively diverse vector sequences, it is possible to accurately estimate the $l_2$ norm using a single dimension $d=O(1)$, whereas in the case of sequences with similar directions, Cotler et et's upper bound $d=O(\sqrt{k \log 1/\delta})$ is already established. Additionally, we examine novel applications involving streaming data with adaptivity levels $p=3/2$, $p=2$, and $p=4$, and novel storage requirements in such scenarios. Our research provides upper and lower bounds for the storage needs of sketching algorithms in various adaptive data settings, with implications for the viability of several techniques used in recent discoveries in streaming data analysis. These discoveries include the estimation of matrix norms, the computation of fast tail bounds, and the analysis of high-probability events in random sketching systems. Lastly, we outline potential future research directions for the information-theoretic limits in streaming data analysis and the associated upper and lower bounds. These directions encompass novel applications in streaming data analysis, new types of sketches, new data characteristics, new dimensions of adaptivity, and novel estimators and testing procedures. We hope that this research will serve as a catalyst for further exploration of these topics in streaming data analysis. Building on our previous research, we established the Convergence Theorem to address compact, singular areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature. This study extends the crucial Corollary 1.4 from that work, allowing us to efficiently remove singular points within a manifold of positive scalar curvature, given certain mild boundaries. This, in turn, enables us to develop a novel decomposition for manifolds of positive scalar curvature, encompassing all conformal structures derived from a given hyperbolic structure. This, in particular, solves the Leeb's problem. Additionally, our convergence theorem facilitates an analysis of the moduli space for compact, singular hyperbolic manifolds, particularly those with negative Euler characteristic, allowing us to prove that it consists of a single point. This outcome may be viewed through the lens of a question posed by Minicozzi. Lastly, we also explore the situation for manifolds of positive scalar curvature with a given conformal structure that is derived from a hyperbolic structure, and demonstrate that the dimension of the moduli space for such manifolds is less than the dimension of the space of hyperbolic structures by exactly $4$. This achievement is also expressed through the language of a question posed by Minicozzi.

As a result, there is a risk that heated plasma will develop a significant entropy due to turbulence, ultimately leading to a instability in magnetic stabilization. This research focuses on a different approach, where highly conductive plasma is replaced with neutral superfluid $^4$He, providing an advantage of being able to manipulate vortex structures using external magnetic field without interference. Future smart grids will rely heavily on high-speed learning and real-time control systems that adapt quickly to changing conditions. Dynamically scaling and optimizing variable generation and storage units within an area are inherently complex tasks that typically require significant data. However, current predictive control methods lack the ability to learn from and adapt to new data in real-time, limiting their effectiveness in these environments. This paper introduces a groundbreaking approach called Real-Time (RT) aggregate adaptability, a first in the field of learning-driven predictive control. By leveraging advanced machine learning algorithms, specifically neural network-based methods, and incorporating their updates into a robust optimization framework, we can efficiently utilize historical and real-time data to refine the performance of individual units in real-time. This results in enhanced system performance, with potential gains of up to 25% in certain scenarios. We demonstrate the efficacy of this innovation with experimental results from an integrated simulation of a smart grid system, featuring 20 variable generation and storage units, and show that it can handle high-frequency updates with minimal computational costs. We introduce SCATTER, a cutting-edge theoretical framework for studying binary systems with highly distorted companions, specifically focusing on x-ray binaries and black hole candidates with accretion discs that are not fully circularized. This innovative model builds upon established shared-envelope frameworks like the Roelofs et al. formalism and Jansen's formalism, improving their performance by incorporating second-order relativistic corrections and enhanced viscosous dissipation effects. SCATTER's unique features include a more precise treatment of gravitational waves, a revised estimate of mass accretion rates, and a dynamic thermal timescale for mass accretion, all derived from an adiabatic conservation principle. Additionally, SCATTER offers a wider range of possible mass transfer modes and a more nuanced description of spin-orbit interactions. By providing a more detailed description of the distortions, spins, and mass transfer patterns, SCATTER aims to bridge the gap between binary system dynamics and spectral observations, and is available for further development at https://github.com/alexjamesarmstrong/SCATTER. A critical aspect in developing numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a long history of investigating and devising preservation techniques for various properties such as maximum principles, entropy, and potential-based properties. Although these preservation methods can be very effective, they often come with a significant drawback: they significantly slow down the convergence of time-stepping methods. As a result, the discretized solutions only accurately represent the preserved property over a limited number of time steps. To address this issue, it is essential to accelerate the convergence of time-stepping methods by employing high-order structure-preserving discretizations. However, even with these advanced discretizations, the convergence of the methods can still be impeded by non-hydrodynamic slow modes, such as oscillatory wave components, especially in problems involving multiple scales. To address this challenge, a new approach is proposed that involves preconditioning time-stepping methods to target specific frequency bands influenced by the physical properties of the equations. By controlling the frequency of the solution within a given range, it becomes possible to accelerate the convergence of the methods by an order of magnitude without sacrificing the preservation of physical properties. This new approach is demonstrated through numerical experiments on a nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and the results show a substantial improvement in computational efficiency by at least an order of magnitude compared to existing structure-preserving methods. We've investigated the early stages of star formation in low-metallicity molecular clouds using a new generation of sophisticated galaxy simulations. Our analysis reveals a previously overlooked category of low-mass star formation, characterized by localized and grain-based explosions in dense interstellar gas. These local explosions, also referred to as "dusty supernovae," occur when internal pressures cause a critical mass of dust to ignite in a compact molecular cloud, combusting any nearby gas. "Dusty SNe" then propel high-velocity gas streams and small dust particles into their surrounding environment, providing a potential explanation for the observed dust particle growth in early star-forming regions. A notable finding in our research is the coexistence of dusty and SN-like explosions in molecular clouds, with approximately 30% of low-metallicity cloud simulations exhibiting both phenomena. A notable subset of these includes "dusty SNe" that fail to eject significant amounts of gas at high velocities, contributing to the overall dust mass in their parent cloud. These additional dust deposits then create an environment ripe for further explosive events, suggesting a positive feedback loop in low-metallicity cloud formations. Our study also uncovers an interesting disparity in SN explosion patterns based on the metal content of the cloud, with "dusty SNe" dominating in low-metallicity settings (comprising 50% of all explosions) and "core-collapsions" and "dusty SNe" equally prevalent in more metal-rich clouds (each making up 40-50% of all explosions). Our analysis suggests a shift in SN explosion types with decreasing metal content, and proposes a possible explanation for the observed discrepancy in galaxy-wide SN explosion rates and star formation rates. Finally, our research highlights an interesting dust accumulation phenomenon in low-metallicity cloud formations, with "dusty SNe" contributing a significant portion of the total dust mass in these environments, a portion that could be substantial enough to support further explosive events, and potentially even facilitate the formation of heavy elements in a subsequent "dusty SN" event, such as in the creation of barium in SSM-18.11. Additionally, our analysis indicates a significant increase in small dust particle growth as a result of "dusty SNe," a phenomenon that could be a major contributor to the overall dust particle growth in low-metallicity star-forming regions. Our analysis also reveals a significant correlation between small dust particle growth and the high-velocity ejection of gas streams in molecular cloud formations, and highlights an interesting discrepancy in small dust particle growth patterns based on the metal content

Detecting three-dimensional objects at a distance is a challenging task, mainly because distant objects appear small in images and often go undetected by conventional two-dimensional bounding boxes used in 2D detection methods. To address this issue, researchers typically employ three-dimensional bounding boxes to capture the spatial dimensions of distant objects more effectively. However, the standard dataset augmentation techniques used in 2D detection, such as rotation and flipping, can disrupt the spatial relationships represented in 3D boxes, thus hindering the detection of distant objects. To tackle this issue, the authors propose a novel far-three-dimensional detection task that focuses on identifying distant three-dimensional objects and develop an end-to-end far-three-dimensional detection framework called Far3Det, tailored to excel in this task. In their study, the authors significantly boost the three-dimensional detection performance for objects at a distance by breaking boundaries and demonstrating the practical implications of far-three-dimensional detection in real-world applications. To facilitate further research on this task, the authors release Far3Det at https://github.com/leimao/Far3Det. To validate the effectiveness of their approach, the authors conduct comprehensive far-three-dimensional detection experiments under the Far3Det setup on the KITTI dataset, resulting in the introduction of a new benchmark called NuScenes Far3Det subset. According to their findings, the existing three-dimensional detection methods fail to generalize to distant objects, thus providing an opportunity for methodological innovations that could potentially enhance the detection of near-three-dimensional objects as well. To this end, the authors propose the Far3Det leaderboard at https://www.leimao.com/far3det-leaderboard/ for both KITTI and NuScenes datasets to encourage the development of novel methods that can handle the far-three-dimensional detection task. To further explore the characteristics of far-three-dimensional detection, the authors conduct an in-depth analysis of the dataset, pointing out the need for more rigorous evaluations that consider not only the three-dimensional detection performance but also the distance metric to ensure the method generalizes well to distant objects. To this end, they introduce the distance-aware detection evaluation metric called DA-AP, which considers both the precision and distance of detected three-dimensional objects, thus providing a more comprehensive assessment of a method's ability to identify distant three-dimensional objects. Chemical reactions research is a critical area where chemistry meets physics, statistics, and mathematics. Due to the high computational costs associated with them, simulations are typically limited to simple systems like hydrogen halides. Recent breakthroughs in quantum computing, specifically the development of the parameterized quantum circuit learning approach, have made it possible to efficiently train quantum circuits using classical machine learning techniques. This paper demonstrates the ability to accurately predict the ground states of molecules like water and methane using this method, even when classical descriptions fail. Unlike traditional configuration interaction methods which are computationally expensive, the proposed framework can handle 100-300 orbitals with relative ease, making it an exciting step towards simulating chemical reactions with quantum circuits. The paper also shows that the learning of these circuits is robust, even when started with random configurations, and that the proposed framework can be used to create quantum circuits that are comparable to experimental observables, potentially paving the way for the development of simulation-based chemical reaction discovery through optimization of these circuits. Due to the small number of controllable qubits in current quantum computers, the paper discusses the potential of applying this approach to nuclear data reconstruction, a related problem involving large numbers but with measurement equipment rather than fundamental processes, and suggests that it may be more feasible than chemical reaction simulations. The paper is concluded by discussing the progress made and the challenges that need to be addressed, particularly the limited availability of data for molecules like water and methane, and highlights future research directions for both theoretical and experimental studies. The paper is a extended version of the authors' previous presentation at the 2022 Quantum Learning Conference. The data used in this paper is now available at https://zenodo.org/record/5814401. The code for the machine learning framework is available at https://github.com/quantummachinelearning/pqc-learning. A significant challenge in neuroimaging analysis involves aligning brain surfaces due to their irregular shapes and large degree of variability. Large-scale evaluations under controlled conditions and real-world applications have yielded promising results with our method outperforming industry standards in accuracy and computational performance. Most modern scene flow methods start with metric learning, establishing a metric that helps match points across images and a video sequence. These metrics are often derived from pre-trained models, which can introduce biases. Additionally, such approaches may over-rely on neighboring information in other images, potentially compromising flow estimation near image boundaries. To address these limitations, this research proposes a novel framework for learning scene flow in a way that minimizes dependence on external information. An adversarial metric is designed to match points within a single scene depth, using a comparison module that assesses a custom dissimilarity measure. This measure, L2-DIF, accounts for both directional and isotropic disparities, which are estimated simultaneously as unknown side effects of matching points under this metric. To prevent the model from leaning on neighboring pixels in other images, a refinement module is introduced, using the adversarial metric to guide the estimation of missing pixels. Notably, this module skips interpolation, instead using the match score to decide which pixels to prioritize. To train the model, both a flow generator and a refinement module are trained in an unsupervised manner using a scene flow dataset. Evaluations using the Lytro Light Field dataset show that our approach matches or outperforms state-of-the-art scene flow methods despite not utilizing external neighbor information or pre-trained models. System implementations and code are also made available online. Furthermore, this research introduces an innovative metric learning method called adversarial metric learning for self-guided scene flow estimation, demonstrating the potential for generalization to other density estimation tasks. As a result, an expanded version of this work, focused on density estimation rather than scene flow, has been published as a separate paper at ICCV 2021 under the name Self-Guided Density Estimation via Adversarial Metric Learning. This paper introduces a new approach called Timeloops, an automated system call filtering technique tailored for secure and high-performance Linux kernel implementations. Building upon existing work, such as seccomp and AppArmor, Timeloops targets containerized microservices and enables them to operate independently, without external input, by leveraging machine learning to determine system call policies. In a demonstration, Timeloops successfully learned and applied system call filters to multiple benchmarking scenarios, including CPUCylinic, XBT, and Redis, across various containerized microservices, achieving a 99% accuracy rate in compliance with predetermined specifications and exhibiting a 1.5 to 3.5 times performance gain compared to optimized secure protocols, such as seccomp-generate. The source code for Timeloops has been made open-source and is available for review. In addition, an upcoming section will outline methods for integrating Timeloops with existing security frameworks and discuss potential areas for enhancement and future research in this area. To address the current observational data, we incorporate a $B-L$ extension into the Standard Model, introducing three right-handed neutrinos whose Nambu-Goldstone bosons are linked to the breaking of $U(1)_{B-L}$. Gauging the $B-L$ force allows for a control of the little Higgses' masses, thus preventing their rapid decaays. Within a viable range for the $B-L$ gauge boson, we explore the possibility of dark matter existence, focusing on a pseudo-Goldstone boson DM scenario. This occurs when the complex scalar, resulting from $B-L$ symmetry, is situated at a point near the parabolic minimum of the potential. We then analyze the constraints from Higgs physics and LEP, as well as the Thompson scattering, LHC direct production, and collosion at LHC and dark matter creation facilities in a comprehensive analysis of our model. We find that a mass range of $164 < \text{GeV} < 833$ is permissible for the pseudo-Goldstone DM, with its production influenced by the $B-L$ force, distinguishing it from the conventional DM models. As a result, even within the most constrained parameter space, our model is capable of replicating the standard model's primary features and achieving a viable, dark matter-dominated closure of the universe. Furthermore, we identify the signature $\text{mono}-\text{Higgs}$ at LHC and ILC, offering a potential for this model to be tested in the future experiments. With the current research, we are able to predict up to 10% of total Thompson scattering cross-section at a planned future electron-proton collider with 100/500 GeV and 0.5/5 TeV, corresponding to 0.5/25 fb. Historical sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with many countries employing various forms of sundials that adapted to their local time standards and environmental conditions. Despite offering practical solutions for determining local time, sundials in Indonesia during the colonial period were often overshadowed by the use of European-style clocks and time standards. As a result of this substitution, many Indonesian sundials from that era have likely been lost over time, making it essential to document any surviving sundials to gain insight into Indonesia's past cultural and scientific developments. This study focuses on constructing a standard method for determining the original time standard of Indonesian sundials, particularly those from the pre-colonial era, using a historical water clock and a sundial collection in Yogyakarta as reference points. To validate this approach, researchers applied it to several sundials in Indonesia, Yogyakarta, and Malaysia, producing results that suggest these timekeepers standardized local time according to the Islamic calendar, with some adapting to the solar time standard used in European clocks introduced during the colonial period. This research is an initial step towards creating a comprehensive database of Indonesian sundials and their time standards, along with any associated historical information, which could contribute to a deeper understanding and preservation of Indonesia's cultural and scientific heritage. This project, titled Suryakala-Nusantara, invites contributions and collaborations from historians, clock and sundial experts, and other stakeholders to further develop this historical database and document any surviving sundials in Indonesia and other Southeast Asian countries. This initiative also presents an opportunity to explore the relationship between sundials, time standards, and cultural developments across the region, with a focus on Indonesia. This study is an expansion of a previous project presented at the 2019 Meeting of the East Asian and Southeast Asian Section of the International Astronomical Union, with an accompanying video available at https://youtu.be/zwQ2D2K0TgA. A cutting-edge Intellect Reflecting Surface (IRS) is proposed that utilizes integrated information and energy resources to support D2D communications in an integrated information and energy network. This D2D communication model is complex and dynamic, influenced by various factors including an integrated information and energy flow constraint, an energy harvesting constraint, integrated information and energy functions for D2D users, and a passive IRS with limited pre-store energy. To optimize the D2D information transfer rate, we develop an optimization problem that takes into account the IRS's limited energy and the dynamic nature of the D2D users. By applying an optimization method and an information and energy flow theorem, we obtain a key inequality that enables us to design an efficient dynamic power splitting and precoding scheme for the D2D users. A suboptimal solution is derived based on this inequality, and we demonstrate through simulation that our proposed solution yields a transfer rate that is close to 90% of the optimal solution. Furthermore, the solution considers various practical scenarios, including an IRS with no energy constraints and an D2D communication model without energy harvesting. The results show that an IRS with no energy constraints can increase the transfer rate by up to 300% compared to an IRS with energy constraints, and that there is an optimal energy storage level for the D2D users that balances the energy harvesting and storage levels. The study provides a dynamic power splitting and precoding solution that can increase the transfer rate by up to 150% compared to a static solution. The results also demonstrate the significant impact of the D2D users' initial information levels on the transfer rate, and the study identifies an optimal initial information level for each D2D user. The study addresses several open research issues, including the optimization of D2D communication in an IRS-based integrated information and energy network with multiple access points and the development of dynamic power splitting and precoding solutions for D2D communication in an IRS-based integrated information and energy network with an orthogonal multiple access (OMA) D2D user. The study is the first to investigate the dynamic power splitting and precoding of an IRS with an information and energy flow constraint, an energy harvesting constraint, and an OMA D2D user in an integrated information and energy network. The study is relevant to the development of next-generation wireless communication systems, and the results provide a dynamic power splitting and precoding solution that can increase the transfer rate by up to 150% compared to a static solution. The study is an important contribution to the field of wireless communication

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. They fail to effectively capture the underlying rhythmic structures and pitch variations present in continuous speech. To address this limitation, a new approach called MaskedDialogue has been developed, combining speech synthesis with a masking technique to consider contextual elements. By masking random segments in the input speech, the model learns to generate not only the unmasked portion but also the underlying contextual features of the next sentence. As a result, MaskedDialogue successfully captures the rhythmic structures and pitch variations of continuous speech. Experimental evaluations revealed that this context-aware synthesis method significantly outperforms the control model in terms of mean opinion score (MOS) and reduction in pitch variation. Furthermore, MaskedDialogue demonstrates pitch and rhythmic superiority when comparing MOS with human raters for both read and spontaneous speech. With minimal additional parameters, MaskedDialogue achieves notable enhancements over the standard synthesis model. To facilitate reproducibility, the model and data used in these experiments are available for download at https://github.com/LOLPenguin/MaskedDialogue. Additionally, a video presentation of MaskedDialogue is available at https://youtu.be/6Q5sL4t6JQo. Experimental results indicate that MaskedDialogue delivers a 20% improvement in mean opinion score (MOS) and a 25% reduction in pitch variation when compared to the baseline model. As for rhythmic accuracy, MaskedDialogue achieves a 10% increase in correct ratings. It is essential to note that while MaskedDialogue demonstrates substantial gains, the evaluation was conducted using a limited dataset and therefore more research is needed to validate these findings with a more substantial data set. We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that combines a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state. Building on this, we classify the solitary wave state as either spectrally or orbitally stable in a broad anharmonic potential context, where we compare the potential's local and nonlocal forms. Additionally, we establish conditions for the existence of integral equations that define orbital stability, under both sub-symmetric and symmetric cases, as well as examine how the anharmonic potential's specific form influences the solution's behavior. A key aspect of our approach involves transforming the problem into a Hamiltonian system and utilizing a conserved quantity to close the map for the integral equation. A notable finding from our analysis is that, in certain cases where the anharmonic potential complies with Klein-Gordon field equations' symmetry properties, we can devise a more streamlined approach for determining stability.
