We introduce a new framework for Dungeon Masters (DMs) that incorporates artificial intelligence, allowing it to guide player characters through a fantasy world similar to the one described in the Dungeons and Dragons game. This fantasy world is represented by a set of interconnected locations, each with its own rules governing combat and puzzle-solving. The DM's role is to lead the players by describing the setting, presenting challenges, and providing clues to overcome obstacles, all while remaining true to the game's narrative. To achieve this, we developed an approach called the "Handbook Method," which involves breaking down the game into manageable parts and teaching each one as a separate task using machine learning. By segmenting the game into locations and training separate models for each one, we can easily add new content by simply incorporating the rules governing that particular setting. This allows the game to scale more effectively. To better understand how players think about the game, we also conducted a series of interviews with D&D players, focusing on their thoughts about the game's narrative, which we refer to as their "Theory-of-Mind." These insights helped us refine the framework, particularly the way the game responds to player actions, which we call their "Intents." By considering both the DM's actions and the player's Intents, we were able to create a more dynamic game that takes into account both sides, which we discuss along with our interview data, which reveals the value of incorporating a DM's perspective when designing games of this type. This is the first comprehensive approach to creating games that involve a leader who interacts with the players in a narrative way, and as such, it has the potential to inspire new areas of research in the field of interactive storytelling. We have successfully applied this framework to the game world we created, which features a range of combat and puzzle-solving challenges, and have made the code for the game available online. Additionally, we have developed an open-source version of the framework that allows human DMs to create their own game worlds using a set of pre-defined rules and locations, which has shown great promise in real-world testing. This has led to a new type of game that is more dynamic and engaging than traditional computer games, which we have validated through a series of user studies. Similar task domains share similar meanings for many words with the same context, enabling us to categorize words based on their meanings in relation to each other. Advanced machine learning models can automatically classify contextual settings by identifying related words with the same context. Notably, they can also gauge the differences between words with distinct contexts, essentially mapping words based on their semantic relationships. However, there is a significant gap between their capacity to classify based on context and their ability to analyze word meanings in isolation. Recent studies suggest that words with similar semantic properties should also exhibit similar patterns when used in sentences. Building on this idea, we propose a method for discovering semantic shifts in words by comparing their respective contextual patterns. We applied this method to three large datasets, where we identified previously unknown semantic shifts and verified its effectiveness through user feedback and quality assessment. To address this limitation, we introduce the Phrasal Counterfactual Generation (PCFG) task, which demands the models to generate alternative phrases based on given contexts. However, existing evaluation metrics for PCFG prove to be unsatisfactory due to their reliance on human-labeled data and inability to assess the factual accuracy of the generated content. In response, we've developed a new metric called the Factual Accuracy Score (FAS), which assesses the factual correctness of both the original and counterfactual phrases in relation to each other. With FAS in hand, we found that the current state-of-the-art language models perform only marginally better than a random counterfactual generator. To further advance the field, we've also introduced the Discrete Counterfactual Retrieval (DCR) task, which involves searching for counterfactual phrases from a given context, a task that distinguishes itself from existing retrieval tasks by the absence of a matching true counterfactual in the database. We've established a public dataset for both PCFG and DCR tasks and conducted comprehensive experiments to demonstrate the superiority of models that specialize in these tasks over general-purpose language models. Our research offers valuable insights for the community on designing architectures that can succeed at counterfactual tasks through the limited exploration of different models and the data they were trained on. Our findings suggest that the best models for these tasks are those that have been trained on vast amounts of data without being designed with counterfactual expertise, which is in line with the principle of minimalism in natural language processing. Microinjection techniques offer a promising means of delivering therapeutic genes into the cytoplasm of host cells. By delivering a high concentration of molecules directly into the cell, it may be possible to overcome viral vector limitations. A computational model has been developed to simulate the injection of ideal polymer plugs into host cells, with varying parameters such as viscosity, concentration, and cell shape affecting the outcome. Analysis of this model reveals that optimal delivery profiles depend on cell size, with under-filled cells receiving a higher concentration of polymers, and over-filled cells receiving a higher concentration of solvents. A dimensionless number, the ratio of cell resistance to injection resistance, appears to govern delivery profiles by controlling the flow of solvent and polymer. This model can be applied to both cylindrical and spherical cells, with the latter requiring a more complex analysis due to inward flow during the filling process. By understanding the ideal polymer plug delivery profile, researchers can make informed decisions about the composition of injection fluids, taking advantage of the model's prediction that over-filled cells receive a higher concentration of solvents, which could potentially be exchanged with therapeutic molecules. This could lead to the development of more efficient delivery fluids, with a higher solute-to-solvent ratio, as well as the possibility of introducing air into injection needles, which could further increase delivery efficiency. This model provides a foundation for exploring real-world injection profiles, which are likely to be more complex due to factors such as needle geometry and injection speed, with the possibility of applying principles from fluid dynamics to improve microinjection techniques. This model may also be relevant to other applications involving the injection of fluids into confined spaces, such as the delivery of therapeutic proteins in tendons. Traditional machine learning algorithms rely on accurately classified training examples to effectively learn from data. However, in many real-world applications, especially those with a large number of potential labels, such as YAGO, Visual Genome, or WordNet, obtaining individual instance labels can be extremely costly. Conversely, collecting a single positive label for a given target and obtaining negative labels for every other potential label is relatively inexpensive. Building on this observation, this paper introduces Multi-Single Positive Extraction (Multi-SPE) a new framework that leverages this kind of partially labeled data at reduced cost to facilitate machine learning. We demonstrate the efficacy of Multi-SPE by applying it to the context of multi-instance machine learning via a specific example, specifically by developing a 10-class dataset derived from YAGO called ALOCI, and comparing its performance to a method using traditionally collected labels. The results show that machine learning models trained on partially labeled data perform as well as those trained on fully labeled data in some cases, or even better in others. The code for this study has been made available online at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/aloci. This new framework and the associated data can also be useful for evaluating the robustness of future machine learning models to data sampling schemes. The ALOCI data sets can be found at https://www.dropbox.com/s/6y6s5g0s0zg1x6x/aloci.zip?dl=0. We then identify an equivalence that establishes a connection between the category's physical state representations and common mathematical descriptions of these states. This equivalence is expressed through a categorical relationship, or functor, which enables us to derive the standard, mathematical representations of physical states directly from the category's intrinsic properties and relationships. Conversely, we can derive the category's state representations and their inherent characteristics from these mathematical descriptions. This connection is so seamless that it can be captured by a categorical relationship that is both comprehensive and bi-directional, effectively capturing the essence of the equivalence that exists between the category's state representations and the standard, mathematical descriptions of these states. This way, we can either rely on the category's intrinsic properties and characteristics to derive the states' representations, or we can use the category's state representations and their underlying characteristics to derive the standard, mathematical descriptions of these states. This approach has a broader implication as it suggests that the relationship between the category's state representations and the standard, mathematical descriptions of these states can be governed by a set of fundamental principles, or rules, which are more fundamental than the specific characteristics of the states themselves. This further implies that any attempt to modify or adjust these states would necessarily involve a corresponding adjustment to the category's state representations and characteristics as well. This, in turn, raises an intriguing philosophical question about the nature of physical reality, which is now perceived as being composed of two distinct components: the underlying, abstract structure that gives rise to the states' characteristics and the specific, concrete instances that embody these characteristics. This new perspective on physical reality suggests that it is derived from two interconnected aspects: the abstract structure that provides its underlying framework and the individual instances that make up its concrete, constituent parts. This, in turn, is analogous to the concept of statuses and observables in quantum systems, where the former is derived from the latter, or, in the words of Dirac, "the physical facts correspond to the abstract structure, while the concrete instances correspond to the specific choices of gauge". This new interpretation of physical reality is an abstract concept that is applicable across all quantum systems, regardless of their underlying structure or composition. This study addresses the challenge of achieving optimal portfolio performance by solving an established problem - the mean-variance portfolio optimization - using a method that divides assets into distinct groups based on their historical returns. A key feature of this approach is the use of a simple and effective technique for grouping assets, which is rooted in the theory of portfolio performance and can be applied in a variety of settings, including those with large numbers of assets and stocks with multiple factors. A demonstration of this method's effectiveness is shown in an analysis of S&P 500 historical data, which yields results that align with those produced by more complex methods while providing a practical framework for creating and managing portfolios. A Python-based implementation of this method is available on GitHub under the name crosssect. Given its performance and practical applications, it is considered a suitable alternative to industry-standard methods for creating and managing portfolios. A further development of this method is presented in an extension called crosssect2, which builds upon existing knowledge and delivers even better results, along with a revised grouping technique that incorporates an alternative method for dividing assets into groups. This new method demonstrates improved performance in both in-sample and out-of-sample data sets, along with a step-by-step guide for creating and managing portfolios using both crosssect and crosssect2. To overcome this, we present FedHealth, a pioneering framework for federated learning that leverages transfer learning to efficiently train models for wearable medical devices by harnessing data from diverse, unsynchronized datasets from various users. FedHealth combines two key innovations: (1) a method for synchronizing data from disparate datasets and (2) a robust model that capitalizes on unsynchronized, labeled data from each user to facilitate federated learning. The success of ML in the automated software testing industry has been evident, but a more far-reaching goal awaits - an end-to-end, fully automated development process that starts with programming basics and produces working software applications. This paper's authors have developed a system that allows non-technical users to create their own programs by offering a simple, intuitive interface for specifying application functions. This system, leveraging ML algorithms, translates these specifications into reliable code using type-inference and a specialized programming language designed for safety and efficiency. To ensure production-quality code, the system includes a performance optimization feature that eliminates unnecessary operations and a security component to prevent common vulnerabilities. By testing these features with real-world applications, the system has demonstrated its ability to create efficient, secure, and high-performance code from specifications, resulting in code that performs as well as hand-optimized code from experienced programmers. This research has resulted in several key innovations, including an optimized coding language, a security framework, and a performance engine with dynamic prediction, all of which have been incorporated into an open-source software framework available for public use. Despite the significant advancements achieved, there are still several issues that need to be addressed, such as handling program errors, improving user interface usability, and supporting more complex program logic, but the authors are confident that the progress made thus far will provide valuable insights for the broader research community. This research has been showcased at multiple top-tier industry conferences and has generated significant interest from key industry players. Two real-world software systems, Apache Kafka and Hadoop, have been successfully redeveloped using this automated software development process, demonstrating that this approach can be applied to even the most complex programs. In addition, this research has resulted in the creation of an open-source, end-to-end development platform that allows users to specify program functions using a simple, intuitive interface and enables non-technical users to develop real-world software applications with good performance, security, and reliability. This platform has the potential to revolutionize software development by enabling non-technical users to develop high-quality software applications on their own, and the authors are confident that it will have a significant impact on the software industry as a whole. We explore an hypothesis with two types of leptoquark particles, where both contribute to unexplained phenomena observed in neutrino behavior, specifically neutrino oscillations and existing limitations on lepton flavor violation. Combining constraints from experiments at colliders and processes involving decay or disappearance of particles, we investigate possible characteristics of these two leptoquark types. Considering their similar mass assumptions, our analysis indicates one of the leptoquarks must have a small mass difference with the other, small enough to be within the reach of the Large Hadron Collider when combined with existing constraints from particle decay or disappearance. This tight restriction significantly increases the likelihood of discovering one of the leptoquark duo by experimenting with neutrino probes at powers of $10^{22}$ times greater than current levels, even if only a small fraction of such processes are observable. Multi-step protocols are commonly used in life sciences but can be difficult to master due to their complexity, involving numerous samples, sophisticated techniques, and precise measurements. These challenges are compounded by the limited expertise of undergraduate laboratory students, necessitating specialized instruction and, in some cases, supervision by graduate students or lab technicians. These constraints, combined with the time-consuming nature of manual data analysis using traditional methods, can impede progress and hinder the development of essential life science skills in future scientists. To address these issues, we present an innovative approach called GuidedLearning, a data-driven method that leverages machine learning expertise to facilitate faster, more accurate assessments of life science data. By combining expert knowledge with current student data, GuidedLearning builds a robust statistical model that can efficiently analyze high-dimensional temporal sequences, even those with brief durations. When applied to a seminal biochemistry assay, GuidedLearning demonstrated exceptional performance, surpassing traditional expert analysis in speed and accuracy while providing a seamless user experience via an intuitive interface. With its potential to streamline data analysis and eliminate the need for manual entry, GuidedLearning can be integrated into laboratory protocols to expedite progress, eliminate errors, and free up graduate students and lab technicians to focus on more demanding tasks. Furthermore, this approach can also facilitate real-time feedback and direct instruction, creating a more engaging and effective learning experience for undergraduate laboratory students. By enhancing efficiency, accuracy, and productivity in life science assessments, GuidedLearning can also contribute to a more significant goal of promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion in STEM education by reducing barriers to entry and minimizing the risk of data loss, errors, and invalidations due to limited expertise, thus empowering every student to succeed and thrive in undergraduate laboratory courses. systemassistant

We have analyzed a comprehensive database of molecular gas observations to investigate the relationship between CI line widths and other properties of galaxies. A key finding is a significant and consistent correlation between CI line widths and those of other molecular transitions, which holds true even when controlling for factors like beam size and gas mass. This correlation is particularly notable in the majority of galaxies with relatively narrow CI line widths (<250 km/s), which are generally narrower than expected under typical conditions. These narrower line widths are associated with smaller velocity gradients in the molecular gas and lower line widths for other molecular transitions, such as CO and HCN, indicating a possible limitation on gas flow velocities due to the low stellar mass fraction in these galaxies. This relationship is used to create a new indicator, the 'CI line width ratio', which could be used to assess the limitations on gas flow in molecular systems and potentially identify galaxies with narrow CI line widths that could be in the early stages of transforming their molecular gas into star formation. This may also provide a means to evaluate the likelihood of water maser emission in galaxies. Line widths for other molecular transitions are generally wider than expected under local thermodynamic equilibrium conditions, which could be an indication of non-thermal energy dominance in these systems. This line width ratio could be useful for selecting a more appropriate excitation temperature for the CI line, with broader lines indicating the need for a higher temperature than the typical 2K. The average CI line width is around 350-400 km/s, which is wider than the average stellar rotation velocity in galaxies by a factor of ~5-6, suggesting that stellar rotation has a significant but not dominant influence on CI line widths. Other factors such as the velocity dispersion within the stellar population, black hole mass, and the flow velocity of gas through the molecular reservoir also have a notable but limited impact on these line widths. None of these factors explain a significant portion of the variation in CI line widths, indicating that other factors such as gas dynamics, the presence of hidden mass reservoirs, or the influence of gas interactions with the host galaxy could also have an influence. We tackle two anomalies seen in $B$ meson decays - an anomaly in their decay rates and an anomaly in their decay into Kaons - by suggesting a new explanation that simultaneously addresses both issues. We propose a simple solution that involves adding two new particles, a long-lived neutral Kaon and a metastable neutral meson, both of which could originate from the same source - a vectorlike system that gives mass to quarks and leptons. This source, which lies at an energy scale of around one TeV, is close to, but not yet within reach of the Large Hadron Collider. This solution can be tested with existing experimental data from the LHC, specifically with searches for long-lived neutral particles that have a non-standard interaction, and a review of recent lattice QCD calculations that can determine the Kaon's lifetime. Additionally, this solution makes testable predictions regarding future observations of the LHC, including predictions regarding missing energy, long-lived particles, and edge effects in top quark decays - all of which are in line with existing expectations for similar experiments. Furthermore, this solution also provides a possible explanation for recent discrepancies between lattice QCD predictions and experimental data regarding the $K^+ \to \pi^+ \gamma$ decay rate, as well as potential outcomes for other meson decays that could be observed with improved sensitivity in experiments at the LHC and in experiments involving the decay of mesons at low-energy colliders and in direct searches for new physics. Lastly, this solution maintains the established composition of the Higgs sector and does not introduce any new free parameters in the Higgs sector that could result in an overproduction of Higgs bosons in future experiments. Furthermore, this solution does not introduce any new sources of CP violation that could result in an overestimation of the electric dipole moment of neutral particles in future experiments. Lastly, this solution prioritizes the elucidation of $B$ anomalies over the elucidation of anomalies seen in other experiments and does not provide a solution that simultaneously addresses all of the anomalies seen in $K$ and $B$ meson decays - instead, it focuses on the decay of neutral Kaons into particles that do not contain any charge, rather than the decay of $B$ mesons into other types of particles that do contain a charge. Therefore, this solution does not result in any potential outcomes for other meson decays that could be observed with improved sensitivity in experiments at the LHC and in experiments involving the decay of mesons at low-energy

Information-seeking questions pose a significant challenge for AI in tasks like answering natural language questions. One important aspect is often overlooked, which is the assumption that most questions stand alone and do not reference surrounding text. This work presents a unique and expansive dataset that breaks with this standard, consisting of 20,000 question-answer pairs where each question is accompanied by up to 64 sentences of context, covering a wide range of topics. This dataset, called Info-Anchor, differs from existing datasets that combine context and relevance, which typically rely on relevance labels rather than explicit part-of-speech tags for the same. Info-Anchor was assembled through crowd-sourcing and incorporates relevance labels and syntactic tags for each question-answer pair, which was achieved by conducting 400 independent relevance tests. When evaluated using these tags, current state-of-the-art models performed at 44.3% in absolute performance, which indicates substantial room for improvement. Info-Anchor offers valuable insights for the community to address the challenge of contextual understanding in question answering through the development of new models and existing ones. We establish that in ASEP, a velocity process can be identified at large times, characterized by distinct phases determined by initial conditions, ultimately leading to coordinated movement in ASEP that is in line with the features of a velocity process it shares with the TASEP. This coordinated movement is, in essence, a result of load-sharing that is facilitated by adjacent particles' interaction, causing delays that are proportional to the number of particles between them. This delay effect divides the speed support of the ASEP velocity process into non-overlapping intervals. Notably, in contrast to TASEP where the speed support is composed of a single interval that is proportional to the rate at which particles are transferred, Exclusion Processes like ASEP exhibit more complex, fragmented speed supports. Moreover, in ASEP, it is possible for particles to exhibit velocity that is not shared with any other particle, as long as it falls within the speed support. We analyze the properties of Majorana fermions, whose realization in physical systems relies heavily on the distinction between two vitally connected modes, often represented as $\delta$ in this context. A parameter typically around ${\pi}\theta\sim {\pi}$, describing the chirality of Majorana fermions, is crucial for their definition. In our investigation, we focus on the long-lasting behavior of Majorana fermions and examine how their properties are influenced by both $\delta$ and $\theta$. Our research reveals that neither of these parameters is confined to a specific range and as a result, neither can be determined with certainty through measurement, leading to an interpretation where the effective character of these fermions becomes Majorana in nature for an infinitely broad range of $\delta$ and $\theta$ values spanning from zero to infinity. In order to validate our analysis, we calculated the anti-correlation between two linear Majorana modes and found it to be in line with predictions made by the Majorana equation. In addition, we investigated the reasons behind the limited range of suitable $\delta$ values, as indicated by some theoretical simulations, and found them to be outcome-dependent and thus, not universally applicable. In the case of systems where the two modes are not linearly combined, nor subject to large interference effects, neither $\delta$ nor $\theta$ needs to conform to specific constraints and as such, neither needs to be estimated. Conversely, in situations where the two modes are linearly combined and significant interference effects are present, neither $\delta$ nor $\theta$ can be confined to a specific range and as such, neither can be determined with certainty, leading to an uncertainty principle similar to the one described by Heisenberg but with distinct properties. In order to demonstrate the practical implications of this uncertainty principle, we calculated the specific limits within which the probability of linear Majorana modes can vary and found them to be influenced by both $\delta$ and $\theta$. As a result, neither of these parameters can be set to a specific value in a way that would confine the probability of these modes to a certain range, leading to a character of these modes that is effectively Majorana in nature for an infinitely broad range of $\delta$ and $\theta$ values spanning from zero to infinity. In order to validate our analysis through yet another approach, we calculated the specific limits within which the average values of linear Majorana modes can vary and found them to be influenced by both $\delta$ and $\theta$. A complex brain tumor, typically categorized into three main types, meningioma (BM), glioma (BG), and pituitary tumor (BP), poses significant challenges for medical professionals treating patients with multiple tumors or tumors in close proximity. Determining the type and precise boundaries of the tumor is crucial for effective treatment and minimal side effects. Although deep learning techniques have significantly improved segmentation accuracy, they can be sensitive to changes in network depth and may fail to focus on critical, tumor-related features. To address these limitations, this research proposes a novel multi-task, directed network called MAG-Net, which leverages two complementary pathways to efficiently process brain tumor segmentation and categorization tasks simultaneously. By integrating a multi-task focus director and using a pre-trained 3D network, MAG-Net ensures that the learned features are both relevant to the task at hand and robust. Furthermore, MAG-Net's directed mechanism allows for the extraction of localized and tumor-specific features, while its multi-task approach facilitates shared learning for segmentation and classification. Experimental results show that MAG-Net achieves superior or comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on both tasks, while demonstrating exceptional focus and providing valuable insights for further optimization of deep learning networks. Specifically, MAG-Net's evaluation on the BRATS2019 dataset yields a Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.923 for segmentation and a precision of 0.983 for classification, underscoring its effectiveness as a straightforward solution that can be easily integrated into various medical imaging applications. Moreover, the paper introduces a novel concept, focus score, to subjectively assess the network's focus on tumor-related features, while providing MAG-Net's code and models for widespread use. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of a multi-task directed approach in enhancing network performance and focus on complex brain tumor segmentation and categorization tasks. In addition to focus score, we propose two magnetic resonance imaging-specific metrics called volume score and categorization score to comprehensively evaluate brain tumor segmentation and classification. These proposed metrics, along with focus score, provide a comprehensive understanding of network behavior and are instrumental in guiding future optimization of deep learning techniques for a variety of medical applications. In particular, we investigate optimal network depth, a critical factor that directly impacts the learning of tumor-related features, while introducing the concept of a multi-task focus directed network with variable depth, which is our solution to addressing the challenge of data size imbalance in brain tumor segmentation. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this innovative approach, referred to as MAG-Net V, in enhancing network focus

Unlike other video enhancements like deblurring and stabilization, deinterlacing has seen limited work in recent years, particularly when it comes to deep learning methods. To address this gap, this study creates a novel approach that specifically targets real-world video deinterlacing challenges. Unlike previous deep learning methods, which often rely on synthetic interlacing data or assume that interlacing occurs at the beginning of the video, this research tackles the more complex issue of instantaneous deinterlacing, which means processing both frames of an interlaced field at the same time. To achieve this, the proposed model leverages a unique architecture that combines a spatial attention mechanism with a non-local operation, and is trained on a relatively small dataset consisting of real-world video frames. The analysis covered a range of 40 - 80 MeV/nucleon in saturation density and focused on the connection between their underlying principles. The study revealed that the neutron radius within the two types of models is correlated but exhibits distinct characteristics. A notable difference emerged at higher densities where the relativistic models yielded larger neutron radii, whereas the non-relativistic models exhibited this increase at lower densities. As a result, the neutron radius distribution is quite broad, spanning approximately 0.4 fm, when considering both models. This diversity exists because the neutron point distribution is only indirectly reflected in the macroscopic properties of nuclei through their collective behavior, as described by the neutron radius. Consequently, this diversity may be attributed to the various competing factors that influence the neutron radius in an average field model, often leading to multiple equilibrium points for the same macroscopic property. Such diversity offers opportunities for testing the underlying principles of these models through precise measurements of the neutron radius in heavy and medium-mass nuclei across a broad density range. In particular, consideration should be given to stable and beta-unstable nuclei that facilitate comparisons between protons and neutrons within the same nucleus, thereby enabling a precise determination of the neutron radius distribution. In addition, studying the electric neutron polarizability as a derivative of the neutron radius at equilibrium may provide additional insights into the point structure of the neutron distribution. Consequently, combining experimental data and theoretical calculations of the neutron radius distribution will facilitate a deeper understanding of the underlying principles of neutron physics. Furthermore, such knowledge can also contribute to the advancement of models that describe the dense and non-dense neutron distribution in nuclei, including within the context of neutron star research. As a result, precise measurements of the neutron radius distribution in heavy and medium-mass nuclei across a broad density range will have a significant impact on the development of these models. Traditionally, this is done with the help of hydraulic models, but they are typically complex and time-consuming to set up, often taking hours to produce results. In this research, a novel approach is presented to predict water depths at a rate of 10,000 times faster, without the need for model setup, using a combination of deep learning and efficient solver techniques. A deep learning network is developed to forecast water depths over extended periods, but with a limitation of only a few minutes into the future. Building on this, a novel hybrid algorithm is presented that can make predictions not just faster, but also more accurate for a longer period, in this case, five minutes. The algorithm's performance is tested on real-world flood data from Melbourne, and the results show significant improvements in prediction accuracy with minimal compromise on speed. The novel approach and the results suggest that this method has significant potential to enhance flood management, particularly in cities with complex drainage systems, such as Melbourne. The code and data used in this research are shared as open-source, allowing other researchers to explore and build upon this work. This revised approach allows the algorithm to handle larger and more complex flood events, and the resulting predictions show significant improvement, exceeding those of traditional methods. This note proves a version of the Mumford conjecture for smooth maps, which is a key component in the b-principle. Specifically, given an appropriate map $f:\Lambda\to\Lambda', both of which are closed submanifolds in respective Euclidean spaces, if there exists a smooth map $g:N\to\Lambda$ such that the composite map $F=f\circ g:N\to\Lambda'$ satisfies certain conditions and can be reduced to a free map under the assumptions of the Mumford conjecture, then the original map $g$ can also be reduced to a free map. Notably, M. Gouezel's recent contribution to the conjecture has led to a simplification and a new form of this result, which is the main focus of this note. This research focuses on a model consisting of two scales, representing plant and animal populations that are influenced by each other's dynamics in an ecosystem with variable light intensity. This framework exhibits complex behavior as it transitions between stable and unstable equilibrium points, exhibiting both rapid oscillations and slow trends that significantly impact its functioning. To better understand these dynamics, we studied the underlying forces that shape the behavior of this model, assessed its variability over time, and developed methods to pinpoint early indicators of major population changes. These methods are particularly useful for identifying changes in the rates at which populations change in response to each other's actions, as well as how variations in environmental conditions impact the rates at which populations and their interactions evolve. By applying these methods to a two-species, two-scale ecosystem, we found several early indicators that could signal significant population changes, shifts in ecosystem dynamics, or changes in the rates at which populations evolve. A crucial aspect in the study of galaxy evolution is the correlation between star formation and mass. This relationship, however, breaks down for massive galaxies above 10^10 solar masses, and a related trend observed in a separate study shows that the mass-specific star formation rate peaks at around 10^9 solar masses. These findings are closely linked, with the latter indicating that low mass-specific star formation in massive galaxies contributes to their deviation from the main sequence. A key factor influencing mass-specific star formation is the presence and size of a bulge. Generally, a larger bulge indicates higher mass-specific star formation, yet below a certain threshold, typically 0.1 times the mass of the disk, the bulge's effect on mass-specific star formation becomes insignificant, allowing for lower mass-specific star formation and thus a higher mass-to-light ratio in late-type galaxies. This threshold varies based on the galaxy, but it is often found at 10^9 solar masses. A more detailed analysis of bulge and disk components in two studies reveals that in massive galaxies with significant bulges, the mass-specific star formation is higher than in those with smaller or no bulges, and a separate analysis of bulge and disk main sequences indicates that the break in the one-dimensional main sequence at around 10^9 solar masses is mirrored by a turn-down in the mass-specific star formation at this point in the more massive galaxies with higher mass-specific star formation. To improve the efficiency of machine translation, a significant challenge remains in accurately transferring sentiment information from the source language. This paper addresses this issue by developing a novel framework that learns multiple tasks in parallel, including sentiment analysis in both the source and target languages. This approach leverages multi-task learning to share knowledge across languages and a range of tasks, extending beyond sentiment analysis to other types of translation-related tasks. We particularly focus on sentiment assessment in target languages with limited annotated data, addressing this issue by incorporating a sentiment-guided parallel selection process. This process enables the filtering of parallel sentences based on the source language's sentiment, ensuring that the selected sentences accurately reflect the sentiment of the source text. This filterd set is then used for target language sentiment analysis. A key aspect of this framework is the inclusion of a synthetic sentiment annotation task for the source language, which involves distinguishing between different sentiment intensities. This task is used to add diverse sentiment-annotated data to the parallel corpus. This enhanced dataset is then utilized to a dataset with the same data distribution, thereby enabling the transfer of knowledge to target languages with limited annotated data. This framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through cross-lingual sentiment assessment experiments, with results showing significant improvements over baseline models, with a mean accuracy rate of 42.1% for Dutch, 41.5% for French, and 38.8% for Spanish, with a 6.3% point gain over the strongest single-task model. Furthermore, this framework's efficiency is verified through a practical application, with a 21% reduction in errors when translating user-generated content from English to Dutch. This framework's code is available at https://github.com/strmlab/xlsa/tree/main/xlsa04. Transactional Memory (TM) provides an abstraction for managing contention in concurrent data structures by isolating threads that conflict. Despite its simplicity, implementing TM is challenging due to the "phased" execution requirement, where transactional operations must only access memory locations acquired by previous operations within the same transaction. This paper introduces two new techniques for repairing phase errors: Self-Invalidation (SI) and Self-Devaluation (SD). SI and SD are both low-overhead methods that incure only one additional memory access per offending transaction. We demonstrate SI and SD to be complementary, with SI proving particularly effective in scenarios with a high frequency of non-transactional memory access, whereas SD excels in scenarios with frequent transactional conflicts. We also introduce a hybrid approach, combining SI and SD (SH), which seeks to minimize memory costs by selecting the most cost-efficient repair method based on transaction history. Experimental results confirm that both SI and SD outperform existing repair methods, with SH delivering superior performance in various use cases and demonstrating substantial performance gains in scenarios with frequent phase errors. Our evaluation also provides valuable insights into transaction patterns that induce phase errors and demonstrate how transactions inducing errors differ significantly from those that do not. Overall, our study provides a thorough evaluation of both SI and SD, as well as SH, which sets a new standard for repair methods, exceeding the performance of previous solutions by at least 2x (4x for SH in certain cases) and offering valuable insights that can be applied across a wide range of data structures and applications. Furthermore, our research with SI, SD, and SH has led to an expansion of our transactional memory system by a factor of 2.5 compared to the original system designed by Guzman et al. without any negative impact on phase fault tolerance. This new implementation, which incorporates both SI and SI+SH, is publicly available as part of the Tval core of the SWAY TM system and can be found at https://github.com/txantrejo/sway-core. Leveraging our extended transactional memory system, we present two new contention management algorithms, SI-based CAS and SH-based CAS, which achieve high performance while maintaining low overhead and provide phase fault tolerance. Both algorithms have been thoroughly evaluated and show superior performance compared to state-of-the-art alternatives, demonstrating that the new repair methods can yield substantial performance gains in contemporary applications. Our research with SI, SD, and SH has paved the way for the development of both low-overhead contention management algorithms as well as transactional memory systems that deliver high performance

Let $W$ denote a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion, which is independent of $B^{H}$. We characterize the set of all points $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ for which there exists a non-trivial Borel set $A\subset[0,1]$ with positive Lebesgue measure, satisfying the condition: the mapping $t\mapsto B^{H}(t)+\lambda t$ takes the same value $x$ for measure $\mu$ in $A$ and for null measure in $[0,1]$. We further investigate the situation when the interior of this set is non-empty. Our findings include the instance where $d\geq 2$ and a projective line in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is reachable by $B^{H}+\lambda W$ for some $\lambda$ if and only if $H>\frac{d}{2}$. Additionally, we demonstrate that if $d=1$ and a point $x$ is reachable by $B^{H}+\lambda W$ for some $\lambda$ if and only if $H>\frac{1}{2}$. Our results extend to reachability under changes of time and space, and are proved using a novel approach centered on the Menger curvature of subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. This research also establishes connections to classical stochastic analysis and several recent papers on fractional Brownian motion. Furthermore, four new open questions are posed within this study. X-ray images contain subtle information that can predict the severity of COVID-19 patients requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission, as evidenced by the successful implementation of data-driven models as described in published studies. To further explore this concept, this research investigates possible image characteristics associated with ICU admission by comparing COVID-19 patient X-ray images, categorized into two groups based on their clinical outcomes. The study utilizes a specialized feature extraction method called Inception Time (IT) to analyze X-ray images linked to ICU admission, as IT has been designed to capture temporal patterns in medical signal series. Specifically, IT was applied to chest X-ray images taken over the course of a patient's illness, with a focus on identifying distinct features indicating a patient's condition will deteriorate to the point where ICU admission is necessary. To validate the method's effectiveness, this research compares results generated by using IT in conjunction with a classifier to the same approach but with traditional image features, leading to the conclusion that data-driven models can identify patterns in medical images that accurately predict the severity of COVID-19 patients. Furthermore, experiments employing radiologists' annotations on X-ray images are used to verify the results and explore the possibility of creating more accurate models that incorporate both expert annotations and features extracted via deep learning. The findings of this study have the potential to contribute to the development of enhanced data-driven models that not only consider clinical data but also incorporate insights from medical imaging, as well as to facilitate collaboration between radiologists and computer-based systems. Additionally, the research may facilitate the creation of more effective search for similar cases based on the severity of COVID-19 patients, as well as the development of better prediction models for patients' outcomes in clinical settings. To further explore the characteristics of medical imaging associated with ICU admission in COVID-19 patients, this study has made the following contributions: (1) proposed a novel approach that combines a deep learning-based feature extraction method in conjunction with a classifier to identify patterns in medical images; (2) experimentally demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by comparing the results generated by using IT in conjunction with a classifier to the same approach but with traditional image features; and (3) investigated the possibility of creating more accurate models that incorporate both expert annotations and features extracted via deep learning. As part of this research, a dataset comprising 1024 COVID-19 patient X-ray images taken at University Hospital in Santiago, Chile has been compiled and made available for download from the following link: https://www.dropbox.com/s/link removed/covid19-xray-data.zip?

The detection of visual relationships relies on removing incorrect pairs from a large set of potential ones. A persistent issue with current approaches is their inability to effectively filter out erroneous pairs by relying heavily on classification methods that are prone to producing false positives. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel two-stage method for visual relationship detection that addresses the source of this problem. Firstly, we propose an improved model that utilizes a contrastive learning objective to focus the detection on a specific class and reduce the number of distracting pairs. As a result, this model produces a set of precise, relationship-specific candidates. In the second stage, we introduce a matching model that accurately selects the correct pair based on these refined candidates rather than the entire pool of potential pairs. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) benchmarks, achieving significant improvements over existing approaches by achieving 0.426 AO on Visual Relationship Detection V1, 0.336 AO on Visual Relationship Detection V2, and 34.3% AO on Visual Grounding V1. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/Erroneous-Positive-Reduction-for-VRD. Additionally, an our model's model has been applied to the Visual Relationship Detection Task at the AICity Challenge 2021, ranking 2nd out of 14 teams. Our model's code for the AICity Challenge can be found at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/AICity2021_VRD. The advancement in deep learning has been accompanied by significant improvements in activity recognition across various settings. Notably, significant challenges persist in recognizing activities from limited and darkly lit video samples. This difficulty is compounded by the need for extensive and well-lit training data, which is often difficult to acquire for certain individuals or in settings with significant privacy concerns. To address this, we've developed an innovative technique called Delta Sampling, which streamlines the training process by condensing essential information from full-light samples. This technique enables the efficient utilization of supplementary light data without over-reliance. Our delta-sampled model, built using a pre-trained R-BERT, has demonstrated exceptional performance in activity recognition, surpassing state-of-the-art competitors in the dark kitchen activity recognition dataset by a substantial margin of 11.8% and 23.4% in average precision and ap@0.5 respectively. Furthermore, our method achieved a remarkable 25.6% improvement in average precision over baseline models trained with dark data, proving the effectiveness of delta-sampling in promoting generalization to light activity recognition. Our methodology has been thoroughly evaluated across multiple experiments, offering valuable insights for future research in the field. To facilitate replication, our code and delta-sampling tool are openly accessible for the dark kitchen dataset available at https://github.com/andersonbatista/delta-sampling and will be presented at the 2023 IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV). Our research provides a pioneering solution for activity recognition from limited and darkly lit video samples, offering a promising avenue for future exploration and expansion across other challenging datasets. Conventional Processors employ a single control unit and a centralized memory, 
which forces them to choose between executing a single operation at a time 
(or instruction) or incorporate a limited number of basic operations within 
a single instruction that can be executed concurrently. This particular design 
has been the standard for over 50 years, yet it is possible to design a 
protection mechanism that allows for the safeguarding of data across multiple 
concurrent processes by deviating from this traditional structure. This research 
paper delves into the in-depth details of data addressable concurrent processors, 
a novel design that diverges from conventional architecture. Here, data with its 
own address serves as both input and output for each individual process, which 
is executed in parallel using an array of identical and fully independent modules. 
Each process unit is capable of operating independently, with the option to either 
execute a single operation or several operations at once. This design offers 
multiple benefits including enhanced security through data process isolation, 
improved system reliability, reduced power consumption, and the potential for greater 
performance through the utilization of underutilized processing resources. This 
research is further illustrated by presenting an actual implementation of this 
design, which is a data addressable concurrent version of the popular 8085 processor. 
This new design comprises of 468 logic cells on a single FPGA chip and is capable 
of executing user programs at speeds comparable to those of the original 8085 
processor. This data addressable concurrent version of 8085 has been put to test 
with a variety of benchmark programs including operating systems like 8085-OS/8080-POS, 
and has demonstrated its performance to be on par with that of the original 8085 
processor. This research is an attempt to revive an idea that was first proposed 
almost two decades ago and is now being presented in the form of an actual 
implementation. This design offers numerous benefits over conventional processors 
and it is hoped that it will inspire other researchers to explore novel designs

Recent studies have revealed that local bulge formation within disks occurs, but the underlying causes remain unclear. We address this by analyzing a sample of galaxies within a z ~ 3 galaxy cluster, where we compare their bulge-developing counterparts and sister galaxies that didn't form a bulge. We found that quiescent lopsided galaxies with bulges and their non-bulge creating siblings at the same stellar mass share the same distribution in terms of specific star creation rates, mass-metallicity relationships and gas content. However, the two groups differ in rotation curves and mass accretion rates: galaxies with bulges have higher rotation curves and lower mass accretion rates compared to their non-bulge creating siblings. As a result, their density profiles shift from anisotropic with a strong radial component before bulge formation to near-isotropic with a weaker radial component after bulge formation. Therefore, we conclude that local bulge formation within disks occurs due to interactions between the anisotropic dark matter halo and the rotating stellar disk, where the dark matter halo plays a significant role in shaping their merger asymmetry and ultimately, their bulge creation. Neural network-based code models have achieved remarkable success in generating high-quality code, but they come with a significant drawback: they require significant computational resources and aren't cost-effective. In contrast, code-based neural network methods have shown great promise in combining the strengths of both worlds, but they typically only tackle limited scenarios due to the complexity of the search algorithm. In this research, we introduce a novel search algorithm called Dynamic Evaluation (DynEval) that leverages strong static code checkers to refine search objectives, allowing for both efficient computation and high-quality code results. When compared to baseline search algorithms, DynEval produced code with a 25% higher code quality metric than other methods, while reducing search time by 5 times. Our code also achieved 94% of the quality of professional code in a real-world scenario, whereas other methods only managed 83%. Our approach and code are now open for public evaluation at https://github.com/google/dyneval. DynEval's efficient computation and high-quality code results make it an exciting development in the field of code generation. Unlike other search-based code generators that rely on weak static checkers to filter out unqualified codes and then perform a breadth-first search, DynEval uses strong static checkers to narrow down the search scope, resulting in significantly reduced search computations. This is because strong static checkers can determine a method's return type based on its parameters, allowing the search algorithm to focus on exploring diverse combinations of code rather than dead ends. In contrast, weak static checkers that assume all types are compatible would require the search algorithm to consider every possible code combination, leading to computationally expensive searches. By leveraging strong static checkers, DynEval's search algorithm is able to explore code combinations at a much faster rate, resulting in code that is not only efficient but also meets professional standards. In particular, DynEval's ability to generate high-quality code was demonstrated in an evaluation against real-world data, with a code quality metric that was 25% higher than other methods. Additionally, DynEval's efficiency was shown to be 5 times better than other search algorithms, making it an optimal solution for large-scale code generation tasks. In terms of qualitative evaluation, DynEval's code also achieved a 94% match with professional code, outperforming other methods that only managed a 83% match. Overall, DynEval's combination of efficiency and high-quality code results makes it an exciting development in the field of code generation. We have derived simplified dynamic equations for relativistic fluid sound waves in viscous fluids. These fluids are modelled using a specific framework that includes both internal and external components, and the derived equations account for the breakdown of continuity due to viscosity as defined by the Brinkman forces. The complex Zel'dovich hydrodynamic equations cannot be directly analytically solved for sound waves in viscous fluids. The developed equations provide a solution by approximating the main equations, and the approximation's validity depends on the ratio of the sound wave wavelength to the mean free path of fluid particles. The equations' complexity varies based on this ratio, resulting in either a second-order partial differential equation or a set of first-order equations including conservation and kinetic equations. The kinetic equations are further divided into two subcases: one where the fluid's viscosity coefficient is constant and another where it changes with energy, leading to different levels of complexity. The resulting equation for a constant viscosity coefficient can be simplified to a second-order partial differential equation with terms representing wave dissipation and the generation of shear stress. A state can compel a user to create an account on a platform under threat of prosecution, but can it forcibly obtain encrypted information from a user who has no intention of violating laws? We examine this inquiry by developing a protocol for public-key encryption that incorporates a user's identity into their private key and is linked to their real-world actions. We then devise a method for the state to coerce the user to perform computations tied to their encrypted data, while ensuring the user retains control over their private key and cannot be compelled to decrypt beyond what their actions in the real world permit. This leads to an innovation in the development of coercion-resistant multi-party computations, where the participants' contributions are made involuntary by the threat of non-cooperation, thus addressing concerns about how to construct CMPC systems that are resistant to persistent coercion over time. This solution is then applied to create an example of secure price auction computation. Our proposal presents an alternative to traditional approaches that rely on the user's willingness to cooperate with the system, offering instead a more realistic model that acknowledges the power imbalance between the state and the user. Ultimately, our solution proves the feasibility of secure computation even in scenarios where users are coerced, while also highlighting the necessity of prioritizing user experience and system usability to ensure the practical feasibility of such systems in everyday life. Our simulation tool can predict the actual performance of an experimental implementation of MDI-QKE, considering various sources of error. It is designed to facilitate the interpretation of real-world experiments related to MDI-QKE, and is particularly useful for identifying the minimum conditions under which secure key exchange can be achieved. Our framework is highly versatile and can be applied to scenarios beyond experimental simulations, allowing it to contribute to theoretical discussions on the minimum requirements for successful MDI-QKE exchanges in realistic scenarios. An integral part of this framework is a feature that optimizes parameter settings to achieve the highest possible simulation outcome, in effect serving as a guide for locating the lowest threshold values for successful key exchange. Our simulation framework is an important resource for both theoretical and experimental research in the field of QKE, and is an essential tool for validating the security of these implementations. It is available online at the provided website, where it can be used by researchers to input their own experimental data and obtain predictions on the outcome of real-world implementations of QKE. Through the simulation of error channels, including loss, channel attenuation, and photon pulse duration, our framework demonstrates its capability to provide valuable insights for improving the performance of QKE exchanges. We have designed a quasi-polynomial algorithm that exactly solves every instance of a general constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) on a sparse and simple graph, weighing each variable freely. This algorithm operates within a polynomial margin of poly(n), N, and P, and is an advancement over the known PTAS for specific CSPs, such as Max-Cut and Chromatic Coloring. We have also developed a PTAS for general CSPs with arbitrary constraints, using a simple and novel technique that first transforms any given CSP instance into an equivalent Ising model with a unique ground state, and then applies a modified version of the NPMTAS for the Ising model. This new method relies on a novel variant of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model with a unique ground state and generates a precise and efficient approximation of the model's partition function, extending the previous NPMTAS for the Ising model to a broad category of models, including those with both variable and edge constraints, and providing a PTAS for solving such models exactly. This algorithm's performance is analyzed and several specific complexity classes are determined, and it is demonstrated that this method can be used as a sub-routine for developing a PTAS for general CSPs with arbitrary constraints and for other complex models, such as Boolean CSPs and Boolean satisfiability problems, through a novel and efficient backtracking algorithm that combines local optima of individual variables into a global solution. This work's novel techniques and its novel use of the XXZ decomposition, the NPMTAS for the Ising model, and a novel variant of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model with a unique ground state, provide a foundation for the study of complex models and may have implications for the study of biological systems and complex networks. Understanding network behavior is crucial when deploying complex neural networks in high-stakes situations. Despite significant advancements in model performance, there has been relatively little progress in understanding how they work and what drives their decisions. In this study, we examine the underlying reasoning behind two prominent neural network models, incorporating both text-based and visual analysis. We employed two leading X-ray model variants and a combination of both for image classification tasks. We gathered a diverse group of 40 participants and asked them to explain their interpretations of network output in writing and through visual presentations. Our findings reveal that, in this limited study, participants' understanding and ability to interpret network output were only around 20% accurate on average. There were some notable individual differences, with some participants consistently demonstrating a higher level of comprehension and interpretation skill than others. Our findings suggest potential avenues for further improvement, such as the impact of dataset diversity on participant selection and the use of more nuanced, detailed instructions in the comprehension and visualization task. Our research is ongoing, and we plan to expand our participant base to at least 100 participants to gather more robust results. Our research findings and data are available for download at the associated webpage. The rapid dissemination of news on the internet poses a significant threat, allowing false information to spread rapidly. This issue is compounded by the small amount of training data typically used for news models. Given these challenges, introducing new false news domains at test time becomes a major obstacle. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that learns false news patterns in the training set and generalizes to identify false information on unseen test domains without additional data. This is achieved through the application of Hypernetworks and Multiple Expert Systems within the context of Neural Process Networks, allowing our model to learn a false news representation while leveraging a meta representation of data points in each domain. This results in excellent performance in false news detection across domain boundaries, as validated by experiments conducted on three diverse datasets spanning social media text, Wikipedia articles, and combined text-image pairs. Notably, our model excels in the absence of domain information, relying solely on a general false news classifier, and showcases impressive performance in the incorporation of expert knowledge through the addition of pre-trained language models as experts. Systematic analysis of Hypernetworks and Neural Process Networks reaches a false accuracy rate of 12% without additional expert knowledge, showcasing the efficacy of our proposed Meta Neural Process Network architecture. This groundbreaking approach sets a new standard for false news detection across boundaries, offering a promising solution for related problems such as adversarial detection and cross-domain recommendation systems. A system that periodically updates information in discrete time is analyzed, relying on the Ber/G/1/1 queueing model. When the system updates information, it takes the same amount of time as a single server service does, whereas the time between updates is seen as n times the time between arrivals. The model's phase duration depends on whether a customer is being served or not, leading to two separate recurrence relations. The model's performance is then evaluated in terms of the expected update frequency and coverage rate. A crucial factor in quantum computing is controlling the interaction between different spin valleys in a two-dimensional material. Researchers have achieved impressive outcomes in isolating adjacent spin valleys in moire systems, however, achieving atomic-scale control over combining isolated valleys with separated spin populations and a target spin valley has remained a significant challenge. By employing atomic-scale scanning, local electrical bias, and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we successfully demonstrated precise control over combining isolated valleys with separate spin populations and a target spin valley in silicon. When a quantum dot is located at an atomic-scale junction between two moire minima, the spin transfer gap can be reduced to near-zero by adjusting the local potential, thus increasing the likelihood of stochastic spin transfer. When placing a quantum dot over a larger moire site, varying the local potential allows us to switch the chemical potential rapidly between the two spin valleys located in adjacent moire minima, a function essential for quantum error correction through spatial spin coupling. Our findings also reveal a novel mechanism of spin transfer mediated by a local atomic-scale potential, proving it an essential factor that influences valley transfer and merging the two spin valleys. This discovery is significant because it indicates that the interaction between different spin valleys in silicon can be controlled through a local atomic-scale potential, a crucial aspect for the material's suitability for quantum computing. However, there are some challenges to be overcome before realizing the potential of silicon-based quantum computing, notably the significant gap between the spin transfer gap and the quantum dot's level when placing it over a larger moire site, as well as the significant overlap between the two spin valleys located in adjacent moire minima, which could impede the implementation of quantum error correction through spatial spin coupling due to the proximity of states within the two valleys. Despite these issues, our research provides a foundation for exploring other methods to control the interaction between different spin valleys in silicon through its unique moire physics. Complex systems, characterized by interconnected components and varied temporal structures, exhibit behavior that cannot be predicted by analyzing their parts in isolation. Due to the difficulty in solving these systems' equations, researchers often turn to simplifying models for better understanding and explanation. In such cases, modeling complex systems often requires both detailed representation of system dynamics and clear explanation of underlying processes. While graph neural networks have shown great promise in processing structured data and modeling non-linear relationships, their potential in capturing the essence of complex systems through temporal graph neural networks remains under-explored. Our work addresses this by presenting a novel framework that leverages temporal graph neural networks to model sophisticated system behavior and extracting a methodology for analyzing system components through neural network weights. Additionally, we apply this framework to two prominent examples: the emergence of synchrony in power grids and the formation of coherent states in spin systems. Our findings reveal that both systems exhibit similar structural characteristics and demonstrate how these can be utilized to design next-generation sensing devices that are both efficient and effective. Our research also paves the way for addressing more fundamental inquiries regarding the interconnection between system variables, state evolutions, and the resultant emergent behaviors in complex systems. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Group-BT/Complex-Systems-Understanding. Our work is also discussed in the thesis titled: Unveiling the Temporal Structure of Complex Systems with Graph Neural Networks available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03008v2. We introduce a family of recursive formulas for computing the counts of specific arrangements of objects in a category, which is based on a key relationship involving a set of symmetric operations. This results in a broad enumeration framework applicable to several areas, including combinatorial objects, monoids, and sets of points in space. Specifically, our counts cover objects such as combinatorial sequences like binary trees and partitions, as well as constructs like finite sets, products of spaces, and quotients of spaces defined by subspaces and inclusion maps. Our formulation is highly versatile, enabling us to derive various well-known counts, such as those from Hermann, Kauers, and Proverbi, and Lagrange, via a simpler proof, and to examine relationships between various areas of mathematics through the lens of our abstract framework. Our general computation framework is demonstrated with the example of computing refined homotopy counts for spheres, which is a significant problem in algebraic topology and homotopy theory. Our method involves using our abstract framework in conjunction with a technique called the homotopy decomposition, which enables us to analyze and compute the refined homotopy counts for spheres in all dimensions up to 8. Our findings reveal intriguing patterns and suggest connections between the homotopy counts and sequences such as the binary tree sequence, the cube sequence, and the sphere intersection sequence, which are all defined using our arrangement framework. Our research also uncovers an interesting property where the homotopy counts for spheres exhibit an alternating behavior when compared to these sequences. Our work lays the groundwork for further investigation into the relationships between homotopy theory and combinatorics through the lens of our abstract framework. Our extensive computations and results, including our descriptions of configurations, our general computation formulas, and our analyses of the relationships between the homotopy counts and the sequences, provide a valuable resource for researchers in both areas. Our research is primarily driven by a desire to explore the connections between homotopy theory and combinatorics but raises additional questions and problems in both areas, which we hope will be of interest to other researchers. Our research is presented in the form of problem statements rather than proofs, which we hope will encourage other researchers to engage with these problems and potentially make progress on them. Clinical experts at tertiary care centers meticulously mark brain lesions in 3D CT scans to aid in further diagnosis and treatment, but this time-consuming process hinders the development of effective training data. To expedite and enhance the quality of these annotations, a novel approach was developed, where a advanced algorithm called the Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PAVAE) efficiently produces accurate lesion entries in 3D brain scans with incomplete annotation points. The PAVA, the base method for this algorithm, outperforms previous variants, particularly in processing complex, unstructured data, such as brain scans, and surpasses state-of-the-art metrics for lesion segmentation and generation, as evidenced by rigorous evaluations using real expert annotations and points, in addition to subjective assessment by clinical specialists. PAVA's adaptability across diverse scanners and centers, as well as its transparent architecture that reproduces annotations in stages, making them inherently interpretable, are its key attributes. This method has been thoroughly tested using over 5000 data points from 100 3D CT scans, with an overall effectiveness rating of 86%, and has been patented in the United States, with pre-trained models available for stroke diagnosis in brain scans at https://pavae.cs.toronto.edu/. Additionally, an interactive user interface at https://pavae.cs.toronto.edu/try-it-out, allows for the input of user-specific annotation points for the generation of tailored brain lesion datasets. These advancements have significant implications for the creation of high-quality training datasets in an ever-expanding field of medical diagnostics aided by artificial intelligence, where data is constantly being generated at a rapid pace, and expert input is becoming increasingly scarce. As a result, there is a pressing need for innovative solutions to produce accurate and reliable datasets in a timely and cost-effective manner, and the proposed PAVA method is an groundbreaking answer to this critical challenge. This groundbreaking solution, PAVA, has the potential to significantly impact various other structured data sets in the field of medical diagnostics, by increasing the quality and speed of annotation, and it is our hope that it will become an industry standard for the generation of accurate and reliable datasets, and will continue to be a source of inspiration for future breakthroughs. We examine a class of multipartite states known as unextendible product states (UPS), which serve as a foundation for quantum nonlocality. Certain UPSs exhibit robust anti-quantum behavior, extending Schroeck's findings in simpler scenarios to complex, unentangled systems consisting of up to four heterogeneous qutrits. These robust, nonlocal connections are demonstrated to withstand any environmental perturbations, as defined by the LPTP criterion, which sets a more stringent standard for complexity than both matrix dimension and system size. Our research also uncovers unique, tripartite states with robust nonlocality that are scalable and may have applications in quantum metrology, outperforming the superdense coding of single systems in both scaling and purity levels. However, all Ups with robust nonlocality in four-dimensional systems do not necessarily exist. We developed a 6-qutrit, 3-system state with nonlocal properties that are resistant to environmental disruptions and allow for high precision measurements, but we were unable to replicate this in a 4-qudit setting with tripartite states. Our findings rely heavily on combinatorial designs and stratified matrix sharing, unveiling their underlying, intricate structures, which hold promise for discovering more complex, nonlocal connections in the future. Our research involves multiple unitary transformations, as well as the application of certain, carefully designed operators that isolate particular, shared matrix patterns, separating and reassembling the components of these states with great precision. Our work lays the groundwork for exploring the interplay between quantum nonlocality and entanglement in complex systems and may have implications for designing robust, nonlocal states with desirable properties in quantum information processing systems. Despite this, TSC showed promise and we believe its principles could be applied to other large-scale distributed systems.
