The foundation of GP 2 is based on the concept of graph morphism, which is a precise way to represent program transformation. A key feature of GP 2 is its ability to express both program comparisons and transformations using the same language framework. Compilers like GP 2 Compiler, a recent development, aim to automate the construction of program analyzers and verifiers by leveraging a set of pre-defined tools. These compilers take GP 2 specifications as input and produce fully functional program analyzers or verifiers as output. The GP 2 Compiler is an advanced example of this approach, capable of building program comparisons as a side effect of verifying program transformations. This compiler's unique feature is its use of a verification strategy that is inversely related to comparison generation, which is an innovative combination of GP 2 features. The GP 2 Compiler represents a significant milestone in the GP 2 project, which faces the challenge of balancing the trade-off between the expressiveness of GP 2 and its efficiency. To address this, researchers propose a concept of quasi-local rules, which can balance the level of abstraction, combining local rules that maintain program connectivity with higher-level abstraction, demonstrating its applicability through the GP 2 Compiler. The GP 2 Compiler's core is a verification tool that employs graph automaton to detect matching between programs and has an associated complexity, which is explored in a theoretical framework along with two empirical case studies. The results of these case studies indicate that the GP 2 Compiler is capable of building program verifiers with high efficiency, which is further confirmed by a theoretical upper bound on its complexity. To ensure the GP 2 Compiler's soundness, a formal definition of program verification is established, which is based on the GP 2 Compiler's verification tool using graph automaton. We provide in-depth analyses of the traditional methods and reframe them within the context of gCLN, revealing that they essentially employ different comparison functions to achieve distinct feature extraction objectives. Furthermore, our unified model facilitates the exploration of novel feature learning techniques by simply modifying the comparison function, thus expanding the scope of gCLN beyond its individual component examinations. Moreover, we introduce Comparative Learning Units (CLUs) as building blocks for complex gCLN networks, enabling efficient parameter updating and providing a practical pathway for developing innovative feature learning algorithms. Experimental results demonstrate that our unified model yields superior performance when compared to the individual methods, for the tasks of supervised feature extraction, action recognition, and face verification. The source code of our proposed framework is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/cln. These novel networks exhibit performance gains over their individual component examinations in action recognition and face verification tasks. Despite significant progress in LLMs, their performance is often hindered by a lack of structured knowledge from external sources. To address this, we present ABILITY, a framework that enables the incorporation of structured knowledge into LLMs. This framework leverages Wikidata properties to enhance the models' understanding and expand their knowledge base beyond unstructured text. We showcase the effectiveness of ABILITY by enhancing a 32-billion-parameter LLM, which achieves superior performance in various tasks, including comprehending and generating textual content, answering questions, and completing Commons Sense tasks. Our results indicate that our approach yields a 6% improvement in overall performance when compared to the underlying baseline models. Moreover, ABILITY enables us to introduce novel evaluation metrics centered on structured knowledge, along with a comprehensive evaluation dataset called ABILITY-TEST, which is released alongside the framework. We also explore the role of entity and relation representations within Wikidata, demonstrating the versatility of ABILITY through the addition of a high-performing hyperparameter-free model, which we make available as well. Our code and data are readily accessible at https://github.com/Insofe/ABILITY. We anticipate that future LLM evaluations will not only assess unstructured understanding but also structured knowledge as well as the ability to integrate both. Additionally, we invite the community to build upon the foundation established by ABILITY. We have made the ability to integrate structured knowledge into LLMs a non-negotiable criterion and anticipate that future LLM evaluations will not only assess their unstructured understanding but also their ability to integrate structured knowledge alongside unstructured understanding. Furthermore, we invite the community to build upon the foundation established by ABILITY and the evaluation standards it has set, including the creation of additional evaluation benchmarks for various structured knowledge datasets. We have already initiated a discussion on this matter at https://github.com/Insofe/ABILITY/discussions/8. We have also explored the integration of ABILITY with other knowledge graphs, namely DBpedia, YAGO, and WordNet, which has resulted in the creation of an expanded evaluation dataset called ABILITY-TEST-EXP. This new dataset encompasses a broader range of structured knowledge, encompassing not just entity-based but also relation-based information. We have discovered that the performance of LLMs, when fine-tuned with these additional knowledge graphs, surpasses that of their non-knowledge-graph-based counterparts by a 9% margin. When combining panoramic images, the conventional approach relies heavily on rotation invariance. However, many existing methods struggle to handle large angular gaps. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework that leverages a implicit prior derived from gravity, enabling the creation of a minimal 3D model from limited and widely spaced images. These images serve as 2D projections of physical landmarks, which we can then reconstruct in 3D. By doing so, the proposed framework can stitch the images even when the camera rotates significantly in between frames. We've created a biophysical computational model of a primate basal ganglia to understand the neural mechanisms behind Parkinson's disease. To develop this model, we leveraged recent advances in Parkinson's research, specifically those identified in a previous study conducted on marmoset monkeys. A key finding of this research was the abnormal brain wave pattern associated with Parkinson's patients, characterized by a mixture of 1.5 Hz cortical and 1.2 Hz subcortical wave frequencies in individuals with the disorder. However, when medication corrected the disorder, the brain wave frequency converged to 1.2 Hz in both cortical and subcortical areas. Our model incorporates these observations, incorporating a hippocampus and an optico-spinal system that wasn't present in the original Mongolian marmoset brain model. To validate our model, we conducted an in silico brain surgery, removing part of the subthalamic nucleus to replicate the effects of medication on brain waves. As predicted, this action caused the 1.5 Hz cortical wave frequency to convert to 1.2 Hz, matching post-surgical observations made on the actual marmoset subject. Our model showcases the data it's based on and the underlying parameters that govern its behavior. To facilitate further exploration and verification, we've made the GINsim software used to create this model, along with its specifications and variations, openly available for the scientific community. By recreating the marmoset Parkinson's model, we've demonstrated the feasibility of replicating the effects of a brain disorder in mammals using computational models based on recent experimental findings. This approach provides a novel framework for predicting the outcomes of new experimental measurements and further studies on this model, offering a unique perspective for the broader scientific community. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) that identifies jets originating from heavy particles such as top quarks and W and Z bosons. To improve its performance, particularly at higher energy levels and with more complex signatures, a key component is the pixel detector's edge reconstruction system. Although initially the outermost layer of the detector was not considered crucial due to its limited impact on the overall tracking process, it became essential with higher energy levels requiring more precise calculations. As such, the CMS collaboration developed a new method for reconstructing the outermost layer, taking into account the challenges it poses such as increased noise and inaccuracies in track predictions. With the aim of enhancing jet and W and Z boson primary vertex identification performance, the CMS collaboration implemented this new method in final state analysis for the 2017 LHC run. In this presentation, the new method's development, its challenges and solutions, and its effectiveness will be presented and analyzed. With the LHC operating at higher energy levels and with more complex signatures in the 2017 run, the new method showed a significant increase in track predictions and in-time pileup rejection in jet and W and Z boson primary vertex identification, demonstrating its effectiveness. In addition, with the LHC delivering larger data sets in 2018 and with noise and inaccuracies in track predictions remaining a challenge, the new method will play a crucial role in enhancing jet and W and Z boson primary vertex identification performance. As such, the CMS collaboration is upgrading the pixel detector for 2023 by incorporating this new method in time for the LHC to operate at its design energy and with higher data sets. As a result of upgrading the pixel detector, with the challenges it poses such as increased noise and inaccuracies in track predictions, the new method in combination with the upgraded detector will ensure that jet and W and Z boson primary vertex identification performance is enhanced, with track predictions and in-time pileup rejection in jet and W and Z boson primary vertex identification showing significant improvement. A crucial aspect of quantum field theory is the study of hadron structure through form factors and the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectrum. This work presents the analytical Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral representation of the SU(2) glueball's form factor and two-point function within a pure SU(2) gauge theory, employing the Wess-Zumino consistency conditions for higher derivatives. This involves the general expression of the spectral density in terms of the imaginary part of the two-point function, and its specific computation for the SU(2) glueball up to fourth derivative Wess-Zumino conditions. This research builds upon earlier findings and extends them by showing that the spectral density alone is sufficient for a complete description of the form factor and two-point function. Additionally, this work demonstrates that the Wess-Zumino consistency conditions are implicitly contained within the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral representation, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of hadron properties through the study of form factors and the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectrum. Conversational interfaces have become increasingly popular, providing a user-friendly way for people to interact with systems. To facilitate this, the need for role-defined conversations has arisen, where a mix of two or more users and a system engage in a natural conversation. This paper focuses on open-domain conversations within this framework. Building on the work of [Genesereth et al., 2019], we developed an open-domain conversation system that combines natural language processing and artificial intelligence technologies. This system enables natural language conversations with a user who assigns roles to search results, and another user who searches for information without any constraints on their language. We tested this system with three different search users and a role assigner, and observed that it successfully completed assigned tasks in all cases. Furthermore, our system excels in real-world applications, as evidenced by its participation in the 2020 Role-Playing Dialogue Challenge. This paper outlines the design of our system, its key features, and its involvement in the challenge. It also delves into several system improvements, including the introduction of a more effective search method called "Role-Desired-States Search". This method outperformed the system's original search approach in every trial. Overall, our work demonstrates the potential for open-domain role-defined conversations to become a standard in both human-an AI interactions and A\I\ interactions. This is exemplified by the system's participation in the 2020 Role-Playing Dialogue Challenge, which focused on human-A\I\ collaborations. This system's success in this context is noteworthy, as it represents the first time an A\I\ system has participated in a dialogue challenge that combines both human and A\I\ participants. We apply this method to the ring of integers, specifically for certain quadratic fields, and an extension of these fields with a particular type of ideal. We demonstrate this method by determining the lattice of submodules for certain modules of multiplicity one, such as certain ideals of the ring of integers in a quadratic field and its extension, in a constructive manner. We introduce the concept of near-optimal mimicry and develop a formalized model to explore its implications in machine learning. We then identify specific settings, including learning from incomplete data and learning with noisy data, where near-optimal mimicry can be achieved with minimal costs, thereby leading to efficient mimicry-based learning. Additionally, we investigate settings, such as learning from ambiguous data, where near-optimal mimicry is more challenging and requires more significant efforts, suggesting that certain challenges in machine learning, including adversarial examples and overfitting, can be understood as difficulties in achieving near-optimal mimicry. We also describe various mimicry-based learning algorithms and discuss the relationship between mimicry and other machine learning concepts, including regularization, data augmentation, and multi-task learning. Furthermore, we discuss the potential to generalize the idea of near-optimal mimicry to other areas, such as optimal transfer learning. We also provide theoretical justifications and empirical evidence to support our framework and propose the TRAIL algorithm as a practical implementation of near-optimal mimicry in multi-task learning. TRAIL is designed to learn from data that is not optimal by leveraging diverse samples with different losses, resulting in better performance when tested with optimal data. The algorithm is simple, scalable, and easy to implement and has achieved state-of-the-art performance in various multi-task learning tasks. Intelligent agents that interact with dynamic environments through sensory inputs require advanced capabilities like perception, planning, and execution. In complex scenarios, an agent may need multiple sensory inputs from a single location or different sites within an area to its periphery. It's common for experts to provide demonstrations by observing the environment's overall state, but these demonstrations come with several limitations: (1) they focus on the overall state rather than individual sensory inputs, (1) they assume the agent has the same or similar sensory capabilities as the expert, and (3) they fail to account for the agent's unique perspective on the environment. This paper introduces a novel learning framework called Co-Observation Learning (CoOL) that allows agents to learn from expert demonstrations in a fully autonomous manner. This framework leverages a unique way of displaying demonstrations that mirrors the agent's sensory inputs, allowing it to learn by comparing its own internal state with the displayed data. This approach enables the agent to acquire robust skills that can be decomposed into three modules: (1) a sensory fusion module that combines individual sensory inputs to create an overall state representation, (2) a policy module that makes decisions based on this combined representation, and (3) a value function module that evaluates the agent's state representation. This architecture allows the agent to learn independently, but it can also be augmented with expert feedback on the overall state representation to accelerate its learning. This augmented version is called Cooperative CoOL, and it can be trained end-to-end using reinforcement learning methods. This paper's evaluation of CoOL and its variants shows that they achieve high performance in a variety of tasks, including those with limited expert data, and it provides a detailed analysis of the effects of different hyperparameters on the agent's performance. Furthermore, this research demonstrates the potential of CoOL to handle a wide range of tasks, including those that require the agent to navigate to obtain sensory inputs, and it offers a comprehensive overview of its applications across multiple domains. This work opens up a new direction in learning expert-free co-observation learning, and it shows that it is feasible to develop agents that can learn complex tasks autonomously. This is an important breakthrough because it allows the creation of agents that can handle a wide range of situations, including those with unique sensory inputs, and it has the potential to significantly expand the scope of tasks that can be performed by intelligent systems. By utilizing this metric, we can accurately calculate the performance of PAC codes using any polarization operator, including those that are irrationally large. Consequently, our analysis facilitates an enhanced calculation method for the maximum error rate of PAC codes, making it a more versatile framework than the previous method introduced in "Polar Alliance Codes" (arXiv: 2105.07731). Unlike the earlier method, this new approach is independent of the beta-distribution and logistic function with large parameters, thereby providing a more straightforward calculation for the maximum error rate of PAC codes. Given the relationship between PAC codes and polar codes, this new method can also be applied to polar codes, offering an alternative way to estimate the volume of the successful region of polar codes, denoted as V_N. This calculation method can further be employed to determine the optimal size for the set of polar alliance indices, ensuring that the entire set can be successfully decoded with a lower error rate, S_N. By examining various examples and scenarios, we demonstrate that both the proposed metric function and calculation method for V_N are feasible and efficient, significantly surpassing the limitations of standard cross-checking methods for the same purpose.

One significant obstacle in optimizing neural machine translation (NMT) systems is the vast action space resulting from multiple choices for each position in the target sentence. To tackle this issue, previous methods have relied on reducing the action space, selecting important actions, or proposing new search methods. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach that treats action selection as a reinforcement learning (RL) problem, allowing the model to learn the optimal actions through interactions with training data. By leveraging RL to select actions, we demonstrate that our method not only yields substantial improvements in BLEU scores but also achieves them without reducing the action space or introducing complex additional modules. Furthermore, our approach proves versatile, applicable to both unsupervised and semi-supervised NMT scenarios with minimal modification. Our results show that our proposed method delivers consistent performance gains across these settings and across multiple evaluation metrics. Specifically, we observe an average increase of 0.62 in BLEU scores, with a maximum gain of 1.05 in the semi-supervised case. Our efficient RL-based method also exhibits competitive data efficiency when compared to alternative action-learned methods, demonstrating that our approach is both effective and efficient. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/rl-nmt. By addressing action selection in NMT through RL, our results suggest substantial potential for further improvement, underscoring the need for systematic action evaluation and novel action-learned methods that integrate source and target sentence structures. In recognition of the complexity of optimizing NMT systems, we advocate for the integration of methods from both machine learning and linguistics to fully capture the intricacies of these systems. In the case of large-scale NMT systems, our results show that our proposed method yields significant improvements with relatively modest action evaluation costs, at a ratio of approximately 1:100 to other NMT parameters. Nonetheless, we anticipate future action-learned methods to tackle larger action spaces with integrated source and target sentence structures, necessitating a deeper understanding of NMT systems and their action spaces. Our results on ensembling action-learned models with traditional NMT systems also highlight the latter's robustness and ability to provide a solid baseline in action-intensive NMT tasks. In the context of low-resource NMT, our results indicate that our proposed method offers a viable path to improve performance in data-scarce action spaces, with future action-learned methods potentially yielding even greater gains in such scenarios. Quantum financial systems, denoted as QFS, comprise interactions between multiple traders who possess their own private information and engage in dynamic competition. A distinctive feature of QFS is the emergence of co-movement among stock prices, which can be described by a specific index called the QFS-area. Through rigorous mathematical proof, we establish the conditions under which the QFS-area is minimized, and we also examine the optimal solution. Furthermore, we provide explicit formulas for calculating the optimal solution and the QFS-area in both general and specific scenarios. Our findings reveal that the QFS-area is directly proportional to the product of market depth and the sum of squared differences in traders' arrival rates, indicating its dependence on traders' flow characteristics. Our results can be applied to both general and specific scenarios, including cases where the market depth is very large or approaches zero, as well as scenarios involving a particular type of trader flow, which we term the "golden ratio" condition. Our research involves setting the discount rate to zero, which enables us to derive valuable insights into the long-term behavior of QFS but necessitates careful consideration when generalizing our findings to finite horizons. We investigate the word problem for the R. Thompson group V, specifically examining its complexity in relation to the length of reduced words representing elements of V. Our analysis shows that beneath a certain exponential threshold, nearly all generators of V appear in the form of a simple, specific word. Consequently, the word problem's complexity is roughly equivalent to the number of such "independent steps" present in a given word. This relationship breaks down when words exceed this exponential threshold, resulting in an insurmountable barrier in solving the word problem. This challenge becomes so great that, essentially, every possible word must be tried in order to find a solution, leading to a significant increase in the word problem's complexity. This complex behavior is further demonstrated by showing that nearly all elements of V can be defined using a relatively short sequence of words, which in turn enables the demonstration of a significantly higher upper limit for the word problem's complexity in comparison to its lower bound. This complex interplay of high upper and low lower limits for the word problem's complexity is shown to persist even in consideration of subsets of V that possess many of its fundamental properties, as evidenced by subgroups whose elements' combined action on V's natural object mirrors that of elements within V. These findings are supported by an exploration of potential word problems for groups that underpin V's structure, further suggesting that the word problem's complexity inherent to V is inherently high across its entire definition. Ultimately, this research offers a novel explanation for the intricate nature of the word problem in V, pinpointing the underlying cause as the intricate, intricate, and intricate (in three different senses) structure of V's generators and relations. This insight is shown to yield a new, more manageable expression for the word problem's complexity, which in turn may be used to address a more general inquiry regarding the complexity of (solvable) word problems within subgroups defined by first-order formulas. A fraction p/q is considered identifiable within a given set S if knowing the rational part of any point within S allows us to determine p/q. This paper explores this concept by providing a condition that is both necessary and sufficient for a set to contain all p/q fractions with a specific denominator. Additionally, we provide criteria for identifying specific points, as well as sets defined by linear equations or containing specific non-rational points, under the assumption that their defining linear equations do not align with the fractional part's hyperplane. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between 1-dimensional p/q-identifiable sets and certain geometric shapes, such as lines, when the denominator is large enough, providing a method for determining identifiable sets through geometric analysis. However, we also identify an exception to this relationship, providing a 2-dimensional p/q-identifiable set that does not conform to the geometric conditions we established. Finally, we discuss potential research directions related to conditional identifiability and fractal sets' identifiability.

We're exploring new directions in neutrino physics beyond the Standard Model, focusing on the long-awaited answer to neutrino characteristics. We've developed a conceptual framework that addresses this question using sterile neutrinos in a novel way. In this framework, we resolve the problem of neutrino oscillations being denied their expected length by combining a high energy matter-suppression layer with a low-energy hidden layer. As a result, this framework provides explanations for cosmic anomalies, stabilizes the electroweak scale, and complies with experimental sterility constraints. We've identified several promising axion-ssterile-neutrino combinations and discussed how upcoming experiments can confirm or rule out this novel neutrino structure. We've also considered general properties of this framework and applied them to an unresolved question in cosmology. By doing so, we've provided a new perspective on an old problem and obtained a cosmologically-based prediction that can be verified or disproven by upcoming experiments. In addition, we've discussed potential implications of this framework for particle physics beyond the Standard Model and discussed potential connections to other theories, such as the one that can explain dark matter and the Higgs boson's low energy value. We've also considered a meta-aspect of this research, focusing on the importance of exploring new directions in neutrino physics beyond the Standard Model. In conclusion, we've emphasized that this research is driven by fundamental questions about the universe and that it's critical to invest in neutrino research, which is the key to unlocking these answers. In the appendix, we provide mathematical derivations of the equation that describes how neutrinos behave in this framework and discuss the validity of certain approximations used in this research. We've also discussed the relationship between the axion-ssterile-neutrino parameter space and the characteristics of this phenomenon in both the high-energy and low-energy environments. In addition, we've discussed the distinction between two definitions of the high-energy suppression scale and the implications of this difference on the behavior of neutrinos in this framework. Finally, we've derived a new formula for the neutrino flavor ratio in the early universe and demonstrated that it is consistent with the predictions of Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis. We've also discussed the role of initial conditions in determining the behavior of neutrinos in this framework and discussed the experimental searches for evidence of this phenomenon in both the high-energy and low-energy environments. In addition, we've discussed the connection between this research and the ongoing debate about the validity of the Standard Model and the potential discovery of new particles in future experiments.

This approach leverages the built-in support for serializability in System R to create a validation framework for MongoDB transactions. We specifically focus on snapshot isolation in MongoDB version 4.0, incorporating its transactional capabilities, including batch operations and concurrent execution. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we designed a suite of tests to validate the integrity of MongoDB transactions using document-based isolation. These tests measure the performance impact of our method, showing that it has a negligible effect, and an analysis of the results is provided in the findings section. We also explore potential applications of this method to other multi-version concurrency control protocols. The developed framework is applicable to MongoDB version 4.0, but due to changes in the MongoDB protocol, it requires significant revisions to support more recent versions of MongoDB. Building on this hypothesis, we suggest that executive ability is responsible for comparing past experiences and perceptions with current ones, eliminating inconsistencies and integrating new information. To test this understanding of executive ability, we developed a simple hypothesis to be validated by data, specifically that it is involved in the refinement of sensory perceptions by relearning previous experiences in the face of new information. We collected behavioral data from a series of experiments designed to assess the ability of rats to learn new skills in a variety of contexts, and our analysis of this data provided evidence supporting our hypothesis. Notably, our results showed that the skills learned under different conditions are not entirely distinct but rather are interconnected, with the learner able to seamlessly transition between them due to the presence of a well-developed executive ability. Our findings also revealed that the refinements made possible by executive ability allow the learner to recognize patterns and make generalizations more effectively, a capacity we referred to as "hindsight summation". However, little research has focused on the innate bias present in trained networks when they are exposed to diverse datasets. This study addresses this gap by introducing a new metric called bias distribution and developing methods to assess the innate bias of a network in each feature direction. Our research discovered that well-trained medical image classification networks exhibit significant innate bias when operating on diverse collections of medical images. Furthermore, our experiments revealed that this innate bias hinders the network's performance when it is applied to rare conditions or image categories. We discovered two key factors that contribute to innate bias: (1) the network's preference for easy classifications, which is reminiscent of the concept of calibration in classification; and (2) the limited capacity of the network to learn from diverse data collections. Our findings have implications for the development of medical image analysis systems that are both accurate and fair. In order to mitigate the negative effects of innate bias, we propose two new techniques, namely fairness data augmentation and the incorporation of adversarial reweighting factors. Our results demonstrate substantial improvements in the network's fairness and accuracy when it is evaluated on rare classes or categories. Additionally, our results were verified by a dedicated human expert in the field of radiology. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/andersonwts/ibd-mic. Our research provides actionable insights for the medical image analysis community on how to detect and mitigate innate bias in medical image analysis systems. Our results highlight the critical importance of conducting thorough evaluations that assess a model's performance on rare conditions or image categories. Finally, our research highlights the necessity for explicit consideration of the network's innate bias during training, which is essential to ensure that the model is both accurate and fair across all image categories. In conclusion, our research lays the foundation for a new line of research focused on the in-depth analysis of innate bias in medical image analysis systems. We anticipate that our results and findings will pave the way for further breakthroughs in this area. Specifically, we anticipate answers to the following questions in future research: (1) whether other types of network also exhibit innate bias; (2) whether the methods proposed in this research can be applied to other types of classification tasks; (3) whether the factors contributing to innate bias are limited to medical image analysis or are a more widespread phenomenon; (4) whether the methods proposed in this research can be applied to models that are trained using other types of data collections;

This research tackles the challenge of sequencing operations at an airport, where flights are mixed with take-off and landing sessions, and adjacent processes have different durations. Errors in scheduling these operations are affected by the order in which they are completed and their individual processing times. To minimize the risk of mistakes, we develop two methods to constrain the possible error rates. The first approach uses a bounding technique to limit the errors based on the order of operations, while the second method creates a priority system to control the errors by influencing the sequence of processing. These two methods are applied to the discrete-continuous shortest path problem, and we show that they can lead to solutions that are close to optimal in certain cases. This research provides solutions to error control problems in scheduling airport operations, as well as other settings with paths, such as the optimization of free flight paths, where sequences of discrete turns influence a continuous trajectory, and both aspects impact the overall journey time. This problem is shown to have an important application in the development of systems that use forecasts of future flights to optimize the sequence of take-offs and landings at busy airports, such as LaGuardia Airport, and can lead to better adherence to scheduled flight times. This can, in turn, reduce the risk of errors in predicting future flights and minimize the impact of such mistakes on flight delays. As a result, flights are completed on time more frequently, which in turn increases the chances of future flights being on schedule. This, in turn, enables the development of advanced prediction algorithms that handle errors in flight scheduling, and this algorithm is one of the best of its kind. This research demonstrates the value of controlling errors in scheduling airport operations, as well as other shortest path problems with discrete and continuous components, and highlights the significance of optimizing the sequence of operations at airports to minimize errors and improve the performance of forecasting systems that rely on scheduled flights. This, in turn, has implications for managing complex systems with interdependent components and tight constraints, and it provides a basis for further research into the development of algorithms for controlling errors in the solution of integer programs used to optimize the sequence of operations in such systems. We've developed a novel approach to creating a Schrödinger operator with rational coefficients that lack monodromy. This method involves utilizing generalized Hermite polynomials, which are an extension of the classic Hermite polynomials. These specialized polynomials are derived from a formula that relates them to a type of Bessel operator and are linked to a discrete Toda lattice. By applying a transformation to a discrete Toda lattice, we demonstrate that this results in a new Lax pair with a monodromy-free Schrödinger operator. This new operator can be expressed in terms of the Bessel operator and its invariant when discretized is explored, particularly in its finite and near-integrable forms. A connection to a q-analog of the Hermite polynomials is also identified. Generalized Hermite polynomials can also be defined through a difference approach inspired by the q-asymptotic algebra, extending the q-Bessel and discrete Toda lattice forms of these polynomials. A new difference Schrödinger operator with rational coefficients that lacks monodromy can be constructed using this approach as well. A discussion on constructing finite and near-integrable forms of the discrete Toda lattice through the difference approach is also presented. Our high-speed camera and force-measuring device analyses revealed that this noise standardizes at 0.32 milliseconds, corresponding to half the time it takes a crack to heal.  The relationship between this standardization and the format changes of the noise remains unexplored, offering a new direction for research in the field of nonlinear dynamics. This research introduces a method where options are valued in a way that reflects their true value, considering the costs of repeatedly hedging their underlying volatility. This approach results in a specific formula for valuing options, taking into account their potential losses in various market scenarios. If an option's value falls below this threshold, it becomes necessary for the option holder to deposit more funds with their broker to cover potential losses. If the value exceeds this threshold, the option holder can withdraw the excess funds from their account. A key aspect of this research is identifying the specific threshold at which an option's value becomes either insufficient or in excess, given the costs associated with hedging. This new understanding can be applied to all types of options and is shown to be a key factor influencing the amount of funds required from their holders. A key implication of this research is that it is possible to design options with thresholds set above their initial value, effectively creating options with built-in stop-loss mechanisms, even in the absence of external regulations. Furthermore, this research is relevant to the current discussion surrounding initial margin requirements, which are based on static delta hedging costs, but has identified a need for a more dynamic approach. A dynamic model of social mobility is proposed that transcends traditional approaches by considering intergenerational connections and professional advancement across multiple generations. A key feature of this model is the presence of what it calls "opportunity spaces," essentially positions that offer prospects for social mobility, which can be occupied by individuals or previous occupants. It is assumed that each new generation seeks to fill these spaces, with the best-equipped filling them quickly. As a result, opportunity spaces are filled by those who have the most "equipment," a combination of innate ability and skills acquired through education, which in turn are obtained by investing time that must be chosen before the game begins. The model leads to equilibrium where the distribution of opportunity spaces reflects the distribution of equipment, with certain implications including the potential for persistent social mobility disparities if certain conditions are met. The model also allows for an analysis of policy solutions, such as education investments, with consideration of potential reactions from future generations. A numerical solution for small-family cases is presented, along with graphical representations for larger family sizes, providing further insight into the model's dynamics. Perfect Crystal Wave (PCW) lasers represent a cutting-edge technology, characterized by advanced features including high power, precise control, seamless integration with optical fibers, and compromised sensitivity. This paper delves into the in-depth design of PCW lasers through the development of a comprehensive linear model, enabling both strategic design decisions and targeted innovations. By leveraging this model's capabilities, we successfully created a new high-power laser system, dubbed HiSw, which features a longer crystal length and a more compact design compared to the original PCW prototype. Analysis of this model also facilitated the reverse engineering of the PCW prototype, providing valuable insights that could be applied to the design of other laser systems, and it identified key performance indicators that could be adjusted during the design phase to meet specific requirements. Furthermore, this model's ability to predict the optimal operating parameters for a given configuration enables the exploration of novel design possibilities and could be employed in the repair of damaged laser systems by reverse engineering and reoptimizing them for maximum performance. Collective findings from both design and analysis phases of this research have the potential to contribute significantly to the advancement of photonic systems, in addition to providing a framework for both strategic design and reverse engineering of these complex systems. This research is primarily conducted within the framework of the European flagship project H2020 PHOTONICS21 with the ultimate goal of creating a next-generation of high-power laser systems that are capable of operating in multiple modes, offering a range of output beam characteristics, and incorporating advanced control features, all while maintaining their sensitivity when combined with optical fibers. This new type of laser technology will have far-reaching implications for a variety of applications spanning the fields of materials processing, biomedicine, communication technologies, and defense systems. However, generating such complex systems requires a multidisciplinary approach that involves both electrical and optical engineering, in addition to precise control techniques, as well as novel design methodologies that can handle the intricate interconnections between these disciplines. As such, design tools and methodologies like the one presented here will be crucial for the successful development of these cutting-edge laser systems, especially in fields such as photonics, biophotonics, and optoelectronics, where the interplay between engineering disciplines can be highly intricate, complicated, and difficult to model using conventional methods. In recent years, Neural Language Models have achieved remarkable success in various tasks including vocabulary ordering. This study delves into the performance of pre-trained models on this task, taking the BART model as a prime example. Our experiments reveal that these models excel at arranging words in a given order but struggle when the order is unknown. This discrepancy is illustrated through multiple metrics. Additionally, our analysis of the BART model's capabilities is complemented by a theoretical framework, which proposes that pre-trained models can leverage both local and global cues to achieve high scores in vocabulary ordering tasks. This framework is supported by a practical word arrangement task we designed, which involves both ordered and unordered subsets of words. Our findings suggest that the BART model's performance is optimal when the order is partially defined, i.e., in the presence of an intermediate-level order. This intermediate-level order is demonstrated to facilitate the BART model's word arrangement by providing a balance between order and disorder. Our research is an initial exploration into the performance of pre-trained language models on vocabulary ordering and paves the way for future studies in this area. The rapid dissemination of deepfake technology prompts the creation of a constantly evolving synthetic media that poses a threat to social stability and credibility. Present methods of detection, while improving, are hindered by their limitations in comparing facial images across time and domain. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a groundbreaking novel algorithm, the MD-CSDNetwork, capable of processing temporal and domain-based continuities in facial sequences. By leveraging a unique cross-sewn network that assesses sequence continuity and domain-based feature correlations, this algorithm outperforms existing benchmarks, including real-world evaluation, demonstrating a substantial boost in accuracy of up to 25.41% in certain categories. Furthermore, MD-CSDNetwork exhibits robustness in detecting deepfakes under various manipulation levels and surpasses current industry standards in real-world scenario testing. The exceptional performance of this algorithm is attributed to its in-depth understanding of temporal and domain-based characteristics in facial sequences. The exceptional performance of this algorithm is further validated through comprehensive ablation testing and comparison with industry-leading benchmarks, including explicit integration of manipulation information, proving its versatility. The code of this algorithm is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/NTUST-CVIG/mdcsdnet. The exceptional performance of this algorithm in real-world scenario testing has prompted the creation of a warning regarding the risks of deepfakes, available at https://www.eea.gov.tw/project/mdcsdnet. Ultimately, the paper concludes that centralized network management based on self-organization has the potential to address the scalability and sustainability issues facing future wireless networks. Karl Menger's 1923 paper introduced the concept of measuring geometric objects using intervals. He defined the Hausdorff measure, a key concept still in use today, and proposed using the measure of a shape's boundary to classify its topological properties. Menger introduced the concept of an "n-dimensional angle space" using this framework and discussed its implications. However, his work contained two unresolved problems from the early 20th century concerning such spaces. The first problem related to whether a 2-dimensional angle space can be 2-dimensional; the second, whether a 1-dimensional angle space is homeomorphic to the surface of a torus. The author of this paper provides the answer to these questions, demonstrating that a 2-dimensional angle space does not necessarily have two dimensions and a 1-dimensional angle space is not homeomorphic to a torus's surface. The author also shows the relationship between these spaces and those homeomorphic to spheres, tori, and projective planes. The solutions to these problems do not rely on order-theoretic methods commonly employed in order topology, instead utilizing a more analytical approach. The author also discusses the underlying metric properties of these spaces, highlighting the role of a well-known function from real analysis in their definition and analysis. The solutions to these problems were first discussed at the 2018 international conference on geometric functional analysis, and now with additional insights, at the 2022 conference on geometric analysis. This formula is applicable to a wide range of HFB configurations, including those involving multiple quasiparticle excitations, and is independent of the symmetry of the HFB wave functions. By employing the Fourier-Bessel transformation, we can efficiently determine the matrix elements of monopole and quadrupole operators, as well as other operators with specific angular momentum properties. Our method provides a crucial foundation for the development of microscopically inspired two-body interactions, and we outline the specific conditions necessary to achieve this goal. We also demonstrate the utility of our approach by investigating the decay properties of quasiparticle states, and we discuss the role of multipole components in monopole pairing, which has recently been observed in experiments involving quasifree scattering. We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units using identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency deviation. We're developing a general performance evaluation metric based on the radar cross-section and certain channel characteristics, and are comparing two specific access methods - CSMA and Slotted ALOHA - in terms of this metric. Our analysis of CSMA shows it offers better results than Slotted ALOHA, and also identifies key CSMA components that influence performance. We've derived an simplified formula for the average radar cross-section in CSMA networks, and are exploring ways to minimize interference in ALOHA networks by implementing a new protocol, CSMA-ALOHA, which allows units that detect the channel is busy to switch to a wait state rather than cut off their transmission. This innovation allows for greater utilization of available time slots, and resulting reductions in required backoff periods can lead to better average radar cross-sections in certain scenarios. A numerical analysis of all three protocols is presented, and indicates that in some cases, the improved handling of busy channel situations in CSMA-ALOHA can result in up to 300% improvement in average radar cross-section over standard ALOHA, and in certain scenarios, CSMA can offer 10-100 times better performance, but there are some scenarios where ALOHA can perform as well as CSMA. We've also found that increasing the number of time slots in ALOHA can also yield significant improvements in average radar cross-section, and have identified optimal time slot settings for both ALOHA and CSMA, and have successfully applied this knowledge in a multiple-access scenario, where ALOHA outperformed CSMA in some cases, but ultimately found that CSMA generally performs better. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information. Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph completion, we introduce a novel method that leverages low-rank representations for events and their corresponding temporal relationships. Unlike previous approaches that require model fine-tuning for each type of relation, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in achieving satisfactory performance without the need for relation-specific models. Furthermore, we investigate the applicability of our approach to large-scale temporal knowledge graphs. We conducted comprehensive experiments on both event and temporal knowledge graph completion, showcasing our method's superiority over existing benchmarks. Our results show notable improvements of up to 14.8% in MRE and 11.1% in Hits@50 metrics on event prediction, and notable gains of up to 5.6% in MRE and 6.1% in Hits@50 metrics on temporal prediction, supporting the use of low-rank representations for temporal knowledge graph completion. We also explore the concept of relation-aware decompositions, presenting an alternative method that achieves impressive results of up to 9.5% in MRE and 10.3% in Hits@50 metrics on event prediction and up to 4.3% in MRE and 5.1% in Hits@50 metrics on temporal prediction. We thoroughly examine our method's representational learning capabilities, uncovering a crucial insight that low-rank representations can be model-neutral, resulting in significant gains of up to 12.1% in MRE and 13.4% in Hits@50 metrics. We have an open-source implementation of our approach on GitHub at https://github.com/zheng-xy/STKG. We have also contributed 13,000 high-quality temporal fact triples to the TData release at https://github.com/zheng-xy/TData. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, requiring us to move beyond static views of data in search of meaningful cluster structures. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach that leverages data to inform the construction of a metriker-based metric, allowing us to define a dynamic distance metric. This dynamic metric is utilized in conjunction with the influence function to identify clusters in temporal data. A theoretical framework is established to guarantee the consistency of our clustering method as the sample size increases. Experiments with real and synthetic data demonstrate the method's effectiveness and efficiency. Notably, we collaborate with astronomers to apply our approach to the analysis of observational data from galaxies in the CHANDRA Cosmos Survey, leading to an innovative discovery of distinct cluster patterns in X-ray brightness. Our research offers a pioneering solution for clustering time series data and showcases its utility in solving an astronomical problem through data analysis. Text generation models like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are typically assessed by their ability to accurately replicate human-generated text. However, training these models proves to be challenging due to the need for high-quality labeled data. In contrast, we propose a novel GAN-based framework called SparseGAN that focuses not on mimicking existing text but rather on producing fresh text data while maintaining class balance and preventing overfitting. In our experiments, SparseGAN showed remarkable performance in class-balanced text generation, achieving state-of-the-art results on the SemEval 2017 Task 10 and 15% improvement in class balancing when evaluated using the F-score metric. Furthermore, our method requires minimal adjustments for extending to multi-class settings, making it an attractive solution for industries dealing with vast datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/ghr43/SparseGAN. 

In Supplemental Section A, we explore alternative sparse training methods along with Section B offering additional generation results in Section C and Section D covering hyperparameter selection through AutoML. Moreover, Section E provides generative sample distribution analysis while Section F outlines future directions for our framework. 

Sparse activation has been successfully applied in various contexts such as image processing, signal processing, and machine learning but its integration into generative models like GANs remains an open issue. Recent work combining generative models with adversarial training has yielded impressive results but has limitations such as requiring extensive labeled data and struggling with overfitting. In contrast, our proposed SparseGAN framework leverages sparse techniques to enhance both training and testing while achieving superior performance in class-balanced text generation without relying on pre-trained models.

Text generation using deep learning methods has gained significant attention in recent years but has been hindered by overfitting and the need for extensive labeled data. In response, our team explored alternative approaches including generative stochastic units, cumulative loss functions, and sparse training methods but found the simplest strategy to be the most effective. Consequently, we propose a novel GAN-based framework called SparseGAN that focuses on producing new data while maintaining class balance and preventing overfitting by incorporating sparse training.

In contrast to deep learning-based generation methods, our proposed framework achieves superior performance without relying on pre-trained models while offering a more straightforward design. Although SparseGAN requires high-quality labeled data for training, our results demonstrate its effectiveness in class-balanced text generation while minimizing adjustments for extending to multi-class settings.

In conclusion, our proposed framework provides a stress-test for deep learning-based generation methods by evaluating their ability to produce new data

The idea that life could be transferred between stars is known as interstellar panspermia, which has its roots in the ancient Greek concept of panspermia. To investigate this theory, we examine various situations in which planetary systems with life could be displaced, focusing on supernovae explosions, massive star migrations, and gravitational waves from binary black hole mergers. Using a statistical approach to assess discovery potential, we consider three detection methods: gravitational wave signals in laser interferometry experiments like LIGO and VIRGO; the five-axial microwave background experiment EDELWEISS and its successor QUBES; and the all-sky gamma-ray bursts observed by the Fermi GBM. Our analysis reveals that the most promising detection methods for extraterrestrial life transfer are gravitational wave signals in laser interferometry experiments like LIGO and VIRGO, with viability scores ranging from 0.13 to 0.27 for specific scenarios and detection tools. These results provide a foundation for future research in this area and emphasize the significance of experiments like the proposed Pioneers for Interstellar Astrophysics and Cosmology which aim to push the sensitivity of detector technology to the limits. Ultimately, such experiments have the potential to significantly contribute to our understanding of the cosmos by either confirming or refuting the possibility of interstellar panspermia. Furthermore, they emphasize the value of multi-messenger astronomy and the importance of continued investment in fundamental science and research. Additionally, the proposed experiment for the Square Kilometre Array, called ViViS, is expected to have a viability score of 0.45 for optical detection of gravitational waves, offering a higher detection rate for transfer events, as well as the detection of local transfer events in the solar system, such as the delivery of life to the Earth from the Sun-like star Skoplj. The score for ViViS is expected to increase to 0.55 with the addition of a next-generation microwave background experiment called QUBES, allowing for the detection of transfer events in the solar system, such as the delivery of life to Mars from the Earth. The detection of gravitational waves by the LIGO and VIRGO collaboration in 2015 has revitalized interest in interstellar panspermia and the proposed experiment for the Square Kilometre Array, called ViViS, is expected to have a substantial impact on the field of astrobiology and the search for extraterrestrial life, providing a robust and direct approach to investigating the possibility of interstellar panspermia. This research suggests that many undiscovered particles wait in the cosmos, their existence predetermined by this chain reaction of symmetry disruptions. Animal population studies often rely on two primary techniques: spatial capture-recapture modeling and resource selection analysis. While these methods individually provide valuable information about population dynamics and habitat preferences, they have distinct advantages when employed in conjunction with the principles of Bayesian modeling. This paper presents an integrated approach that utilizes capture-recapture data and resulting encounter history information to inform the estimation of abundance and utility mapping parameters in a spatial capture-recapture model, leveraging the flexibility of the R package JAGEN for efficient computation. This method enables a more robust estimation of population parameters, considering factors such as density, visibility, and trapping efficiency, and allows for the generation of posterior predictive distributions of encounter history probabilities and density maps. This approach was applied to data collected in Alaska during a study of moose population characteristics, yielding reliable estimates of population density and detailed utility maps that account for factors like visibility and trapping efficiency. The resulting models and data are also compared to traditional spatial capture-recapture models, demonstrating the former's ability to produce comparable but more accurate density estimates. This approach is deemed an enhancement to standard capture-recapture modeling, offering enhanced understanding and visualization of population characteristics and habitat preferences through the integration of capture-recapture data and resource selection information within a Bayesian modeling framework. Network polarization measurement techniques are diverse, reflecting varying views on the subject. Some researchers differentiate between network polarization as a state and phenomenon, and others see it solely as a state. Consequently, there is a lack of consensus on testing the validity of measurements in detecting network polarization. This study aims to categorize and standardize polarization measurement methods by distinguishing between those indicating the presence of polarization, those assessing its degree, and those ignoring its nuances. We propose a framework for evaluating the sensitivity of these methods and developed three procedures for assessing method reliability. Our evaluation of 10 methods against four protocols revealed the need for method developers to consider several factors including protocol compliance, scaling properties, reliability in distinguishing polarization from other network states, and sensitivity to blockmodel representations. Ultimately, our study advocates for a robust and precise definition of network polarization to guide future research. Additionally, our findings can be utilized as reference guidelines for creators of structural polarization measurement methods. Our research team is open to feedback and suggestions from experts in the field. The study's findings, together with method creator feedback, will contribute to development of a standardized framework for evaluating network polarization measurement methods. This unified framework will provide clear criteria for method creators to follow and ensure that future methods are creator- and model-agnostic, focusing solely on detecting and measuring network polarization. We explore how a strong internal connection within each layer affects the spread of information between the two layers, specifically when there are varying degrees of connection between the layers. Uncovering this phenomenon, we find that an extremely internal connection can either hinder or enhance interlayer transmission, depending on the levels of connection between the layers. When the connection between layers is weak, increased internal connection speeds information transmission. Conversely, when the connection between layers is strong, excessive internal connection slows transmission, only to accelerate further as it reaches a critical point. This complex behavior is further displayed in our findings on how this system responds to an external force. When the connection between layers is weak, some internal connection is required to resist the external influence. In contrast, when the connection between layers is strong, a significant amount of internal connection is needed to overcome external resistance, similar to how increased connection in a single layer would. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for Transformers through prompt-based learning. In this setup, HyperNetworks craft customizable prompts for each token in the input sequence, enabling a single model to excel in multiple tasks by providing tailored contexts. By formulating the prompts as learned outputs rather than fixed strings, HyperNetworks take on the responsibility of generating context, allowing for flexible integration of knowledge into the input sequence. This allows for the incorporation of external knowledge to be injected into the input sequence, even if it's not originally part of the input data. Through extensive experiments on diverse tasks like translation, summarization, and classification, HyperPrompt demonstrates its capacity for adaptability and achieving high performance across a wide range of tasks with minimal hyperparameter tuning. Notably, HyperPrompt achieves exceptional results on multi-task translation and zero-shot translation, outperforming other prompt-based models by a significant margin. Furthermore, HyperPrompt shows a notable advantage in generality, achieving a 6.5% improvement in supernet score as compared to other HyperNetwork-based models. In quantum field theory, parity-symmetry plays a significant role in the interaction between light and heavy particles. A particular subset of interactions, known as Cassini interactions, maintains parity symmetry, leading to distinct emission patterns for particles with the same mass but opposite parities. Our analysis reveals that these unique interactions can result in bundle emissions consisting of multiple particles, a phenomenon not observed in Rarita-Schwinger interactions, which are affected by parity symmetry violations, especially in a strong interaction regime, characterized by large values of the coupling constant. A key feature of Cassini interactions is the presence of a parity-symmetry-guarded bundle emission nonperturbative order, which can be probed in experiments using collisions of heavy ions at high energies, such as those produced in heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and LHC. Theoretical models predicting parity-symmetry violations can also be tested against Cassini interactions, providing new avenues for the study of parities in quantum field theory. Furthermore, our research raises fundamental questions regarding the origin of parity symmetry in nature, potentially shedding light on the subject through the lens of quantum field theory. In addition, we propose a novel concept, parities in quantum field theory bundles, which can serve as an interpretative framework for experimental data on parity-symmetry violations, even in cases where the underlying mechanisms are not yet understood. Ultimately, our exploration of parity symmetry within the context of quantum field theory poses an intriguing philosophical dilemma: whether the underlying parities are an inherent, objective property of nature or a construct of our observational methods, shaped by the constant interplay between nature and our observational tools. This enigmatic enigma is an existential aspect of all experimental inquiries and serves as an underlying thread throughout our research. In conclusion, our research on parity symmetry in quantum field theory rekindles the timeless debate between E. P. Wigner and A. S. Wightman concerning the role of parodies in the observation process, while our analysis on Cassini interactions and bundle emissions provides a critical foundation for exploring more intricate parodies in quantum field theory, such as those present in loop-level phenomena, like neutrino emission, which awaits experimental verification. Furthermore, our research paves the way for an in-depth examination of the relationship between parity symmetry and the fundamental principle of localism, setting the stage for an engaging theoretical debate on the interplay between these two fundamental principles in quantum field theory. In addition, our exploration of parity symmetry in quantum field theory has profound implications for theoretical models predicting parity-symmetry violations

A key challenge in designing an self-adaptive network is estimating network properties such as its size. This task is particularly difficult in small-world graphs with incomplete and unreliable information, especially when a small number of malicious nodes can compromise the fleet. In this research, a novel algorithm named Antisocial Neighbor Counting is developed to address this issue in small-world graphs under the influence of malicious nodes. The algorithm enables nodes to estimate the network size accurately, extending to a range of applications including efficient cleaning of malicious nodes and optimal resource allocation. A critical aspect of this solution is a new definition of small-world graphs properties, specifically degree and node failure probabilities, which is established as a fundamental theorem. A realistic simulation model is introduced to evaluate the algorithm's performance, showing ANTISOCIAL counting can achieve precise results even in networks with malicious nodes up to 10% of the total, in a network of 7000 nodes, in a time frame of 20 seconds. This algorithm is open-sourced and available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. This research is also accompanied by a short paper presented at Awerks 2020, reproduced in the appendix. Building on this work, a new algorithm named ANTISOCIAL counting called MultiPath has been developed, offering enhanced performance and wider applicability to large-scale networks, presented in a companion paper at Awerks 2021, also included in the appendix. This research is an extension of an earlier conference paper titled "Small World Network Size Estimation in the Presence of Malicious Nodes" presented at Awerks 2020, and "MultiPath: A New Algorithm for Small World Graphs" presented at Awerks 2021. Both of these conference papers are included in the appendix along with their review processes. We present a novel nonparametric method for estimating short-term queue sizes at road junctions using simple measurements from probe vehicles. Our approach requires minimal assumptions and doesn't rely on traffic model parameters. We utilize existing data from Los Angeles and New York City to test our method and find it consistently outperforms existing techniques in the field. Specifically, our evaluation shows our proposed function for estimation is more accurate than existing parametric and combinatorial approaches by significant margins in both cities, with an NME of 103.2 meters in Los Angeles and 121.5 meters in New York compared to estimated queue sizes of 54.9 meters and 65.5 meters for parametric and existing combinatorial methods respectively. We also explore how our method behaves over time and discover it is able to adapt quickly to changes in traffic conditions. Notably, our proposed method can provide reliable short-term estimations even with as few as 10-20 minutes of historical data from Los Angeles and 30-60 minutes from New York, providing a useful solution for applications that require rapid processing of traffic data. We also explore an extension to our basic method that utilizes additional data from inductive loops, which further enhances its performance, suggesting it holds promise for enhancing traffic monitoring systems using existing infrastructure in urban settings. Furthermore, our proposed method can provide precise short-term estimations for relevant practical applications such as calculating average queue sizes, determining percentages of roads with congestion and estimating the number of stopped vehicles. Lastly, our evaluation confirms the method's effectiveness in complex real-world scenarios, indicating it has the potential to become a valuable tool for traffic monitoring and management in urban areas. We also provide the method's implementation along with its evaluation on additional datasets from Los Angeles and New York, as well as further testing with additional urban settings in the U.S.A, namely from Chicago, Houston, and San Francisco, which is also included in the paper's supplementary materials available at https://drive.google.com/drive/foldes/1c6-8Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q1Q

This results in a more robust and accurate method for solving the Einstein Field Equations, one that eliminates the need for artificially narrow transition zones and can naturally handle complex interface dynamics. Recently, pre-trained models have achieved remarkable performance in various natural language processing tasks. However, due to their large size and high computational requirements, it's impractical for individuals or small-scale companies to use these models directly. Model aggregation through a process called knowledge distillation has been identified as a viable solution. In this method, a set of smaller models (teachers) train a single larger model (student) by comparing their output distributions with the outputs of the teacher models for a specific loss function. Although successful in some cases, this approach has its limitations as it solely relies on the comparison of output distributions and does not utilize the labels during training. As a result, the student model may not benefit as much as it could from the knowledge of the teacher models. We propose a novel framework called PILE that incorporates the labels as well as the output of the teacher models to calculate a loss function. During training, this framework allows a set of teacher models to calculate the logits of the classification layer for a given sample and then combines these logits through an iterative process to obtain a new set of aggregated logits. It then uses these aggregated logits along with the original logits from the teacher models to calculate a pairwise loss function that takes into account both the similarity and difference of the teacher models. We also introduce a label-guided loss function to ensure the student model focuses on the task at hand. The results of our experiments show that PILE achieves significant improvement over the baseline models and outperforms them in nearly all cases. For example, our model achieves an F1 score of 92.6% on the SST-2 dataset while the baseline models achieve an F1 score of 89.4% and 91.3%. We also find that our method is particularly effective when the number of teacher models is limited, which is often the case in real-world scenarios. We believe this is because PILE allows the student model to make the most out of the limited information provided by the teacher models. We apply our model to three different NLP tasks, including Sentiment Analysis, Semantic Role Labeling and Text Classification, and find that it generalizes well to these tasks as well. We also provide a comparison with other models that were also trained on the same datasets and found that our model performs at least as well as them in nearly all cases. The success of cutting-edge astronomy relies heavily on the involvement of the public in massive, automated data analysis projects. A crucial component in this endeavor is the operation of a large-scale citizen science platform, featuring numerous users working in unison on complex tasks through user interfaces powered by advanced machine learning tools. Here we present the technical components and operational frameworks of our platform, which incorporates a suite of machine learning applications to streamline data processing and facilitate remote participation. This infrastructure has enabled significant boosts in productivity and data handling speed, with an average user achieving analysis rates of ~200 seconds per object using the COLOS machine learning tool designed for galaxy morphology. With over 2,500 registered users and a diverse team of 28 institutions, our collaborative effort has analyzed ~10^7 objects across ~10,000 fields in a year's time frame, with an average of ~7 million objects analyzed per month by the user base of ~1,000-2,000 active participants. Our platform has shown great potential in inspiring interest in astronomy among the participating community, with an online survey indicating a notable increase in astronomy-related searches on Google among users over time. As a result of its effectiveness, this platform has become the default approach for conducting large-scale, remote, and high-throughput citizen science projects in the field of astronomy and beyond. With the upcoming launch of the Roman Space Telescope, a massive data set with unprecedented scale and complexity will be generated, requiring a significant increase in analysis speed and efficiency. To achieve this goal, we plan to enhance the performance of the COLOS machine learning tool by a factor of ~10 through a major upgrade, along with the development of more advanced machine learning applications and a new interface designed to facilitate easier participation among a broader community, including school-age children and young adults. This upgrade will be implemented in conjunction with the B612 Foundation, a leading non-profit organization dedicated to space safety and science education, with a focus on promoting STEM education and inspiring interest in astronomy among the participating community. With this upgraded version, we anticipate analysis speeds of ~20 seconds per object and the ability to process ~10^8 objects within a year's time frame, paving the way for a new era of collaborative data analysis in astronomy and beyond.
