We employ photonics to enhance the processing of astronomical catalogs by integrating three methods: matching templates, nearest neighbors, and tree-based searching. Specifically, we utilize silicon photonic technology to design various templates that can be cross-matched simultaneously, significantly improving processing speed compared to traditional methods. Our approach is highly adaptable and has been successfully tested with real astronomical data, resulting in accurate matches that match existing methods. Our findings are easily applicable to other fields that involve spectral cross-matching, and we outline a feasible path for implementing this technology using astrophotonic solutions in a real-world observational projects, such as the CHORDS survey. Our design for this large-scale project demonstrates a matching speed of around 10,000 times that of traditional methods, indicating that astrophotonic solutions are viable for handling massive astronomical datasets. We also explore the potential benefits of integrating machine learning algorithms with astrophotonic solutions to achieve even greater matching speeds and accuracy. Our design for silicon photonic templates has been featured in a Silicon Photonics Manufacturing Line, and we are in the process of integrating the waveguides with relevant astrophotonic components. We anticipate that this project will contribute significantly to the development of astrophotonic solutions for cross-matching methods and may pave the way for the integration of machine learning algorithms with silicon photonic technology. Our research is an extension of the work presented by Grobusch et al. (2020) and is an ongoing collaboration between the University of the Witwatersrand and the University of KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, the University of St Andrews in the United Kingdom, and the University of California, Santa Barbara in the United States. Our findings are also an outcome of the 2019 DST-NRF South Africa Research Chair Innovation Grant and the 2020 SARChI Research Grant. Medication pairs can sometimes have adverse effects if not monitored, prompting an interest in advanced computational methods to identify them. Our investigation offers a comprehensive analysis of relational machine learning methods in medication pair scoring by drawing from existing research and scoring techniques. A framework integrating principles of relational learning, CohRel, has been established to explain the performance of these approaches. CohRel comprises five key components derived from medication pair scoring studies, covering separate feature representations for medications, the incorporation of relationship characteristics, the integration of additional information, the handling of auxiliary relations, and a focus on combining scores via maximum likelihood estimation. A quantitative assessment of 15 scored medication pairs along with their adherence to industry standards revealed varied levels of accuracy. Nonetheless, an examination of medication pair scoring literature and a survey of healthcare experts identified several key issues, including the absence of openly accessible data and reliable scoring metrics, along with difficulties in replicating and comparing results. A survey of healthcare professionals also highlighted several limitations of existing approaches, such as cohesion and extrapolation challenges, along with an observed disconnect between features used in modeling and those found in medical literature, and the need for more transparent and explainable models. This extension addresses paths that, while not necessarily stationary, still exhibit a persistent structure and are characterized by a Hilbert space-valued stochastic integral. For supervised machine learning projects, using diverse data is crucial, but due to data privacy constraints, accessing a large, unified dataset can be difficult. Typically, researchers gather datasets from various sources, but these datasets are often dispersed and independent. In this paper, a novel Random Stroll Method is introduced to tackle these challenges by allowing independent datasets to participate in a learning process. Each participant creates smaller subsets of data and generates models through stochastic training, after which they enter a "stroll" phase where models are updated locally using a unique two-step optimization process. This process involves first updating the model using a subset of data from the current dataset, then refining it using a subset of data from other participating datasets. This process is repeated for each participating dataset until a predetermined number of steps is reached. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields models on par with those trained on unified, larger datasets, even when those datasets are not jointly sampled. This method shows particular promise when dealing with datasets that are independent and scattered, requiring minimal communication and coordination among participants. Our results also highlight the method's potential for producing interpretable models through integration of knowledge-based constraints. Our implementation and data sets are publicly available to facilitate replication and exploration of this method in various machine learning contexts. Our findings suggest that, even with small models, the RSM is efficient, with an average communication cost per participant more than 10 times lower than that of a single unified training iteration. Our code is written in Python using the PyTorch framework and is accessible at https://github.com/andersonbott/Stroll-for-Education, and our datasets are available at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1xQ5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5

This study validates the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum in numerical simulations of rotating viscous fluids undergoing moderate Reynolds numbers. The spectrum in question, first proposed by Zakharov and Kolmogorov, is a specific kinetic energy distribution pattern. Specifically, we are verifying the $k^{4/5}$ relationship for the spectrum's slope within the inertial wave range in the context of three-dimensional turbulent flows. Our analysis involves multiple independent numerical data sets obtained from high-resolution direct numerical simulations, and confirms that these results consistently match the $k^{4/5}$ model over a broad $k$ range within the inertial wave regime, despite initially deviating due to specific simulation conditions. This verification was achieved by employing an invariant measure technique to eliminate any finite Reynolds and grid number effects, thereby providing a more rigorous confirmation of the spectrum in question. This confirmation is further supported by an analysis of the anisotropy of the spectrum, which shows it to be in line with the Kolmogorov hypothesis, and thus contributes to a more comprehensive validation of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum within the context of three-dimensional inertial wave turbulence. This validation is significant as it provides a theoretical basis for explaining the generation of gravity waves in geophysical flows within specific parameter ranges. This research was supported by an ERC grant and simulations were conducted using HPC resources at CINES and GENCI. The code used for these simulations is publicly available on GitHub under an open-source license. Due to the complexity of these simulations, a significant amount of computational power was required, specifically up to 10 TF of sustained wall-clock time on 10,000 cores for certain runs. This verification of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum has confirmed previous stochastic model predictions and has provided a more precise understanding of inertial wave turbulence, which may be applicable to various turbulent flows in both planetary and lunar environments. This understanding could be utilized to develop new turbulence-reducing flow control strategies in various applications and could also be employed to improve existing scaling laws for the dissipation of energy in turbulent flows. Lastly, this research has demonstrated the feasibility of conducting high-resolution simulations of inertial wave turbulence on large HPC clusters and has identified several areas for future research in this field. This research has also provided a more precise validation of the anisotropic three-dimensional turbulence models and has contributed to a better understanding of the relationship between turbulence and anisotropy in various flow applications. This research involves a simulation-based framework, leveraging a novel method that incorporates elements from systems thinking and quality improvement, to analyze the effectiveness of mandatory mental health therapy for convicted individuals within the criminal justice system. The model, with the participants' input, identifies key factors influencing the mental well-being of this population and assesses the impact of mandatory therapy as part of their rehabilitation on overall mental health. Results indicate that, even with existing systemic challenges, the criminal justice system's mental health support services display improvement with mandatory therapy for convicted individuals, with further reductions in mental health-related issues over time. Additionally, the model's results are validated through real-world data from the Texas Department of Criminal Justice. With the simulation model's capability to adapt to diverse system settings, it offers a valuable tool for the criminal justice system to enhance mental health support and overall well-being through data-driven decision making. A common issue in medical image segmentation, especially under low-labeling conditions, is the risk of overfitting due to limited annotation data. To address this challenge, researchers often employ regularization techniques in deep learning models. In this study, we introduce an unconventional strategy to prevent overfitting, drawing from the concept of data consistency. By applying a straightforward form of consistency regularization, we effectively expanded the effective use of unlabeled data without introducing significant computational expenses or complex configurations. Our experiments demonstrated that this technique yields consistent outcomes when compared to segmentation models incorporating adversarial and total variation regularization, as well as Graph Attention Networks, across multiple datasets, including brain and colon segmentations. Furthermore, our study uncovered that this simple regularization technique is a competitive alternative to more intricate methods, requiring no additional parameters or complex optimizations, which could be of use to practitioners and researchers in the field of medical image analysis. Our code is publicly available for reproducibility purposes. Our research discovered that, in certain scenarios, this simple method outperformed models incorporating unlabeled data, which warrants further exploration and is an open issue for data experts. Additionally, our experiment's CR metric indicated that the model's performance improved at a slower rate than baseline models, which could be an interesting aspect for additional analysis. Our study's findings suggest that deep learning models incorporating this technique may need more data to achieve optimal results, which could be an interesting aspect for further investigation. Between 2015 and 2018, the Large Hadron Collider delivered 25 Fourier momentum transfer values ($\mathbf{nb}$) of integrated luminosity, enabling the ATLAS collaboration to conduct in-depth analyses of jet metabolism at higher energies previously unexplored. As a result, the number of events exceeding the experiment's jet-based signal threshold in the full $\eta$ range increased substantially, posing a significant design limit on the 2014-built ATLAS jet trigger system. To maintain above 99% efficiency in picking up high-energy jets below 1 second, the system was re-designed and re-engineered for the new data conditions. This effort involved creating a new zero-suppression trigger decision module based on an FPGA circuit featuring 256-bit wide and 5-GBps read and 3-GBps write capabilities, powered by a custom-designed multi-Gb/s serial transceiver. This new module, which provides 3 simultaneous 32-bit unsigned integer outputs with up to 50 M 32-bit words per second each, provides a useful demonstration of the capabilities of modern high-speed digital design and could serve as a useful reference for other experiments facing similar challenges. This talk outlines the design of the new zero-suppression trigger decision module and presents the reasons and design choices made during its development. This project also involved creating a custom 8-bit 1.6 GHz RISC-V processor, a custom 256-bit wide 160 MHz non-volatile memory controller, as well as an 8-bit 3.2 GHz microcontroller, all of which were designed using a 5-layer Ultrascale+ FPGA board. This talk will cover the architecture of these custom cores and their performance in comparison to commercial equivalents. This project was carried out as part of a research collaboration between the University of Toronto and NRC Canada. This talk will be delivered at the 2019 DATE conference in Grenoble, France. The growing interest in immersive, interactive technologies like virtual reality and gaming prompts the development of advanced visual simulation methods. To create realistic, articulated characters for these platforms, researchers face significant challenges in producing visually appealing, accurate animations, especially in scenarios that go beyond simple, linear movements. Existing approaches to visualizing structured shapes, like human avatars, fall short in this area because they typically rely on superficial, two-dimensional representations rather than comprehensive, three-dimensional models. To address this, we propose a novel methodology, called Articulated Neural Rendering, a comprehensive framework that can generate highly realistic, detailed animations of virtual characters from any perspective, using only minimal, two-dimensional reference images. In contrast to existing methods, ANR utilizes a holistic, three-dimensional model of the avatar and employs a sophisticated neural network to transform two-dimensional reference frames into accurate, articulated poses, thereby providing a more comprehensive visualization of the avatar. To demonstrate the capabilities of this method, we created a range-extended dataset featuring over 200 high-resolution, animated poses, and showed that it outperforms existing techniques in visual simulation, delivering far more realistic results. ANR has significant implications for the development of realistic character animations in virtual reality, gaming, and other visualization applications, and is available at https://github.com/antoniopadova/ANR, along with the new dataset at https://antoniopadova.github.io/ANR-dataset/. Through this work, we aim to contribute to the advancement of computer graphics research in the articular visualization domain and to facilitate the development of high-realism character animations in various visualization applications. ANR is particularly suited for rendering human avatars in virtual environments and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual simulation. To facilitate further research in this area, we introduce a new evaluation metric called Articulated Structural Similarity, which assesses the quality of animated shapes, and provide evidence that optimizing ANR using this metric yields animations that are preferred over baseline models in user studies. Building upon ANR, we explored several extensions to this method, including an improved neural network architecture called Articulated Multi-Resolution NeRF, that can generate high-realism animations from sparse pose data, and a new dataset called Animations in Motion, that features over 3000 frames of realistic, light-field animations. These extensions and the associated data are available at https://antoniopadova.github.io/ANR-dataset/. Ultimately, we envision ANR to have a significant impact on the development of high-realism character animations

Building on intuitive neural network techniques and leveraging our experimental capabilities, we've created a method to measure time-dependent system dynamics through a simple, interpretable neural network that ensures the accuracy of its results. When applied to the example of quantum Haar chaos, our approach yields a clear, meaningful connection between system mixing and attractor localization within the neural network's framework. This has allowed us to link neural network performance to established indicators of quantum chaos, demonstrating the value of our graph neural network in exploring the relationship between system chaos and the behavior of neutral atoms in optical lattices. Furthermore, we've established the principle that our approach can be universally applied to any time-dependent spectral transformation of a system's spectrum, and we're using this understanding to design a neutral atom array-based experiment to determine whether systems with similar characteristics but different implementations, such as neutral atoms versus trapped ions, also behave similarly. In doing so, we're establishing the foundation for using our experimental data to drive advancements in theoretical models of quantum chaos through supervised machine learning, even in situations where the models are initially agnostic regarding the system's spectral properties. Ultimately, we're delivering a framework for identifying and reaching the boundaries of quantum chaos through a critical intersection of experimental research, graph neural networks, and machine learning. Additionally, we're exploring the broader implications of our findings for the study of complex systems in other areas, and we believe that our approach will enable a new era in interdisciplinary research where the interpretation of experimental data is guided by theoretical models, and conversely, the design of experiments is informed by the principles of data analysis. A new method is introduced for obtaining an optimal estimate of the mean parameters of a mixture model, without requiring knowledge of the underlying component distributions. This method is based on an expansion of the Kullback-Leibner divergence and results in a feasible solution for a standard optimization problem. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in several scenarios, including the creation of synthetic datasets and sampling theory, and show that it yields more efficient results than existing methods. Specifically, we find that the proposed method leads to a significant increase in the accuracy of estimated means in synthetic datasets, and a notable improvement in the coverage probability of confidence intervals for the true population mean. This method is applicable to a broad class of mixture models and can be implemented using widely available computational software. We have also developed an extension to this method that enables the estimation of components of a mixture model, and this method is currently being explored for potential applications in sampling theory. All of the computational software used to develop and evaluate this method can be made available upon request.

Knowledge tracing has achieved remarkable performance in recent years with the advancement of machine learning and educational technology. This paper demonstrates that this space retains closure under composition, provided $X$ is rational and has only a finite number of non-compact components. The closure of the space of elliptic differential operators on $X$ is shown to be equicontinuous when $X$ is projective and compact. The primary goal of this research is to prove that the closure of the space of elliptic differential operators on $X$ contains all differential operators with holomorphic coefficients when $X$ is irreducible and non-compact. As the number of mobile devices contributing to a learning model grows, synchronizing updates can become inefficient. To address this issue, researchers explored asynchronous learning methods but were limited by the requirement for a gradient constraint, hindering the participation of devices with large batch sizes. This paper introduces a novel asynchronous approach that allows unconstrained gradients and eliminates the need for a constraint. In our proposed method, updates are stored in a buffer and accumulated until a connection with the server is established. This allows devices to learn from mini-batches of any size, free from constraints, and significantly reduces the communication frequency required. Our results show that this method achieves comparable performance to FedProx, the current state-of-the-art, while enabling the participation of up to 76% more devices with large batch sizes. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengdianxiao/Unconstrained-Buffered-Async-FL. This work was done in collaboration with Google's Pixel team and has been presented at ICML 2021. Our team's subsequent research built upon this foundation and explored the integration of our proposed approach with existing algorithms, resulting in the development of Buffered Ascynchronous Coordinated Parallel Learning. This new method was found to be robust against fluctuations in device participation and allows for the seamless addition or removal of devices at any time. Our results with this new method have shown further improvements, indicating that it is capable of supporting up to 85% more devices with large batch sizes. This finding, combined with our previous results, suggests that our proposed approach can facilitate the participation of at least 75% more mobile devices in federated learning settings. Our team's research on this topic has also led to the identification of a key challenge in FL, which is characterized by the uneven participation of devices. This issue has been addressed in our research through the development of BACP-FL, which is designed to counter the fluctuations in device participation patterns. Our results with this new method have shown significant improvements over existing methods, which is attributed to its ability to efficiently utilize the gradients from devices that participate frequently. To accelerate and reduce costs in speech recognition training, we've developed a novel approach that leverages pre-trained models from other languages for data-scarce languages. Our method involves two transfer scenarios: a) using pre-trained models with limited data from one language (L1) for another language (L2), and b) combining data from two languages for L1, and using that data to train L2. We've conducted experiments in both English and Chinese, and our results show that our rough-to-fine strategy achieves 8.3% better word error rate (WER) and our cross-language strategy achieves 10.3% better WER compared to training alone in each language, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/lys0m/xf-xlm-xlsr. Furthermore, we've observed that our cross-language strategy can achieve good results even with a) L1 having abundant data and L2 having scarce data, and b) the two languages being dissimilar, resulting in 12.5% and 18.8% WER reduction in these scenarios respectively. Our findings suggest that our method is a powerful tool for reducing data requirements in multi-speaker and robustness evaluations, and has potential in natural language processing tasks like text-to-speech. Our model's resilience to noise is an added benefit, as it reduces the need for specific speech augmentation techniques, allowing 30% less data compared to baseline models. Our research paves the road for further exploration of our method in low-resource speech recognition, especially with the constantly growing disparity between supply and demand for annotated data. Our model's performance in some cases is close to that with data-specific fine-tuned models, yet it has the advantage of being highly versatile and adaptable to a wide range of setups, including those encountered in real-world scenarios, for which we provide qualitative analysis. Our work also highlights the significance of open-unlimited evaluation, as it highlights the difference in WER by up to 11% when comparing it to the one reported by the evaluation script. By examining various decay modes and applying quantum mechanical principles to particles like kaons and pions, as well as charm and bottom quarks, we aim to identify key signatures that can aid in experimental verification of $\rho^0(1450)$. However, there has been no concrete theory to connect these two to the 1.5 GeV scalar and related structures until the proposal of the "dark meson" model, which posits they are all members of the same non-quark-based meson family, with $\rho^0(1450)$ being the most likely candidate to explain $f_J(1500)$. Using a Monte Carlo method with an exactly calculated phase diagram as a guide, we've calculated the critical exponents and critical dimensions that distinguish different universality classes in the model for both its symmetric and asymmetric phases. Additionally, we've investigated the critical behavior of the Higgs order parameter in all evaluated universality classes and have identified several of them, including the Ising and scalar conformal universality classes, which can be realized depending on the potential's parameters that are near its triple point where superfluid, Ising, and scalar conformal phases coexist. These coexistence points can be located by calculating the dimensions of all relevant primary fields on the boundary between any two coexisting phases, which are typically given by sets of linear equations that are also provided with this submission. Our research provides an extensive collection of critical exponents and critical dimensions that can be used to describe coexisting phases in the model and we believe that some of these values will also be applicable to other models that feature Higgs field representations of the SU(Nc) gauge group. Our simulation's data, along with an extensive list of tested model parameters and all calculated critical exponents and critical dimensions, is available for download as part of this submission. When marine robots navigate, they need to balance exploring their surroundings with minimizing risk. Our research focuses on this challenge under the name Marine Navigation, a newly defined problem. Unlike existing problems that involve balancing exploration and safety in changing environments, Marine Navigation takes into account the fact that environmental variations usually occur over extended periods. Taking a stochastic process view of the changing environment, we propose a novel approach, SPAN, which utilizes a Gaussian process to model both the underlying state and temporal changes within the state. Taking into account that many environmental states are known to be stationary and stable over time, SPAN incorporates an adaptive threshold to filter out unnecessary models, thus preventing unnecessary exploration. Taking high-dimensional observations into account, SPAN also uses a neighbor-based approach to efficiently learn across smaller, more manageable subsets of features. Through simulated experiments in diverse underwater scenarios, SPAN consistently demonstrates its ability to learn from limited observations, efficiently navigate its surroundings with minimal risk, and effectively compare against models that either rely on strong assumptions about the environment or are computationally infeasible for real-world applications. SPAN is available online at https://github.com/ethan-ai/SPAN. SPAN is an important breakthrough for solving Marine Navigation, a newly defined problem, and temporal variation learning in general, and is an important step for future work in this domain which will be further explored in future research. Due to the low spatial density of star-forming regions in a galaxy, it's challenging to map its two-dimensional structure. A key obstacle lies in distinguishing a galaxy's intrinsic features from those projected by observing the star-forming regions three-dimensionally. By comparing various projection views of a galaxy's three-dimensional structure, a method is developed to distinguish a galaxy's intrinsic two-dimensional structure from its projected two-dimensional appearance. Using this approach on a sample of 38 spiral galaxies, a known spiral pattern type 'Multi-Element' is identified for nearly half of them. A Multi-Element galaxy features multiple separate spiral arms. The proposed method builds upon a novel approach to classification, where a base model is used to generate features from COVID-19 images, and these extracted features are then compared to corresponding patient-relevant features. To improve the accuracy of the model, contrastive mixup classification is employed in multiple stages. The introduction of noise is also used as an augmentation technique to enhance model performance through the reduction of overfitting. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, resulting in improved results when compared to existing models. Specifically, our model achieved 72.76% accuracy in the COVID-19 severity classification task, representing a 5.32% improvement over the baseline model. Furthermore, the model's performance was found to be robust in scenarios involving limited dataset conditions and noise addition. We established a few key factors that influence domain transfer in GER, including the quality of source and target languages, with potentially negative consequences if they clash. Researchers and survey takers often encounter situations where single responses are rounded to the nearest integer to the closest hundred for a total estimation. This study reveals that, statistically, the estimated totals generally fall within a specific range of $\pm 26.5$ around the actual total when there is no information loss. When rounding to the nearest integer, estimates become binned, leading to potential overestimation or underestimation of actual totals ranging from -$99.5 to infinity or -$\infty$ to $99.5$, depending on the specific range in question. A new model is introduced to handle these issues by taking into consideration both the specific range in question and the standard deviation of the estimates, now referred to as the "ambiguity". Through simulation, this model demonstrates effectiveness in estimating actual totals more accurately than traditional methods in various scenarios, particularly when standard deviations are high. This model is applied to two real-world data sets, yielding results that are either on par with or more accurate than alternative estimation techniques. Notably, this model performs notably better than other methods in scenarios with high standard deviations or significant information loss, achieving actual totals estimates that are either overestimated or underestimated by no more than half of the total estimation range of $99.5$. This model is made available for public use through an R package called "estimround". This research offers a new approach for estimating actual totals based on rounded responses and provides an R package for replicating and extending the model's findings. The model is designed to handle rounding to the nearest hundred but can be adapted for rounding to the nearest ten or other specific ranges. This study is an important step in addressing survey nonresponse and data quality issues that arise from rounding actual responses to the closest integer. These findings are relevant to any research involving single-response rounded to the nearest hundred and have the potential to be applicable to other research scenarios that involve rounding in different units. This research is an important contribution to the statistics and survey research communities, and the R package it introduces is a valuable resource for replicating its results and extending its findings. The study's findings are also of use to any researcher dealing with rounded data and actual totals estimates that range from -$99.5 to infinity or -$\infty$ to $99.5$, and the model it presents is a crucial tool for improving actual totals estimates when standard deviations are high or information loss is significant. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, was initially classified as an irregular galaxy by 1958 and a spiral by 1971 observers. A notable absence of HII regions along its outer rim was noted as early as 1971. We have obtained high-resolution H-alpha and R-band images with the Gemini GMOS, showing that this missing portion is not an edge but rather a distinct, low-density disk that has been kept collisional by nearby spiral galaxies. This outer ring at a distance of roughly 82 kpc measures 101 kpc in length and exhibits a constant density. We have calculated the total mass of its surrounding halo to be in the range of 10^11 to 2 x 10^12 solar masses based on several key factors, including the density of the disk, the velocity of the galaxy, and the lack of HI absorption. A similar phenomenon was observed in the nearby spiral galaxy UGC 6095 with a much larger diameter of approximately 185 kpc, and we have made a hypothesis about the possible existence of a small, faint spiral galaxy pair near UGC 8839.

Re-identifying individuals across different video datasets based on their visual characteristics is a challenging task in video-based re-identification. This task is made even more complex by the absence of re-identification labels in extensive datasets. In this paper, we introduce a novel unsupervised re-identification approach that leverages contrastive learning to match individual frames within a given dataset to each other, thereby learning a robust feature extractor that yields compact and discriminative visual representations. To efficiently explore the dataset, we employ random walk strategies to effectively expand the initial pairwise comparisons through sequential matching, thus learning a holistic understanding of each individual's appearance. To evaluate our method's effectiveness, we conducted comprehensive experiments on nine diverse individuals across seven million frame pairs from the MARS, iQIYI, and VIOLET datasets, demonstrating its superiority over baseline models by a significant margin of 21.3% in mean average precision and 10.5% in mean average recall compared to the state-of-the-art unsupervised re-identification method RFL. Notably, our method achieved impressive results even without relying on external datasets or re-identification labels, setting a new standard for unsupervised individual re-identification across extensive datasets. Our code and models have been made publicly available for further research. In addition to individual re-identification, our method exhibits potential applications in action recognition and object re-identification, as evidenced by its superior performance in action recognition tasks, with improvements of 6.3% in top-1 accuracy and 5.3% in top-5 accuracy on the VisDA-2019 action recognition benchmark, as well as re-identifying individuals in object detection datasets, as shown through thorough experiments and analyses presented in an accompanying supplementary document. This work sets a new high mark for unsupervised individual re-identification on the MARS, iQIYI, and VIOLET datasets with a score of 0.2946 at 10,000 frames per individual, offering valuable insights for future research in the field. Using the lattice QCD, we calculate the correlation between two flavor fields within a pion, which yields the squared magnitude of pion's charge form factor. Our simulation, conducted at nearly physical quark masses, takes advantage of two flavors of exact quark propagation and an O(a^3) improved lattice action for the pion's momentum. As a result, we obtain reliable form factor data at multiple momentum values up to Q^2=1 GeV^2 in the large momentum regime. A comparative study with lattice QCD's cross-correlation and Ioffe-Quark Model reveals that our direct two-flavor correlation method provides a more comprehensive understanding of the pion's structure. Moreover, our lattice data for the pion's electric and magnetic form factors are consistent with each other's prediction, demonstrating a key property of hadron physics. Ultimately, this study paves the way for further investigations of the pion's structure using our correlation observables, which can be related to other physics phenomena. For instance, we discuss the connection between the pion's correlation and decay constants, as well as WPCHE (Ward identity-derivable Polarized Quark Conditional Histograms Effective action), which can be used to describe the quark's role in the meson's polarization. Therefore, improving our understanding of the pion will have implications for our comprehension of quark's internal structure and the meson's interaction with other particles. Lastly, this study highlights the significance of exploring hadron correlations on the lattice, a theme that will be the focus of our forthcoming research in this domain. Our research is also relevant to JLab 12 GeV and the E18, E18-01 experiments, providing a theoretical framework for the experimental measurement of the pion's structure. Our previous research revealed an underrepresented phase of classical T Tauri stars during their transition to full hydrogen burning, which we termed the "Post-Main Sequence (MS)" stage. To further investigate this stage, we assembled a new sample of 57 T Tauri candidates in the Chamaeleon II and III star-forming regions using the VOSHI all-sky survey and SPARKS photometry. We particularly focused on XX Cha, a prototype of the Post-Main Sequence stage, and observed its behavior as it entered the phase due to its unique position in our data set. Based on light curve fluctuations, specifically using generalized Lorenzian amplitude and FRICK variability indexes, we distinguished two different accretion patterns in our sample: a primary group that follows a linear relationship between accretion and light curve fluctuations, and a secondary group that shows an offset from this line. XX Cha fell into the secondary group, exhibiting an abnormal relationship between its light curve fluctuations and accretion behavior. This discrepancy led to an overestimation of accretion rates among T Tauri stars with fluctuation similar to XX Cha when using light curve fluctuations as an indicator. We also calculated a new threshold for light curve fluctuations above 0.25, which differentiates primary and secondary groups, and discovered a wider dispersion of accretion rates in T Tauri stars than previously reported due to biases in earlier studies. This new study provides a revised definition for the Post-Main Sequence stage in T Tauri stars, specifically those with fluctuation above 0.25, and estimates a duration of this stage at around 2-3 million years for all T Tauri stars in the Chamaeleon II and III regions. XX Cha's unique accretion profile led to an overestimation of its age when comparing it to other stars in the same regions, resulting in an age of 2.3 million years for XX Cha, an age that supports the initial 2-3 million year estimate for the Post-Main Sequence stage. Finally, we discovered a correlation between light curve fluctuations and the presence of a disk in T Tauri stars, as well as an increased variability among T Tauri stars with a disk, which contributed to an increased dispersion of accretion rates among T Tauri stars with fluctuation above 0.25. Social inequality varies significantly based on the economic system in place, prompting the inquiry as to which aspects contribute to its persistence. Chances and income play a crucial role in this dynamics, as they have a dual impact: can either concentrate to exacerbate disparities or diffuse to reduce them, depending on specific circumstances. The term "inequity of chance" refers to the situation that arises when there are initial disparities in chances, leading to varying income outcomes, regardless of whether this inequality is inherent or developed over time. This concept is the focus of this paper, which explores its implications through mathematical modeling and simulation. The results indicate that inequity of chance leads to income reallocation, resulting in increased overall variability, in addition to stimulating the development of new inequalities and causing existing ones to worsen, as seen in both stochastic and deterministic models, and particularly in their mean-field and Ising versions. These findings are particularly evident in the latter, as they allow for the emergence of multiple distinct inequality levels. The sensitivity of these phenomena to temperature, order, and interaction parameters was examined, and the observation made that certain parameter settings can give rise to situations where chances become less important than income in determining overall inequality, as well as the occurrence of ferrimagnetic behavior and the creation of new inequalities at higher temperatures. The potential applications of these results to policy decisions are also discussed, along with the need for further empirical research into how chances and income relate in different economic systems. The ever-expanding use of machine learning (ML) through online services necessitates more effective and transparent data preparation for these systems. A significant obstacle in achieving this transparency is related to the opaque nature of ML models, which hinders their users from identifying data issues and taking corrective actions. To address this challenge, we introduce an innovation - data troubleshooting through the computation of Shapley significance values. Initially, we calculated these values for individual data points by using an ensemble of ML models to classify them as normal or anomalous. Next, we calculated these values for entire data subsets by breaking down the performance of the ML model using a data-driven approach. Finally, we experimented with these methods using an open-source platform for end-to-end ML pipelines, and the results showed that we can identify the most significant data points and subsets that contribute to the model's anomalies. Our data-driven approach for sub-sets outperformed a comparable model by 15% in accuracy and 1.5 times in computation time compared to our baseline method. Our research provides users with online services that use ML with a valuable tool to maintain the quality of their data and improve their classification performance. The mysterious origins of radio galaxies in distant globular clusters remain an unsolved puzzle. To tackle this, the MAVERIC (Mapping the Absorption towards the Centers of Extragalactic Radio Sources in Globular clusters) survey utilizes CHANDRA to map absorption in front of 26 radio galaxies within 10 kpc, coupled with optical observations to identify the host clusters, their masses, and core properties. This targeted approach concentrates on low-luminosity radio galaxies in a critical breadwinner population, and studies how their number and power correlate with cluster mass and core conditions. CHANDRA observations revealed three primary patterns: (1) Source absorption in vacuo, (2) Colliding winds in both the host cluster and at the galaxy's core, (3) Evidence of activity inside the cluster due to a straying black hole, despite no central star formation. Ultimately, the MAVERIC study discovers that one-fifth of low-luminosity radio galaxies within 10 kpc possess sufficient cluster mass to generate their observed power, while the remainder's energy sources remain enigmas yet to be solved. The MAVERIC study opens up possibilities and paths for the investigation of radio galaxies in clusters across the universe, and within our own Milky Way. The full data set of the MAVERIC study, featuring 24 radio galaxies towards the Center of the Milky Way, will be released in a follow-up paper. The MAVERIC study's resources are also made available at https://archive.stsci.edu/maeviz/ and zooniverse.org/ project/maeviz, for researchers and the public to explore. The MAVERIC study breaks new ground in radio galaxy research and paves the way for the investigation of numerous unknown sources of radio energy within our own Galaxy and beyond. The MAVERIC study's findings and methodology set a precedent and establish a new standard for future research in this field. We work on a frequently encountered problem in computational biology and other fields, where hyperedges representing interacting entities are used to describe complex systems through a graph. However, due to noisy or limited data, a hypergraph approximation is often sought for better understanding and prediction. This task can be viewed as a sparse hypergraph reconstruction issue on a background grid, which we address using a novel method that leverages a previously established scoring function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to a real-world dataset from the ENCODE project, comparing its performance to alternative methods. Our results show that our method achieves higher accuracy and efficiency in predicting interacting entities in a complex system compared to existing methods, which can be extended to other hypergraph construction scenarios. Furthermore, we explore and identify key parameters that influence the performance of our method, which involves a score system that prioritizes certain attributes over others. We propose an advanced concept for predicting directional emission patterns in microcavity lasers by combining entropy with their electromagnetic field analysis. This approach goes beyond existing methods that rely on intensity or intensity-related measures, providing a more comprehensive understanding by considering the complexity of electromagnetic field patterns. We apply this idea to several examples of microcavity lasers with various geometries and photon confining capabilities, demonstrating its effectiveness and accuracy in identifying regions of low entropy, which indicate directional emission patterns. Our research reveals that low entropy regions often resemble those predicted by vectorial beam transformation and the entropy change of resonant modes, but can also predict new modes of directional emission in lasers with high symmetry and strong photon confinement, describing their emission patterns in terms of soliton-like modes, and showing that increasing the asymmetry of a microcavity laser reduces the entropy of resonant modes. Our findings can help researchers design microcavity lasers with optimal properties and understand the relationship between electromagnetic field patterns and entropy in confined environments. We believe our research can be applied to other areas where confined electromagnetic fields play a crucial role and influence each other's behavior. We investigate the connection between thermal atoms in a gas and the photons they emit, specifically focusing on the link between the temperature of the atoms and the statistics of the photons. Our analysis reveals how the Wigner function's negativity indicates the presence of collective influence between the atoms, and this effect is most evident in photonic intensity distributions from systems with large spatial separations. Our theoretical findings are supported by experimental data from thermal rubidium vapor. As the temperature of the atoms decreases, the photonic intensity distribution transitions from a thermal pattern to one characteristic of laser light. Notably, the boundary between these two behaviors is marked by the phenomenon of thermal light parabolic distribution, which occurs when the atoms are closely packed and there is a significant influence between them. When the atoms are farther apart, the parabolic distribution gives way to a two-dimensional thermal distribution within a certain temperature range. When the atoms are very distant from each other, the photonic intensity distribution is similar to that produced by a coherent laser source, and the associated correlation between photonic intensity and position is a manifestation of the large spatial separations. This means that even when the atoms are no longer influenced by each other, the photonic intensity distributions can still reflect the collective influence present in the thermal vapor, effectively encoding this information in a way that is accessible through the study of photons emitted from thermal atomic groups. As a result, it becomes feasible to non-invasively gauge the temperature distribution and correlation structure of thermal atoms by analyzing the emitted photons. This raises the possibility of utilizing the photons emitted from these atoms as a means of detecting the presence of influence in thermal vapor, a phenomenon that may have implications for our understanding of open quantum systems and the effects of environment on coherence and entanglement. In addition, this discovery may also provide a foundation for developing novel methods for temperature control in atomic systems through the management of photonic intensity and correlation in real space and time. As well as offering potential for improving the performance of optical communication systems by utilizing thermal light sources with specific temperature conditions, or by exploring new ways of generating and utilizing multi-mode non-Gaussian states in optical communication networks. Furthermore, this research may also facilitate the realization of novel quantum imaging methods that take advantage of the unique properties of thermal light and its interactions with matter. Additionally, this breakthrough may also facilitate the development of novel approaches to study open quantum systems, coherent and correlated matter systems, and may also provide new avenues for exploring the effects of environment on quantum coherence and entanglement. Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning methods are crucial for data-efficient training in settings with vast numbers of episodes and diverse exploration paths. Many current methods focus on learning from individual experiences but may struggle with complex tasks that require coordinated actions between agents. To address this challenge, we introduce an end-to-end framework for learning from positive trajectories in offline multi-agent reinforcement learning settings. In contrast to existing methods that require constructing an individual policy for each agent using their individual experience trails or neighboring agents with similar state-action profiles, our framework leverages a single unified model that can handle the interdependencies between agents by maximizing the mutual information between their respective state-action profiles. In experiments, our method achieves superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art baselines in multiple challenging multi-agent reinforcement learning scenarios with significant coordination requirements, including complex cooperative tasks and competing agents in a grid world and Multi-Agent Transportations. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghs85/MPMRLP.

We developed a novel method for aligning MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to converge on alignment settings. However, these methods are often hampered by low-quality megavoltage images, which can impede convergence and yield suboptimal results. In contrast, our approach involves training a Convolutional Neural Network to directly output transformation parameters between images, bypassing the need for iterative optimization. By doing so, we are able to bypass image similarity metrics and associated challenges, instead relying on the network's ability to learn relevant cues from the images. In 2D, we demonstrated alignment between MV and MV images, using a dataset with substantial variations in position, rotation, and skimming. In 3D, we demonstrated alignment between MV and KV images, with a focus on addressing position and rotation discrepancies. In both 2D and 3D settings, our network achieved highly accurate results, with mean error rates of 1.3 mm and 2.5 degrees in 2D, and 3.5 mm and 5 degrees in 3D, respectively. Furthermore, our method demonstrated robustness and efficiency, with minimal reliance on dataset pretreatment and relatively fast processing times (approximately 20 seconds per pair). Overall, our Convolutional Neural Network-based image registration method offers an effective and efficient solution for aligning MV images, particularly in scenarios where IT-based registration is impractical. In addition to clinical applications, this method is also applicable to megavoltage images in radiation therapy research. In conclusion, we are releasing our network architecture and training framework as an open-source platform, with code available on GitHub, in an effort to establish a foundation for further research in this domain. An object can be genuinely nonlocal if it manifests nonlocality, even when it is isolated from other objects. In quantum mechanics, the most straightforward manifestation of nonlocality is associated with entanglement. However, not all entangled states display nonlocal effects, and certain nonlocal effects can arise from non-entangled, separable states. As a result, entanglement is not a universal indicator of nonlocality. One particular nonlocal effect is the ability of an object to steer its unentangled counterpart, resulting in a nonlocal effect that can occur with a single particle, as demonstrated in this study. The provided theorem identifies all single-particle states that can exhibit this effect and demonstrate that certain quasi-local states can steer their surrounding environment, leading to the proposal of modified versions of entanglement-based nonlocality tests that could be more efficiently applied with Gaussian states, as well as the exploration of unique properties of rotating quasi-local states. The object's ability to steer its surroundings also implies its capacity to exhibit nonlocal effects in certain scenarios, as demonstrated in this study. The proposed theoretical approaches can also be applied in experiments to identify situations where nonlocal effects occur, and specific near-optimal states with maximum steering capacity in one-dimensional scenarios have been found and could be produced in opto-mechanical systems using a variety of methods, including the application of squeezed vibrations, rotating waveplates, and photon additions, as well as discussions on the broader implications of single-particle steering and its relationship with other nonlocal phenomena. One such connection is single-particle steering with respect to multiple parties, which could provide additional insights into the object's ability to exhibit nonlocal effects. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classical nova-like explosion in 2018, has been analyzed in further detail. These features, along with the presence of a unique, temporary hump during the post-outburst phase and ongoing dwarf nova-like dips in light curves, suggest that V392 Persei is an exceptional binary system where the nova-like outburst and dwarf nova-like dips are both actively contributing. With no signs of decline in the six-year post-outburst period, V392 Persei is distinguished from other classical novae. We propose a novel approach to designing codebooks and reducing the feedback load in FDD systems. Our method leverages GMM modeling from large-scale TDD training data, enabling us to develop a codebook that effectively captures the GMM characteristics. By sharing the GMM parameters instead of codebook indices, our scheme achieves significant feedback reductions, with an average saving of 7.44 bits per user, in exchange for slightly increased encoding costs. Our codebook and feedback encoding framework delivers a 2.18% performance improvement at a 12.5 kbps feedback rate, outperforming existing methods, and showcases robust adaptability in large-scale systems, supporting up to 32 users. Our findings demonstrate that our codebook design and feedback encoding approach yield rate enhancements of 2.18%, 2.55%, and 2.85% at 12.5 kbps, 6.25 kbps, and 3.125 kbps, respectively, and our method's scalability in multi-user scenarios is consistent with theoretical gains. By integrating our codebook and feedback encoding framework into an OFDM system, we achieve rate improvements of 2.18%, 2.55%, and 2.85%, and our solution is suitable for 5G systems. We are investigating a new concept, "topological emitters," which could offer more precise control over photons interacting with matter through waveguide QED. To achieve this, we are developing a 2D model using a honeycomb lattice, where a strong interaction between atoms and photons is induced by coupling them through a photonic channel. We show that in this setup, we can create a one-way flow of photons between two distant points using a single control laser. Additionally, we find that by adjusting the strength of the atomic-photonic interaction, we can manipulate the emittance of photons from the source, even when there's no control over the direction of emission. We also discover that a strong reaction between atoms and photons is required to produce the desired topological properties. Finally, we propose a realistic experimental implementation using a diamond substrate and a laser-cooled ensemble of nitrogen-vacancy atoms. Shining a laser on these atoms could generate a variety of phenomena, including topological emission, using techniques similar to those that produced Bell-state emission and entanglement between two remote points. This fundamental concept can be applied to the set of functions defined by the equation $f(n) = \frac{p_n}{k_n}$, where $p_n$ represents the $n^{th}$ prime number and $k_n$ is an integer related to function $f$. By examining the composition of these functions, we can establish a prime-based counterpart, resulting in a new sequence of functions defined by $F(n) = \frac{P_n}{K_n}$. When $F$ is applied repeatedly, it demonstrates a fascinating property where its $n^{th}$ iteration, denoted as $F^n$, is equal to $F$ raised to the power of the $n^{th}$ prime number ($P_n$). This remarkable finding provides a solution to the problem of determining fixed points for prime numbers, where a fixed point occurs when a function of this type, in this case $F^n$, equals the identity function, resulting in the identification of specific fixed points and their associated functions. Ultimately, this airtight framework allows us to draw parallels between the behavior of prime numbers and that of functions under iteration. By exploring special cases of these functions through explicit calculation or using advanced mathematical techniques such as Landau's theorem, we can gain insight into the values of prime numbers at specific points or across broader ranges, while also analyzing the overall behavior of the functions, including whether they are recursive or not, and even establishing links between them, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of the intricate relationship between prime numbers and functions under iteration. We propose a novel concept called resonant x-ray diffusion spectroscopy, which could be used to study nuclear stages in hibernating stars by employing next-generation facilities like the High-Energy Facility at the SPring-8 or the High-Brightness Synchrotron Radiation Source at Hefei. This method involves directing resonant x-rays at a particular target to produce a broader x-ray spectrum through a process known as diffusion, which can be used to create a signature that is unique to each nuclear stage and allows for its identification via spectroscopic means. We have outlined a strategy and a framework for this method, which would also provide insight into other essential components of hibernating stars, such as latent phases, mixed phases, and critical points, by considering theoretical models and simulations of two specific cases, including one for hyperonic matter in neutron star mergers and another for magnetic nuclear matter in magnetars. The feasibility of this approach has been confirmed through numerical simulations and potential limitations, including the current capabilities of facilities and data processing constraints, have been acknowledged as areas for improvement. We believe that the implementation of this method will contribute significantly to our understanding of hibernating stars and the behavior of matter in compact objects under extreme conditions of density and magnetic field strength. We invite the participation of researchers in this field to join this research by sharing their expertise and knowledge. We have made the code for this project publicly available for further development and improvement. We have also outlined several path forward for this project including the exploration of new facilities, new research fields, and new theoretical models such as the phenomenological phase diagram of neutron star mergers, quark matter, and dense double-neutrino scattering in neutron star mergers. We have defined several metrics for the success of this project including the advancement of the field through new research, the development of new skills in young researchers, and the demonstration of the feasibility of this method for future facilities. We have discussed the relevance of this project to multiple research areas including nuclear physics, astrophysics, and gravitational physics and we have outlined the potential for this project to contribute to the development of new research facilities and the training of young researchers. We have also discussed the potential risks associated with this project including the risk of not being able to complete the project within the allocated time frame and the risk of not being able to secure the necessary funding. We have outlined several risk mitigation strategies including the development of a detailed project timeline, the identification of potential risks during the project planning phase, and the development of contingency plans

The success of quantum computing relies heavily on controlling and mitigating errors during operations. For this purpose, quantum error correction codes are essential, particularly when running circuits that are otherwise impractical to perform in bulk. Building on previous research, we develop a method to analyze the set of feasible error locations that could arise from no-input quantum states, applying this to various classical codes based on spin models. Utilizing quantum channel length as a practical indicator of circuit complexity, we identify regions of error locations that are accessible given certain classical stochastic processes, demonstrating how this understanding can be utilized to optimize the implementation of quantum error correction protocols through feedback-controlled quantum channels, even in scenarios beyond small-scale rotations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that certain classical codes based on interacting spin models have unbounded classical complexity, implying that only a tiny fraction of this complexity can be explored over time in scenarios where quantum interactions are limited or absent, leaving room for further theoretical investigations into the relationship between classical complexity and quantum behavior. Additionally, we explore the possibility of simulating multi-qubit interactions by combining weaker interactions between single qubits, along with various other applications and extensions of our method.

We propose a concept for a spin-valve switch that utilizes a single helical magnetic layer in close proximity to two separate layers of superconducting material. This proposal takes advantage of the chiral magnetic properties of a helical magnetic layer to achieve exact opposite effects on each superconducting layer. When a specific external magnetic field is applied, the helical magnetic layer's influence on one superconducting layer switches from suppressing to promoting superconductivity, or vice versa. As a result, by adjusting the external magnetic field, it's possible to design a spin-valve switch that can effectively control the superconducting current in one layer while the other layer remains unaffected, even in the presence of an opposing magnetic field. Additionally, we demonstrate that it's feasible to use this kind of spin-valve switch in a device that can output a significant signal, using a simple numerical model that considers the spin-valve switch's fundamental components. To address this, DiscSense a method we propose, conducts an exhaustive semantic analysis of all indicators at once, using each sentence's embedded representation to categorize it into a predefined semantic class from a comprehensive taxonomy. To address this limitation, we integrated Glauber dynamics into the Ising model, thereby obtaining the Ising-doped voter model. This modification allows us to study both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, as well as central and asymmetric positions within a graph. We examined the balance between two opposing states – in this case, the voter and Ising configurations – and measured the associated balance gap. Notably, in the absence of doping, the balance gap is zero for both central and asymmetric initial conditions. However, this unity is disrupted when we introduce doping, as distinct proportions of Ising and voter agents result in unique balance gap values. Furthermore, these gap values exhibit unique characteristics in both the large-$k$ and small-$k$ regimes, displaying a unique structure that is fundamental and irreducible. This fundamental structure is also reflected in nonequilibrium scenarios. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for investigating the intricate balance between opposing states in nonequilibrium systems. Systems governed by Glauber dynamics and ferromagnetic interactions exhibit unique characteristics that are fundamental and irreducible, resulting in unique balance gap values in both graph and lattice settings. Our research also uncovers unique relationships between degree distribution and nonequilibrium dynamics. Deep learning models inherently yield uncertain results, which can be critical in interpreting their output in scientific contexts. This study delves into the aspect of uncertainty representation, specifically ambiguity quantification, in machine learning, where the focus is on evaluating the variability of model predictions rather than their absolute accuracy. We examined six prominent uncertainty quantification methods, including Monte Carlo, Bayesian approaches, and five techniques for quantifying ambiguity in scientific machine learning, such as the MC dropout and K-folding. We explored 13 metrics for comparing these methods, considering three aspects: ambiguity quantification, data efficiency, and computational cost. We applied these methods and metrics to three image classification datasets under varying conditions of data quality and ambiguity, consulting with experts in three fields (astronomy, geology, and medicine) to provide insights into the practical aspects of uncertainty quantification in machine learning. Our comprehensive evaluation revealed distinct patterns in the performance of uncertainty quantification methods depending on the dataset and conditions, coupled with nuanced feedback from the expert consultations. Notably, the scores of the methods were often highly disparate, with some receiving the highest rating in one aspect but the most negative feedback in another. Ultimately, this study underscores the complexity of ambiguity quantification in machine learning, emphasizing that there is no single universally superior method and that the choice of technique depends on the specific problem at hand. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of accounting for variability when interpreting results from machine learning models, particularly in scientific contexts, and suggests that future research prioritize exploring alternative uncertainty quantification methods and rigorous evaluations of existing ones. Additionally, it notes that collaborating with domain experts and practitioners to refine the evaluation of uncertainty quantification methods can be beneficial, as can exploring connections between these methods and other aspects of model behavior, such as interpretability, as they are integral components of the machine learning pipeline, especially for applications involving complex datasets. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) employ convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture for image classification, which has reached near-human levels of accuracy. CNN plays a key role in INVID, a system designed to automatically classify military vehicle videos. Following the discovery of hardware manipulation attacks on INVID, researchers explored the application of hardware error tolerance techniques. This paper delves into the security justification for this approach, focusing on utilizing activation interval supervision with floating-point implementations of CNN. Although floating-point computations appear inherently insecure due to their widespread use, our analysis reveals that introducing round-off errors within specific activation ranges significantly impede an adversary's ability to manipulate INVID outputs. Our findings show that activation interval supervision with floating-point CNN can prevent malicious modifications in over 99% of test cases, as measured across a comprehensive dataset of 51,000 images, including a variety of real-world scenes and vehicle classifications. This analysis provides a basis for examining the security of deep neural network architectures in various settings and offers insights into the design of more secure, robust error tolerance frameworks. As the incorporation of round-off errors raises questions about the inherent security of floating-point computations, this research may yield valuable outcomes for investigating the security of floating-point implementations in other contexts. An evaluation of the hardware costs associated with activation interval supervision reveals that this supervision technique can be efficiently integrated into error tolerance systems with minimal additional cost, equivalent to less than one second of computation on a state-of-the-art CPU. This research may serve as a starting point for exploring ways to design and develop more secure and robust deep neural network architectures in various applications, including those utilizing CNN and incorporating real-world dataset examples from 50 Categories dataset, Animals with Fences (AWF), and Vehicle-in-Distance (ViD. dataset. The concept of firm-settling has been recently introduced in the field of dynamic competition with asymmetric information, focusing on resolving moral hazards that arise from firms' incentives to manipulate system revenues. This issue is particularly evident in the Romanian Ministry of Finance's experience with advance tax payments, where it is seen as a major concern that needs to be addressed. Building on previous work by Julliard and Krylova (2016), we develop an innovative algorithm to determine optimal tax payment obligations for firms, considering their individual productivity levels, relative productivity comparisons, and private information about their productivity. This new approach goes beyond the existing literature in several ways, offering a more efficient solution than the one proposed by Julliard and Krylova (2016), and providing insights that can be applied to broader contexts of firm-settling problems. Leveraging these findings, we design an communication game between the Ministry and firms, demonstrating how our algorithm can address the issue of tax evasion and lead to cooperation, resulting in socially desirable outcomes. Analyzing this game allows us to derive several testable implications and provide an application to the Romanian Ministry of Finance's data, revealing that firms' productivity is higher than previously estimated and provides evidence supporting the model's predictions regarding the use of payments in the second period. Additionally, we observe payments made by high-productivity firms in the second period are lower than payments made by low-productivity firms in the first period, and offer a quantitative estimate of the efficiency loss due to firm-settling, showing it is substantial. Furthermore, we find that firms with intermediate productivity levels have an incentive to manipulate their productivity, and provide a numerical solution to this problem, as well as a qualitative analysis of the role of payments in the second period in solving the model. This research contributes to the understanding of firm-settling in the context of advance tax payments and provides a new framework for addressing this issue, which has implications for designing mechanisms to address similar problems in other contexts. Additionally, it highlights the importance of taking into account firms' relative productivity levels and their private information about productivity when designing mechanisms to address firm-settling. This research also provides a new perspective on the experience of the Romanian Ministry of Finance with advance tax payments and offers a quantitative solution to the problem of firm-settling, which can be applied to other contexts of dynamic competition with asymmetric information. Building on this research, new directions for future research are also identified, which can provide further insights into firm-settling and dynamic competition with asymmetric information. This study creates a unified semantic space that spans multiple languages and allows for consistent clustering across those languages. Unlike previous approaches that used a single type of clustering, we developed a method to employ not one but three forms of clustering for different purposes. To achieve this, we employed three types of constraints that are applicable to three distinct sub-domains within a unified semantic space. Specifically, we defined constraints for clustering domain and sub-domain structure, synonyny, and hyponymy. Additionally, we proposed a novel method to generate cluster-consistent word representations that account for these varied clustering goals by applying different transformations to the three types of clustering constraints. This method enabled us to present word representations that not only reflect the structure of clusters but also the relationships between words. To validate our approach, we conducted three-fold assessments of the consistency of clusters in three languages. Interestingly, the results showed that English performed the best, followed by Spanish and French. To further examine our method, we conducted a cloze test to assess the semantic quality of the word representations generated by our approach. Surprisingly, the quality of these representations was found to be lower than those produced by traditional methods but still showed promise. On the other hand, our method was comparable to state-of-the-art methods in terms of clustering consistency but lagged behind in terms of semantic quality. To explore the potential of our method in real-world applications, we tested its performance in a monolingual task, namely, semantic similarity classification, and discovered that it not only outperformed the baseline models but also the strong mainstream models that rely on multiple negative sampling techniques. To extend our method to multi-lingual settings, we introduced the novel concept of cluster-consistent cross-lingual word representation mapping. To achieve this, we proposed a method that leverages three types of clustering constraints to generate a mapping function, thereby enabling the mapping of words across languages based on their cluster structure. To evaluate our approach in a multi-lingual setting, we conducted an assessment of the consistency of clusters in three languages and found that English once again performed the best, followed by Spanish and French. To further validate our approach, we conducted a cloze test to assess the semantic quality of the cross-lingual mapped word representations. Interestingly, the results showed that the quality of these representations was found to be lower than those produced by traditional methods but still showed promise. On the other hand, our method was comparable to state-of-the-art methods in terms of clustering consistency but lagged behind in terms of semantic quality.

Dialogue state tracking (DST) is a crucial component of multi-step dialogue management, with various approaches relying heavily on labeled data to inform their policies. However, the accuracy of these labels has not been thoroughly validated. Previous studies have revealed that certain labeled data categories exhibit significant variability in their representations, with some being too broad or too narrow. To address this issue, a new dataset called Multi-Woz 2.0 has been created through a crowdsourcing re-labeling exercise, but it still poses challenges for DST models due to its imperfections, including labeling errors and inconsistencies. To tackle these issues, a new approach called ASSIST has been developed, taking into account the following factors: (1) labeling errors result in performance fluctuations across different domains, (2) labeling inconsistencies lead to discrepancies in how states are formatted, and (3) the need for domain and state-specific generalization. To mitigate these issues, ASSIST has been designed with three key components: (1) a robust loss function that minimizes the effect of labeling errors, (2) a joint optimization framework that addresses inconsistencies by learning from both formatted and unformatted data, and (3) a simple yet effective strategy for generalization, with experiments showing that ASSIST achieves superior performance over strong baselines in multiple datasets affected by label imperfections. When evaluated on the Multi-Woz 2.0 dataset, ASSIST achieves a 12.81% improvement in the overall joint accuracy, with gains of 10.87% and 14.55% in single-domain and multi-domain accuracy, respectively. Furthermore, ASSIST demonstrates comparable performance to state-of-the-art models when tested on the original Multi-Woz 2.0 dataset, with an overall joint accuracy of 77.11%. Additionally, the model exhibits strong generalization capabilities in various datasets affected by label imperfections, with ASSIST achieving 73.19% overall joint accuracy in the Multi-Woz 2.0 dataset, a 5.41% improvement over the strongest baseline, with gains of 4.87% and 6.11% in single-domain and multi-domain accuracy, respectively. When evaluated on the Multi-Woz 2.0 test set, ASSIST achieves 76.19% overall joint accuracy, with gains of 75.19% and 77.19% in single-domain and multi-domain accuracy, respectively. Moreover, the model exhibits strong generalization capabilities in various datasets affected by labeling errors and inconsistencies, with ASSIST demonstrating the ability to generalize across different domains
