Ethynyl derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene have been detected for the first time in the TMC-1 molecule cloud using radio telescopes. Ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) and 1-deutero ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H4D CCH) in addition to their protonated counterparts were successfully discovered. Additionally, two variants of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH and C6H5CN) were found with higher sensitivity than previous detections. Abundances of these ethynyl derivatives in comparison to their cyanogen counterparts indicate lower cyanogen to ethynyl ratios (12.6 for C5H2 and 5.5 for C6H2), suggesting a possible link between the two molecules that could be influenced by magnetic fields. Observations of ethynyl cyclopentadiene and benzene provide a deeper understanding of the formation of cyanogen, a complex molecule found in molecular clouds. For benzene, observations of ethynyl and cyan derivatives (with ratios of 5.5 for CCH to CN), suggest benzene itself may have a relatively low abundance compared to cyclopentadiene (in ratio to CCH), implying that it may not form efficiently during the chemical development of molecular clouds. Column densities for the new detections were calculated through a comparison of observed spectra with simulations made using a collisional radiative model for cyclopentadiene and standard models for benzene and cyanogen, resulting in values of 1.01 x 10^12, 9.6 x 10^11, 2.3 x 10^12 and 2.3 x 10^12 for C5H5CCH, C5H4D CCH, C6H5CCH and C6H5CN respectively. Isotopic ratios of 12C/13C for cyclopentadiene and benzene, calculated using the same methodological approach as previous measurements for cyanogen and other molecules in TMC-1, showed a slightly lower value for 12C/13C in cyclopentadiene (6.25 vs 6.44 for benzene and 6.47 for cyanogen), with uncertainties that need to be clarified through further observations. These discoveries and measurements provide a deeper understanding of chemistry and molecular formation processes in TMC-1 and offer valuable comparisons with results from observations made with ALMA

In neural machine translation, the source sentence is typically processed sequentially from left to right. However, when the target sentence is translated word by word, each source sentence element can be related to any target sentence element, introducing unnecessary complications. This work suggests that attention within the source sentence follows a look-forward pattern and seeks to optimize the attention network accordingly. A novel attention model is proposed that assumes each source sentence element only depends on previous elements and incorporates a memory mechanism for elements that have been processed. This model's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments, showing it achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods while reducing the number of unnecessary connections between source and target sentence elements. Our best model yields significant improvements, delivering a 1.04 $p$-score improvement and 0.16 $bpec$ gain over strong baselines. Our analysis of the learned networks reveals a strong match with the proposed theoretical framework. Systematic experiments covering six language directions are conducted to validate our findings, indicating that this look-forward attention framework holds universal value for NMT. Effective curiosity in learners is a crucial factor that can significantly influence the learning process and ultimately lead to better outcomes and a deeper understanding of subject matter.  Curiosity has been extensively studied in individual learners, yet its dynamics in collaborative learning environments remain an area of uncertainty.  This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by investigating the curiosity levels of learners within a small group setting.  A theoretical framework combining self-determination theory and the situational interest model was used as the basis for a measure of situational curiosity in learning contexts.  This research is innovative due to its use of multimodal data collection methods, specifically combining physiological signals with speech patterns and written communication to create a comprehensive picture of learners' curiosity levels.  A learning analytics system was developed to analyze these data and provide a curiosity score for each learner in real-time.  This score was validated through self-report surveys.  The results of this research reveal that there are strong correlations between the scores generated by the learning analytics system and the self-report surveys conducted on learners.  In addition, this research identified two primary factors that contribute to the curiosity levels of learners within a collaborative learning environment.  These factors were used to create a conceptual framework that describes the curiosity levels of learners within this setting.  This research provides valuable insights that can be used to inform the design of learning environments and tools to support the development of curiosity levels in learners within collaborative settings.  Two case studies were conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of a learning environment designed with the recommendations of this research in mind.  The results of these case studies showed significant increases in the curiosity levels of learners within this environment.  This research offers a foundation for the development of learning environments and tools that can support the development of curiosity levels in learners within collaborative settings. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for assessing uncertainty in complex systems, and their integration with Dirac delta functions through Mat\'ern kernels significantly expands their capabilities, especially in analyzing isotropic data. This research adapts Mat\'ern kernels, which account for data isotropy, for use in non-isotropic settings by incorporating Gaussian processes on graphs. This approach is mathematically represented in a theoretical context and showcases its practical applications through two real-world studies: one exploring temperature distributions across Europe and the other analyzing gene expression within a biological cellular process. This work also invests in computational methods, developing an algorithm for efficiently handling Gaussian process predictions in graph-structured data, and making the associated R package, MatGraph, available for others to use. This research provides significant insights on modeling non-isotropic data using Gaussian processes on graphs and highlights the value of data-driven approaches to identifying optimal graph neighborhoods. This includes a novel observation from the temperature distribution analysis, indicating that a relatively small neighborhood can suffice for accurate predictions when comparing it to the expression data within a cellular process, which demands more precise modeling of boundaries. This research is further expanded upon through an ongoing project, presented in this document, where Gaussian process models are integrated with particle filters to anticipate temporal variations in complex systems, and this framework is applied to forecasting gene expression across cellular process examples. This research is primarily presented in a theoretical context but promising results warrant the development of this framework further. The growing interest in optimal urban road network exploration is driving research in efficient detection methods for road types, particularly in urban settings. While previous studies have focused on methods using GPS data from individual vehicles, our research leverages a more powerful tool: ridesharing vehicles equipped with advanced sensors, capable of detecting surrounding roads at a higher rate and with greater precision than individual vehicles. We addressed the problem of maximizing the detection of road types by developing a real-time algorithm that prioritizes vehicles based on their detection capabilities and network characteristics. Our results showed that this approach yields significantly better performance compared to traditional methods, with a significant improvement of 5.6 times in road type detection in the New York City network and 3.5 times in the Los Angeles network, even with a more conservative detection rate. Our findings also provide valuable insights into designing optimal routing protocols for road type detection. This work introduces Multivariate Functional Singular Spectrum Examination (MFSE), a framework that delves into the singular spectrum of multivariate functional data across multiple dimensions. Unlike traditional methods that rely on second-order moments for multivariate methods and first-order moments for functional data, MFSE utilises all available moments for a comprehensive analysis. Building on the principles of Functional Singular Spectrum Analysis (FSSA), MFSE explores the singular spectrum in the functional domain through the representation of multivariate functional data in operator-valued integral operators. A new representation theorem enables the application of MFSE in a manner analogous to its scalar counterpart, revealing hidden patterns and structures in the data. Furthermore, MFSE offers a clustering system where data is clustered based on the spectrum of the integral operators representing the multivariate functional data. A simulation study is conducted to assess the clustering performance of MFSE. A notable finding is that MFSE exhibits an improvement in clustering results when compared to its functional and multivariate counterparts. A statistical analysis of intrinsically low-dimensional brain signals using diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI) is presented as a real-world application of MFSE. The analysis employs a large dataset consisting of 394 subjects with 334 cortical regions of interest. The results indicate that the majority of the brain signals exhibit an intrinsically low-dimensional structure, whereas a few high-dimensional regions are identified in all three dimensions. Deep learning-based attacks and defenses have achieved remarkable stability in successive iterations, yet they continue to fall short of ideal performance. To address this, we undertook a comprehensive analysis of modern adversarial attack methods within machine learning spectra. Our findings reveal a troubling pattern where attacks become excessively sensitive, surpassing the range of intended movements, and we term this problem overresponse. We further establish that, in certain situations, overresponse and overstability are interlinked, as well as show overresponse can be measured independently. Next, we investigate the underlying causes of overresponse and find that it is primarily attributed to the excessive scaling factor needed to balance exploration and exploitation in search processes. Overresponse is also found to be present in other exploration-based methods such as BEAR-CL and to be present in all three attack frameworks examined (AES, UAT, and RFG). We explore potential solutions to overresponse, including the use of intrinsic regularization, and find that both successful defenses (DeepSpeed and EfficientSD) in fact address this very issue. One of these successful defenses (EfficientSD) is found to be explicitly designed to counter overresponse and we gain insight into its inner workings. We also investigate alternative solutions, including the application of intrinsic regularization and the proposal of a new method called bounded factorization which shows promising results. Lastly, we highlight the significance of overresponse in attacks and the potential risks it poses, as well as the need for further research into this previously under-explored aspect of machine learning. Our work lays the foundation for a more in-depth examination of overresponse in machine learning and the development of more effective methods to tackle it head-on. Given the widespread adoption of machine learning models in safety-critical domains, it is crucial to give due consideration to this previously under-studied issue. Our research is an initial step in this direction and we are confident that our contributions will inspire a more in-depth exploration of this previously under-studied aspect of machine learning. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany utilizes a plasma generator that operates in two modes: a vacuum glid-to-metal discharge and a helicon discharge. This study focuses on the plasma characteristics when the generator is operating in helicon mode and verifies that it mimics the plasma found in the private sector ITER neutralizer under similar conditions. It is found that when the generator is in helicon mode, the plasma properties, including density, electron temperature, and flow velocity, match those of the sector's neutralizer, except for a discrepancy in the ion velocity, which is higher in the helicon mode by about 150 m/s. Additionally, the study measures the characteristics of the plasma when the generator is turned off and finds that the density and electron temperature return to their initial states, while the flow velocity and magnetic field strength remain elevated for a more extended period. It is proposed that the increased flow velocity could be caused by the lingering effect of the neutralizer's flow velocity. It is also observed that when the generator is in helicon mode, the plasma density and electron temperature follow a linear relationship with the power input, while the flow velocity is proportional to the square of the power input. It is suggested that the flow velocity's dependence on the magnetic field strength and the type of gas used could be the reason for this non-linear relationship. It is proposed that the elevated flow velocity could be mitigated by decreasing the magnetic field strength, but this could result in a non-uniform plasma distribution. In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial biopesticides offer numerous advantages, including higher target specificity and reduced environmental pollution risks. To address this challenge, a new methodology has been developed to identify and eliminate these external state and reward variables, thereby stabilizing the training process. This methodology first detects the latent variables determining state and reward dynamics, and then constructs a self-sustaining reward signal from these variables. It then develops a reinforcement learning algorithm that leverages this reward signal to train a stable policy. This algorithm achieves optimal performance by eliminating the external influence, and is demonstrated in simulations and experiments for both model-free and model-based learning in multiple scenarios. The results show significant improvements in learning efficiency and performance when the external state and reward variables are eliminated. Achieving this alignment requires a thorough validation process, ensuring the accuracy of the code against the specifications from its initial development phase through to its eventual deployment on the blockchain. Building upon this principle, our system HELMHOLTZ validates Tezos smart contracts with a refined type relationship between the Michelson language and Tezos runtime, successfully putting refinement type theory into practical use. Moreover, HELMHOLTZ's design allows for the detection of errors at development time, eliminating the risk of contract failures on the blockchain. This application paper details an investigation into the virtual origin synthetic aperture (VOSA) Ultrasound beamforming technique and its effectiveness in enhancing displacement estimation in elastography.  A numerical study examined the advantages of real-time and robust data processing, followed by experiments under controlled conditions and in vivo examinations of breast and prostate tissue.  The results demonstrate that VOSA outperforms other beamforming techniques in terms of lateral resolution and displacement estimation precision, offering potential for enhanced diagnostic accuracy in elastography.  In contrast to model-based elastography, VOSA Ultrasound data offers greater flexibility for a wide range of applications beyond elastography, including optimal probe placement and accurate localization of lesions in ultrasound images.  Therefore, VOSA is an ideal choice as a precursor to model-based elastography and related image analysis tasks.  The study also demonstrates that VOSA can be integrated with elastography to achieve more precise displacement estimation and enhanced diagnostic performance compared to conventional ultrasound elastography and phase-sensitive ultrasound. Recently, deep learning techniques have significantly boosted the development of low-dose CT (LDCT) image enhancement, enabling medical diagnoses with reduced radiation exposure. A key challenge in this area involves matching the intensity of enhanced images to match original images from normal-dose CT scans, particularly given the diverse range of CT scanners used in clinical settings. To address this issue, this study introduces an adaptive inception point-to-global average pooling (AdaIN-IGAP) layer that identifies valuable global information from cycle gan (CycleGAN) learned features and adapts its use in image synthesis. By incorporating this layer into a CycleGAN framework, it becomes possible to incorporate global information from undosaged CT images, enhancing the generative model's ability to produce high-quality, radiology-diagnosable LDCT images with natural variability. To further improve image denoising, this research combines CycleGAN with a U-Net architecture, allowing the two methods to complement each other's strengths. Notably, the proposed method achieves comparable or better performance compared to state-of-the-art cycle-based methods and UNet-like architectures, as evidenced by quantitative evaluation using LDCT images derived from CT dose index phantom images, as well as qualitative assessment of actual LDCT images obtained at two different medical centers. Moreover, the proposed method exhibits efficient training and real-world applicability, demonstrating the extraction of over 95% valuable global information from undosaged CT images during training. Moreover, this research provides the first open-source code for cycle-based unsupervised LDCT denoising available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/AdaIN-Switchable-CycleGAN, as well as the first qualitative evaluation of LDCT denoising images at https://sites.google.com/view/ldct-denoising-evaluation, providing a critical framework for the evaluation of LDCT denoising methods. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 11.19% in CT dose index phantom evaluation, as well as a structural similarity index (SSIM) of 0.819 and a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 25.403 in actual LDCT image evaluation, underscoring its effectiveness and efficiency in producing high-quality, radiology-diagnosable LDCT images with natural variability. Furthermore, this research provides the first open-source code for cycle-based unsupervised LDCT denoising available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/AdaIN-Switchable

To study the characteristics of distorted halo nuclei, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions obtained from the GOGNE-DWBA approach.  This method effectively accounts for strong interactions through the renormalization of single-particle strengths and removal energies.  Our calculated intrinsic wave functions for $^{42}$Mg, $^{44}$Mg, and $^{46}$Mg, which exhibit distorted halo structures, show that they possess prolate deformations and unique rotational symmetry.  However, when angular momentum projection is applied, these properties are broken due to shape uncoupling effects, resulting in the mixing of rotational symmetry and the formation of triaxial shapes in the ground states.  The influences of shape uncoupling effects on rotational momenta are demonstrated through the analysis of ratio spectra.  Specifically, the ratios of energies for $K^{\pi} = 2^{+}$ and $4^{+}$ states exhibit variations with different values for different rotational momenta $I$.  This phenomenon provides a practical indicator for identifying distorted halo structures.  It is also found that the magnitude of energy ratio changes with $I$ is directly correlated with the strength of s-wave removal energies for $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg but not for $^{46}$Mg, suggesting that other factors influence this property.  Additionally, the proposed relationship between energy ratio changes and s-wave removal energies can be utilized as an experimental signature to verify the distorted ground state of these halo nuclei.  The theoretical framework employed in this study is applicable to other distorted halo structures found in light exotic nuclei.  Furthermore, the presented findings suggest that rotational momenta should be precisely determined in experiments to avoid confusion and to facilitate a deeper understanding of exotic nuclear structures.  The effects of shape uncoupling have the potential to be probed through magnetic moment measurements in future experiments, and the proposed indicator for distorted halo structures can be validated through the analysis of ratio spectra and in-band $\gamma$-ray transitions.  Ultimately, the interplay between shape uncoupling effects and other factors like configuration coupling in multi-particle systems should be explored further in research.  The potential role of ab initio calculations in uncovering the intricate relationships between strong short-range and weak long-range forces in nuclear systems cannot be understated.  It is also crucial to investigate the connections between distorted ground states and various decay modes such as halos, molecular structures, cluster formations, and two-neutron drop structures. In multi-task reinforcement learning, achieving high performance across a range of tasks is essential. This is because each task represents a distinct goal, and the agent must balance its learning to adapt to new environments by default. By contrast, a well-known property of model-based multi-task reinforcement learning is that it typically exhibits goal fragmentation - the tendency to break tasks into sub-components due to overfitting the model, resulting in destructive interference of performance. This phenomenon arises because the agent learns an explicit representation of how actions affect rewards in each environment, a challenge that is exacerbated as the action space increases. Our research demonstrates that imposing structural constraints on the agent's models through separate components for each task can prevent destructive interference and enable the learning of general, useful representations by limiting their complexity. We validate this approach by achieving notable improvements over baseline methods across various multi-task reinforcement learning scenarios, including those with complex goal spaces and high action costs, in a range of simulated and real-world tasks. Our findings suggest that modular models can facilitate the learning of general, useful representations by limiting their complexity, and this technique has the potential to be applied to a broader range of reinforcement learning settings. By dividing the agent's models into distinct modules corresponding to each task, we can prevent destructive interference of performance and enable the learning of general, useful representations. This research paper focuses on establishing local approximation theorems for several types of equations, including the porous medium type and the rapid diffusion type, within a noncompact metric measure space that has a compact boundary. We primarily leverage the concept of local uniform gradient approximation, denoted as UGAF, for functions to demonstrate these results. UGAF is introduced as a local technique to approximate the gradient of a function by a linear function, in contrast to the global approach which relies on compactness assumptions. Building on this foundation, we prove several key results: (1) we demonstrate that equations belonging to the porous medium type or the rapid diffusion type can be approximated locally using a linear function, (2) we prove that these approximations are equivalent, and (3) we show that these approximations can be used to derive local boundedness results for the original equations. These findings are then applied to a broad class of equations, including the porous medium type and the rapid diffusion type, resulting in the establishment of local boundedness and one-dimensional symmetry results for these equations. Notably, in the case where the ambient space has more than two dimensions, these results provide novel contributions. We synthesize the life stories of four logicians from the 20th century, Alan Turing, Alonzo Church, Kurt Godel, J.B. Rosser, Stephen Kleene, Emil Post, Rudolf Carnap, Alfred Tarski, and Nicolas Bourbaki. Our account is presented in four chapters corresponding to these logicians. Godel's discovery of a fundamental property about first-order logic served as a significant milestone in the development of modern computer science and philosophy of science. After World War II, the Amsterdam Conference saw important contributions from Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Church, among others, though one author, J.B. Rosser, made a crucial advancement in the theory of Turing machines that allowed for unbounded computation resources to be circumvented. Following the Amsterdam Conference, the development of theoretical computer science and related fields continued to evolve, marked by important milestones such as the Kolmogorov complexity theorem and the undecidability theorem, ultimately laying the foundation for Nicolas Bourbaki's constructive topology. Two appendices provide a historical context for the Amsterdam Conference and a formal proof of the unsolvability of the decision problem using Godel's incompleteness theorems, as well as a discussion on the Church-Turing thesis.

In chapter one, we explore the early lives and contributions of Alan Turing, Alonzo Church, Kurt Godel, J.B. Rosser, Stephen Kleene, and Emil Post.

In chapter two, we delve into the pre-war achievements of Rudolf Carnap, Alfred Tarski, and Nicolas Bourbaki, before shifting to the Amsterdam Conference in 1946-1947 and the post-war era.

In chapter three, we examine the life stories of Stephen Kleene and Alan Turing in greater detail, as well as the development of computer science and the philosophy of science in the mid-20th century.

In chapter four, we analyze the discovery of the property about first-order logic by Kurt Godel and the contributions of Kurt Godel, J.B. Rosser, Rudolf Carnap, and Alfred Tarski at the Amsterdam Conference in 1946-1947.

Two appendices are included: one provides a historical context for the Amsterdam Conference in 1946-1947, while the other offers a discussion of the Church-Turing thesis and a formal proof of the undecidability theorem using Godel's incompleteness theorems. This thesis is an extension of Peter J. Taal's undergraduate thesis

When conducting surveys in a geographical area, it is often necessary to collect data in a balanced manner. Traditionally, researchers employ techniques like equal interval sampling with a systematic approach to achieve this balance. However, these methods can be challenging when operating within a confined space with an irregular layout. A novel sequence-based method is proposed for sampling in geographical balanced sets, enabling the collection of balanced data even in areas with irregular layouts. A theoretical imbalance risk assessment is provided for this proposed method, and it is demonstrated through simulations and real-world applications that it is highly effective. A notable example is derived from the National Household Characteristic Survey in Brazil, which showcases the method's capability in handling large, diverse data sets. The proposed method is an open-source Python package called seq-gbs, which is available on GitHub under the MIT license. It offers a versatile solution for data collection in geographical balanced sets, and is an important contribution to the field of sequence-based statistics. Additionally, two new open-source Python packages are introduced alongside seq-gbs, which are (1) seq-gbs-view, a 3D data visualization tool, and (2) seq-n4d, a 4D data visualization tool. These methods provide data analysts with a suite of sequence-based statistics tools for discovery and validation. Equipping robots with a camera mounted in their grasp allows them to identify and manipulate objects with greater precision. However, adjusting the position of the camera within the hand to optimize object recognition can be a challenging task. One possible solution to this issue involves training machine learning models on a large dataset of images, including variations of the object's appearance as the camera is moved. Yet, assembling such a comprehensive dataset of images is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. This study explores an alternative approach, which involves training the models directly on images obtained after the camera has been adjusted by a human operator to allow them to identify the object. By applying this method to two different scenarios involving the recognition of objects, the researchers demonstrated that it is possible to achieve comparable or even better performance compared to traditional methods requiring large datasets of images. The results of these experiments are presented in the paper, along with a discussion on the limitations of the method and possible ways to enhance it. The eye-in-hand (EiH) camera adjustment problem aims to optimize object detection by adjusting the camera's position within the hand's coordinate space. Unlike other optimization problems with clear mathematical formulations, this one lacks a defined objective function due to the complex, non-linear relationships between camera settings and image features. Machine learning models can be trained to predict this unknown function but typically require large datasets of images at varying settings, which are hard to collect. This paper proposes an alternative framework for training models without explicit datasets, leveraging the information contained in images obtained after a human operator adjusts the camera. By applying this approach to two object recognition tasks, the paper's authors demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency, showing that it yields performance on par with or even surpassing that of traditional methods. One such technique involves training a conditional generator in conditional GANs to produce high-quality images from low-quality input. To address this issue, we propose a novel $K$-regularized conditional GAN, which introduces two key advancements. In our experiments, we applied this method to noise removal, deblurring, and super-resolution tasks, achieving comparable or superior results to state-of-the-art methods while significantly reducing the risk of over-feature-extraction and related issues. This paper introduces a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to circumvent the limited duration issue of WaveNet. Typically, WaveNet generates audio in real-time using a non-causal dilated convolution structure that mirrors the quasi-periodic nature of the human voice. To account for varying pitch, QPNet incorporates a pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural network with a compact pitch-encoded input. During each time step, QPNet's neural network assesses the current quarter-period and incorporates that information into its output. Experimentation reveals that QPNet surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in both subjective quality and naturalness, outperforming them by a significant margin. Notably, QPNet achieves this with a relatively modest model size. To validate its generative capabilities, we conducted a singing voice synthesis evaluation, with results indicating that QPNet's samples closely mimic professional recordings. With the ability to generate lengthy audio at once, QPNet offers a promising solution to the duration issue affecting current state-of-the-art WaveNet-based models. To solve the Isolation Problem with Majorana modes, we need a more precise method of identification. Superposition of local Majorana modes on a mesoscopic scale may resolve this issue, but even then, an additional challenge arises - different topological and non-topological states can have very close energies and may not be easily differentiated just by having a superposition. We propose using tunneling spectroscopy with Ohmic damping and resistive electrodes to overcome this difficulty. By sending a strong tunneling current through a small bias and observing the resulting tunneling curve under Ohmic damping, we can differentiate between high-energy peaks, including Majorana peaks, regardless of the presence of a gap in the system. The proposed method explains previously observed peaks in mesoscopic systems and demonstrates the potential for distinguishing between different states using tunneling spectroscopy. It can also determine whether a peak is shifted due to interaction with a bath or remain at the same position, providing further evidence for the presence of Majorana modes. We suggest building a tunneling microscope with a variable temperature setup, a fast switching circuit for pump ports, and an average measurement time of at least a few hundred times the switching time to implement this technique. We also discuss an alternative method involving the measurement of conductance as a function of frequency instead of chemical potential, which may be more suitable for experimental implementation using transport measurements. Ultimately, we believe that tunneling spectroscopy with Ohmic damping and resistive electrodes holds great promise for identifying Majorana modes unambiguously and resolving the Isolation Problem. We demonstrate the feasibility of this technique by analyzing and explaining the results from recent experiments, demonstrating that the proposed technique can distinguish between different states and peaks, including those with a high energy and without a gap in the system, providing further evidence for the presence of Majorana modes. However, the scale of these networks poses a challenge for maintenance teams, who often struggle to identify and repair critical issues in a timely manner. Existing methods rely on visual inspections by trained professionals or a combination of technological approaches paired with user-generated data, but these methods are often fragmented and fail to provide comprehensive, real-time insights. To illustrate the capabilities of this platform, we share results from a pilot study conducted in partnership with a leading highway authority in Singapore, highlighting the detection of highway defects and assets using a drone-based approach and highlighting key considerations for the adoption of such technologies in large-scale infrastructure management settings. A model consisting of a resonator coupled to a circuit automatically generates a high-amplitude mechanical motion, and this interaction forces the resonator to operate at its nonlinear switching threshold even when driven by a low-intensity light. This leads to the heating of the mechanical motion rapidly, resulting in increased power transfer. A general analysis shows that there are specific parameters, such as small optomechanical coupling and a large phonon number, that result in a compression of the optomechanical potential and an increased power transfer. A case study involving a hybrid circuit-resonator setup shows that it is possible to achieve high-power transfer without the need for intense light, and this could have implications for the development of better optomechanical lasers that operate in the saturation limit. We present a novel framework for understanding delay discounting behavior, which deviates from the standard exponential model commonly used in economics. We argue that a generally applicable framework should meet three criteria: firstly, it must be mathematically equivalent to the standard exponential model when the Tsallis parameter is set to one; secondly, it must accommodate varying levels of decision-making efficiency; and thirdly, it must be supported by a clear decision-making process. We propose a delay discounting framework based on the Tsallis exponential distribution, which meets these criteria and provides a plausible explanation for observed discounting behavior and decision-making anomalies. We demonstrate that our framework and its special cases such as the Kable framework can explain a wide range of data without assuming subjects maximize expected utility or employ hyperbolic discounting. Instead, our results suggest that delay discounting behavior can be explained by a combination of decreasing sensitivity to delayed rewards and declining decision-making efficiency over time. We also investigate the implications of our framework for delay discounting, including the relationship between discount rates and decision-making efficiency, and propose a method for estimating this parameter. We validate our framework through a series of economic experiments, which provide further insights into the factors that influence delay discounting behavior and decision-making efficiency. We offer a critical review of existing delay discounting theories and experiments, and highlight the limitations of previous studies. We argue that the failure to account for declining decision-making efficiency over time has led to a misinterpretation of data and incorrect conclusions regarding the discounting process. We propose a new approach for estimating delay discounting parameters and demonstrate that our framework offers a more efficient and accurate method of data analysis. We investigate the relationship between delay discounting behavior and decision-making efficiency in different contexts, and explore the implications of our framework for our understanding of delay discounting behavior and decision-making in different domains. We acknowledge the contributions of previous researchers who have suggested modifications to the standard exponential model, and highlight the similarities between our framework and the proposed alternatives. We outline a program of research aimed at further investigating delay discounting behavior and decision-making efficiency in different contexts and domains. We anticipate that our framework will provide a useful tool for researchers and practitioners working in the field of economics, psychology, neuroscience, and decision-making. We discuss harmonic gauge choices in the context of Einstein's general relativity, examining both its simplified and complex forms. When complexified, the harmonic gauge yields a first-order hyper surface equation, enabling the elimination of the conformal factor and subsequent simplification of the Einstein field equations. This results in a set of linear wave equations for each conformally distinct metric component. This analysis extends to Einstein's general relativity with a cosmological constant, Lambda. In this case, the harmonic gauge gives a second-order hyper surface equation, leading to a simplification of the Einstein-Lambda field equations into a mixed order hyper surface equation and a set of linear wave equations. This analysis is performed in both Riemannian and pseudo Riemannian spaces. We also explore gauge choices in teleparallel gravity and extended Einstein teleparallel gravity. When complexified, these theories behave similarly to general relativity. We conclude by examining the potential of harmonic gauge choices in both simple and complex forms to clarify and simplify substantial gravity theories. We call a gravity theory'substantial' if it describes the physical world accurately, without relying on the introduction of an arbitrary imaginary time. In such theories, complex harmonic gauge choices may lead to unstable solutions due to the presence of oscillatory modes from the hyper surface equations, potentially resulting in solution divergence. On the other hand, real harmonic gauge choices may still provide valuable insights into the nature of gravity by facilitating the decomposition of gravitational fields into conformally distinct components. We suggest that real harmonic gauge choices may offer a more stable framework for the study of substantial gravity theories. We also outline a plan to investigate real harmonic gauge choices in both simple and complex forms in future research. This paper will discuss negative absolute temperature's promising implications in the context of quantum chemistry, focusing on its potential to address challenges in molecular dynamics that have proven insurmountable with conventional methods. We will examine the method of temperature introduction and its relationship to time-dependent versions of equations such as the Schrödinger, Dirac, and Boltzmann equations. We will also explore the relationship between negative absolute temperatures and the direction of time, as well as examine a new statistical mechanics framework that could provide a solution to Parronhuber's equation by incorporating negative absolute temperatures in a way that is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics. We will refer to this new framework as NAT-SSM. Within the scope of this discussion, quantum hydrodynamics and the Hartree-Fock method will be of particular interest. Finally, an overview of an ongoing project will be given, which aims to evaluate the efficiency of quantum models that incorporate negative absolute temperatures through the new NAT-SSM framework by applying them to a range of benchmark molecular systems. This evaluation will involve comparing the results obtained with the new method to those obtained with the parabolic approximation and the original time-admitted matrix equation, with a view to presenting the outcomes at an international conference in the future. Key aspects of this project can be found in the list of figures and tables provided at the end of this document. In conclusion, negative absolute temperatures hold great potential for enhancing our understanding of molecular systems in a way that could, in turn, contribute to the advancement of chemical reactions under controlled conditions in the future. Histological analysis by a trained pathologist, aided by imaging techniques, achieves this goal. However, this process is both time-consuming and subject to human error. UniToPatho is an open-source histological dataset containing 8160 annotated regions, designed to support the classification of colorectal polyps and evaluation of adenoma dysplasia using morphological features, specifically tailored for H&E stained tissue samples. UniToPatho is unique in its comprehensive nature, covering four categories of intestinal epithelial lesions, including normal tissue, hyperplastic polyps, adenomas with low, medium, and high dysplasia, and malignant carcinomas. To facilitate easy access, the dataset includes detailed information about the associated clinical data and lesion morphology. UniToPatho is now available for researchers and developers to explore and download from the UniToPatho website. For the task of classification, UniToPatho is an expanding dataset that is currently open to contributions from the scientific community. UniToPatho is also the foundation for a recently introduced challenge focused on adenoma detection and characterization, known as ICCV 2023 Adenoma Detection and Characterization (ADC) Challenge. The challenge aims to advance cutting-edge technologies capable of detecting and evaluating the severity of adenomas from digitized biopsy slides, thereby supporting the development of more effective surveillance and screening strategies for colorectal cancer. The ADC Challenge is currently accepting submissions from innovative algorithms and machine learning models. A statistical analysis using a large dataset of similar isotopic measurements revealed a similar yet distinct trend. Since these isotopic signals are resistant to isotopic equilibration during planetary formation and differentiation, various scenarios were explored to explain these findings in reference to the formation of the solar system. One possible explanation is that a distinct population of dry inner solar system planetesimals broke down into smaller components during the early stages of the solar system's formation, releasing free metals that could accrete with silicate materials due to sticking together in the gravity field. This scenario would provide evidence for the accretion of dry inner solar system material into the forming Earth, supporting research suggesting that a similar body in the asteroid belt, known as the "Moon-analog", could exist. This discovery would also provide a solution to the Earth-Moon's distinct isotopic composition, with the Moon having a higher content of metal grains than the Earth. Speech translation bypasses the written intermediate step between listening to spoken language and speaking a different language. This task is complicated by the presence of multiple source and target languages. For instance, if someone is speaking English and you need to respond in Spanish but didn't learn any English, the task becomes significantly harder. Until now, it had been assumed that each combination of source and target languages required unique skills. However, our research reveals that a single neural network can accomplish all speech-to-speech translations with ease, even across vast linguistic families, provided it can learn from labeled data for each language pair. We demonstrated the efficacy of this single-firm approach by achieving superior results on six pairs of languages, including English and Spanish, in comparison to industry standards. Our novel system also excelled in zero-shot voice translation, where the target audience is unknown, at both automatic and human evaluation levels, outperforming a leading speech-to-text and subsequent text-to-speech model by a considerable margin. Our model's capabilities can be extended to any new language pair without the need to redesign it, thanks to its zero-shot adaptation ability. Within the most fundamental scoto-seesaw (sSS) matrix model, we perform a comprehensive analysis of both dark matter and Higgs vacuum stability issues. As a first step in the sSS approach, this study focuses on the simplest form of the framework, where only one non-zero neutrino mass is considered. By incorporating the minimal supersymmetric standard model, we examine the dark matter problem and Higgs vacuum stability within this framework. Our findings indicate that radiative neutrino mass generation and neutrino oscillation phenomena are naturally explained when one neutrino mass is significant. Regarding dark matter, we found suitable masses in the range of $O(100)$ GeV to $O(1)$ TeV, which is consistent with WIMP-like behavior. In addition, we identified regions of parameter space where the Higgs vacuum remains stable up to the grand unified theory (GUT) scale without the need for a high-scale GUT symmetry. The minimal sSS model with only one non-zero neutrino mass already addresses the dark matter and Higgs vacuum stability issues, thus eliminating the necessity to incorporate the full scoto-seesaw framework in search of WIMP dark matter and Higgs vacuum stability solutions. Nonetheless, the full sSS matrix model with multiple nonzero neutrino masses continues to provide more extensive and varied avenues for investigating these fundamental problems in a more intricate but more realistic neutrino standard model. Finally, our analysis reveals several suitable dark matter phenomenology benchmarks, such as direct detection rates in the $O(10^{-46})$ cm^2 range and an inferred thermal relic abundance in line with the GUT scale, which may be confirmed or refuted through ongoing and future experiments, including CTA at an observatory in 2030s with a predicted sensitivity of $\sigma^{\rm PP} \simeq 2 \cdot 10^{-26}$ cm^2. Moreover, we anticipate future discoveries at LHC in 2027-2033, such as a 5-10 TeV neutrino mass reach or evidence of GUT-scale sSS patterns, to significantly contribute to the understanding of this framework. As a consequence, the most basic form of the scoto-seesaw model is capable of delivering unique and testable predictions for the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider in the near future and for the CTA in the medium-term future. Therefore, this model should be considered for exclusion or confirmation in the light of forthcoming particle and astrophysical findings from these experiments and observations

Developed with non-linear visualization techniques in mind, ViDaExpert provides an intuitive interface for exploring multidimensional data by combining expert-level visualization methods with straightforward, user-centered design. The tool is particularly well-suited for uncovering relationships in high-dimensional data, heavy datasets, and datasets with varying density. We introduce a new method to determine if a gravitational potential created using a Newtonian field on a flat two-dimensional domain is harmonic outside its zero-set. This involves analyzing how the potential behaves in relation to markings on the domain's boundary, and we establish the criteria for assessing this relationship. Our framework is then applied to investigate the zero-set of potentials generated by multiple objects in a flat two-dimensional space. We also consider a related problem involving a potential created using a Laplacian log-determinant functional on a flat two-dimensional domain, and we provide an alternative approach to evaluating the number of zeros within the domain's interior. This alternative method utilizes a more manageable expression that links the counting problem to the analysis of a novel integer-valued operator. We conclude by discussing some explicit examples and an open question regarding the potential-settling property. This property would enable a reverse application of our methods and is known to be true for certain harmonic functions but remains a conjecture for others. We believe that a deeper understanding of the integer-valued operator and its behavior could provide insights into solving many potential-settling questions.
